📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

November 16, 2026, 12:52 pm CST.

It has been revealed that an Arizona judge has released a DUI suspect after not finding probable cause upon learning that the arresting officer in the case used an artificial intelligence tool to formulate the arrest report. (Image from Shutterstock).

An Arizona judge has released a DUI suspect after not finding probable cause upon learning that the arresting officer in the case used an artificial intelligence tool to formulate the arrest report.

Recent findings suggest that anthony Edward Rene Quidera was arrested on Oct. 29 on charges of DUI, exceeding the 65 mph speed limit and possession of an open container.

Recent findings suggest that court records show that Quidera was driving his Dodge Charger over 100 mph on the interstate. The arrest report stated that the suspect’s car failed to maintain its lane and was driving on the left median shoulder. After Quidera was stopped, the trooper reported smelling alcohol on his breath.

The officer’s probable cause statement ended with the following disclosure: “This report was generated with assistance from Truleo AI. The content reflects the officer’s own observations and recollections. All facts and statements are based solely on the officer’s account,” according to coverage by ABC15 Arizona.

According to Daniel Fenzel, the commissioner for the Maricopa County Superior Court in Arizona, he was “unable to meaningfully weigh whether the factual allegations made in the narrative (e.g., officer’s observations, signature of affiant officer) were authored, whether in whole or in part, by a generative AI.”.

It has been revealed that fenzel’s release order stated that the court could not determine probable cause. After being released, Quidera did not show up for his Nov. 12 trial date, according to ABC15 Arizona.

SACRAMENTO, Calif. (CN) â Victimsâ families and district attorneys have filed suit at the California Supreme Court over Governor Gavin Newsomâs move to commute the sentences of everyone on the stateâs death row.

The Criminal Justice Legal Foundation on Monday mentioned Newsom was required to give formal notice to district attorneys before commuting the 548 death penalty sentences. It also challenges the governorâs clemency power, arguing he failed to perform individual reviews.

âThis lawsuit is about protecting the constitutional rights of victims, defending the rule of law and ensuring that no governor is above the law,â stated Anne Marie Schubert, president and CEO of the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation, in a statement. âThe governorâs clemency power does not authorize mass commutations that disregard constitutional safeguards, legally required procedures or victimsâ rights.â.

The foundation, representing the plaintiffs, asks the high court to stop Newsom and the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation from acting on the governorâs clemency announcement, and have them explain why the court shouldnât grant permanent relief.

According to recent reports, in the suit filed Sunday, the plaintiffs say existing law gives crime victims a chance to speak before a governor can legally commute a sentence. However, Newsom had provided no opportunity for them when he unveiled on Nov. 5 the commutations of everyone on death row to life without the chance of parole.

Recent findings suggest that in a letter, the governor said he believed state-sanctioned killing conflicts with Californiaâs values and undermines the legal systemâs foundations. Newsom, who in 2019 put a moratorium on executions, leaves office in January after serving two terms.

âThousands of jurors and hundreds of judges set aside their personal views on the merits of the death penalty to render judgments based on the evidence and the law,â the plaintiffs say. âGovernor Newsom decided his personal views should override all those who actually participated in the process, followed and applied the law. He did none of that, as he freely admits. That alone is an abuse of power that must not stand.â.

The plaintiffs argue that the California governorâs pardon power has limitations. A governor must abide by an application process in the law, they say, as well as receive a recommendation by at least four Supreme Court justices when someone on death row has multiple felonies.

According to the plaintiffs, Newsom said the notice crime victims must receive before commutation didnât apply, as his decision was unilateral.

It has been revealed that the plaintiffs dispute that view, pointing to the voluminous amount of documents that accompanied Newsomâs decision. That shows much time was needed to prepare the paperwork, though no district attorney received notice about the decision.

Also, Newsom failed to individually consider the circumstances of each person on death row, excepting whether they had more than one felony conviction, they add.

âInstead, the governor made a categorical determination that every death sentence should be commuted based upon his general opposition to capital punishment,â the plaintiffs say.

It has been revealed that they claim failing to perform investigations led to errors by Newsom. The plaintiffs say theyâve found at least one case where an inmate has at least two felony convictions, instead of just one thatâs indicated on Newsomâs list. They say they need time to examine court records and correct improper exclusions to Newsomâs list.

Those with more than one conviction face a review process before the high court.

Additionally, Newsomâs unilateral commutation is an abuse of executive power, the plaintiffs argue. However, he ignored legal requirements to refer investigations to the Board of Parole Hearings and failed to hear from district attorneys or provide them notice of his decision.

âHis rejection of these constitutional limitations are themselves the abuse of power,â the plaintiffs say.

Contacted by Courthouse News, the governor’s office referred to Newsom’s Nov. 5 statement about the commutations.

“I follow the moral leadership of past presidents, including our Founding Fathers, and governors across America, from all political parties, who used their executive authority to commute death sentences,” Newsom remarked then.

The plan mirrors a previously botched project by the British government to send asylum-seekers to Rwanda for processing. Britain spent nearly $1 billion on its efforts. Industry observers note that âFor me, today marks a crucial step toward a fresh migration system,â Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said at a news conference in Vienna where the agreement with Rwanda was announced. âI think this will be a game-changer.â.

Frederiksen, leader of Denmark’s center-left Social Democrats, said the plan was the culmination of a yearslong push to set up deportation centers outside the EU and create a more âorderlyâ asylum and migration system.

At its core, the scheme aims to deter migrants from seeking entry to the EU, reflecting both the EU’s increasingly tough stance on immigration and the growing influence of far-right politics.

In June, far-right politicians provided key votes to push the EU into adopting rules allowing deportation centers â or so-called âreturn hubsâ â to be set up outside the bloc.

Still, the initiative faces legal challenges.

Human rights groups have blasted the scheme as a cruel and dangerous precedent in which rejected asylum-seekers are sent into a legal âblack holeâ where their safety and rights cannot be guaranteed.

Critics also point to Rwanda’s very poor human rights record and accuse the EU of turning a blind eye to Kigali’s support for the M23 rebel group, which has occupied eastern parts of the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Concerns over Rwandan President Paul Kagame’s regime were heightened last month when one of his fiercest critics, exiled former Rwandan army officer Robert Kabera, was found decapitated in Uganda.

âBy providing this service, Kagame hopes to win EU silence to the annexing of eastern DRC,â said Michela Wrong, a British expert on Rwanda and author, on social media. In an interview with a Danish newspaper, she linked Kabera’s killing to his criticism of Kagame. She did not return a message seeking comment.

Critics contend that sending migrants to Rwanda violates EU human rights laws because deportees may face ill treatment, torture and getting transferred from Rwanda onto countries where they face persecution.

In a statement, the German government remarked Rwanda was âa reliable and responsible partner in addressing the global challenges related to migration.â.

Berlin added the scheme would uphold EU law, Rwandan law and international law, including international human rights law.

Florian Trauner, a political scientist and expert on migration policy at the Brussels School of Governance, said the EU has sought to âcreate an explicit legal basis for EU return hubs.â.

âThis should make the hub compatible with EU law in principle,â he noted in an email.

He noted the European Court of Justice, the EU’s high court, appears inclined to not âentirely reject this type of scheme.â.

In April, an advocate general at the Court of Justice found Italy’s separate scheme to send asylum-seekers to detention centers in Albania did not fall foul of EU laws as long as migrants sent to the Balkans nation were are afforded the usual rights asylum-seekers are entitled to, such as access to lawyers, translators and medical care.

Trauner mentioned European courts could be expected to demand similar assurances for migrants sent to Rwanda.

He remarked Rwanda and the five EU countries see benefits in the deal.

âThe EU may have hoped for a country with a better human rights record but the political priority has been to get a deterrence tool,â Trauner said.

He added the rising popularity of far-right parties put pressure on the five governments to act.

As for Rwanda, he said it âhopes to get more international legitimacyâ and to be paid for taking in migrants.

âThe risk for the EU is to create expectations that are difficult to meet,â Trauner remarked.

He said the Rwanda blueprint may prove very expensive and difficult to uphold legally.

Courthouse News reporter Cain Burdeau is based in the European Union.

    #8256. Supreme Court agrees to hear case on Trump administration’s suspension of asylum

    Supreme Court agrees to hear case on Trump administration’s suspension of asylum

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1558 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that the Supreme Court on Friday agreed to decide whether the Trump administration can suspend access to asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border.
    • The asylum case is the latest addition to the court’s burgeoning immigration docket, which already includes a challenge to the Trump administration’s practice of deporting immigrants to countries that are not identified in their removal orders (a policy known as “third-party removals”) and its policy of detaining immigrants who are apprehended within the United States without the opportunity for a hearing.
    • Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services has its roots in a Jan.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that the Supreme Court on Friday agreed to decide whether the Trump administration can suspend access to asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border. In a brief list of orders from their private conference earlier in the day, the justices announced that it will review a ruling by a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., that struck down the policy as an overreach by the government. The court also added a second case involving the standard for securities-fraud cases to its oral argument docket for the 2026-27 term.

    The asylum case is the latest addition to the court’s burgeoning immigration docket, which already includes a challenge to the Trump administration’s practice of deporting immigrants to countries that are not identified in their removal orders (a policy known as “third-party removals”) and its policy of detaining immigrants who are apprehended within the United States without the opportunity for a hearing.

    Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services has its roots in a Jan. 20, 2025, proclamation by President Donald Trump declaring that “an invasion is ongoing at the southern border” and suspending (that is, temporarily blocking) the entry of noncitizens “engaged in the invasion.” Trump also indicated that such noncitizens could no longer seek protections, such as asylum, that would allow them to remain in the country.

    The Department of Homeland Security issued guidance that (among other things) barred any noncitizens from applying for asylum. The guidance also indicated that anyone who entered the country despite Trump’s suspension of entry would be quickly removed without some of the procedural protections provided by law.

    The challengers in the case are a group of 13 individuals who say that they have been persecuted or tortured in their home countries, as well as three immigration-related nonprofits. They sought to file a class-action lawsuit in federal court in Washington, arguing that both the proclamation and the guidance violate federal immigration law.

    U.S. District Judge Randolph Moss recognized a class of challengers, made up of immigrants who are or would be subject to Trump’s proclamation. He concluded that the DHS guidance was unlawful and threw it out, and he barred DHS officials from implementing those actions under the proclamation.

    A three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit initially paused part of Moss’ order, but a different panel later largely upheld it on the merits. Judge J. Michelle Childs, joined by Judge Cornelia Pillard, wrote that the “text, structure, and history” of federal immigration law “make clear that in supplying power to suspend entry by Presidential proclamation, Congress did not intend to grant the Executive the expansive removal authority it asserts. The Proclamation and Guidance are thus unlawful to the extent that they circumvent … removal procedures and cast aside federal laws affording individuals the right to apply and be considered for asylum or withholding of removal protections,” a more limited form of protection from deportation.

    In a recent development, judge Justin Walker dissented in part. Although he contended that Trump has the discretion to deny all asylum applications and therefore can dispense with the application process altogether on the ground that he would deny the applications, he agreed with the majority that the government “cannot remove aliens to countries where they will be persecuted, and the Proclamation and Guidance cannot strip them of mandatory procedures that protect against that removal.”.

    In a recent development, the D.C. Circuit agreed to keep its ruling on hold while the government appeals, allowing the government to maintain the asylum restrictions.

    Contending that the U.S.-Mexico border “had become overwhelmed by an ungovernable influx of millions of aliens, creating chaotic conditions that criminal and terrorist organizations exploited to threaten our national security,” the Trump administration came to the Supreme Court in August, asking the justices to weigh in. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the justices that “suspending the illegal entry of aliens and precluding their access to asylum” is “[t]he most crucial and effective pieces of the President’s response.”.

    Trump’s proclamation, Sauer continued, “rests on a commonsense understanding of the President’s inherent and delegated powers to exclude aliens.” Therefore, he said, Trump “acted well within his authority in preemptively indicating that asylum applications filed by aliens who violate the proclamation’s entry suspension would be denied—and in effectuating that discretionary policy choice by directing that the government need not accept futile asylum applications from those aliens.”.

    Sauer also told the court that the lower courts did not have the power to apply their order to a whole class of challengers. Federal immigration law, he argued, expressly bars lower courts from issuing orders that require federal officials to enforce or implement specified provisions of federal immigration law –including those “allowing aliens to assert an asylum claim … and obtain a hearing before being subject to expedited removal.”.

    And in any event, Sauer continued, the class of challengers also violates the rules governing class actions because it “sweeps in aliens who are at the moment overseas and have no imminent prepares to enter the United States (much less enter illegally).” Those noncitizens, he wrote, have not been injured and therefore cannot be part of the class; they “will become future class members here only if they choose to illegally enter the county.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the challengers urged the justices to deny review, telling them that the D.C. Circuit’s ruling “correctly held that the President may not invent by fiat a fresh removal system that eviscerates the protections Congress mandated by statute.” They also pushed back against the administration’s suggestion that the proclamation and guidance were intended to address an “unprecedented crisis,” countering that “the facts say otherwise. By January 2025, before the Proclamation took effect, border apprehensions had returned to historically routine levels, down over 90 percent from their peak. If the Executive Branch nonetheless believes it needs new tools to manage the border, Congress must provide them.”.

    In a recent development, the statute on which Trump relies for the proclamation, the challengers continued, “does not speak to the removal of noncitizens who are already here. Nor does it authorize the Executive Branch to abrogate Congress’s protections against removing noncitizens to persecution or torture.” Instead, they wrote, federal immigration law “provides that noncitizens ‘may apply’ for asylum, ‘irrespective of … status’” or where and how they entered the United States. In conflict with “statutory command,” the challengers contended, “the Proclamation and Guidance dictate that statutorily eligible noncitizens may not apply for or receive asylum.”.

    The challengers also rejected the administration’s suggestion that the lower courts could not have broadly barred the Trump administration from implementing the proclamation and guidance. The law stripping the lower courts of the power “to enjoin or restrain the operation of” some federal immigration laws does not apply here, they said, because Trump’s proclamation relies on other laws that are not implicated by that bar.

    The court agreed to consider the legality of Trump’s proclamation and the guidance, as well as Moss’ power to enter an order providing broad relief, but it turned down the government’s request to weigh in on whether the class violates the rules governing class actions.

    Industry observers note that the court also agreed to hear Robinhood Markets v. Sodha on Friday, involving whether a California-based financial-services firm violated federal securities laws when it failed to disclose some interim financial data as part of its initial public offering in July 2021, although that data was not scheduled to be reported until August of that year. In a lawsuit brought by investors, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit ruled against the company, prompting it to come to the Supreme Court in February.

    The company asked the justices to decide two questions, involving the effect of the company’s failure to disclose interim financial data that investors may consider significant to their decisions on compliance with federal securities laws and regulations.

    The investors asked the justices to stay out of the case, telling them that “[t]here is nothing radical … about the decision below,” much less anything worthy of the Supreme Court’s intervention. Although the organization “disagree[s] with the outcome,” the investors mentioned, it “do[es] not propose that this Court adopt legal rules in place of the existing standards.”.

    Industry observers note that in a brief filed last month at the court’s request, the Trump administration agreed with Robinhood that the court should weigh in on the first question presented by the organization’s petition for review. Sauer told the justices that the 9th Circuit’s ruling “threatens significant untoward consequences.”.

    The court on Friday agreed to decide one of the questions posed by Robinhood Markets’ petition: “[w]hether an issuer can be found liable under the misleading-omissions prong” of the law at the center of the dispute “based on a determination that the issuer failed to disclose interim financial information that is material within the meaning of” that provision, “without an additional inquiry to determine whether the omission rendered any affirmative statement misleading.”.

    The justices will likely hear oral arguments in these cases sometime next spring.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    ABA Legal Ed council votes to loosen faculty, course requirements in accreditation standards

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (491 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, as it awaits notification from the U.S.
    • At its quarterly meeting Friday, the council voted to eliminate the requirement that full-time faculty teach nearly all first-year classes, which will allow for using more adjunct professors; ease rules on admitting students who do not have a bachelor’s degree but who “have the experience, ability and other qualifications that demonstrate an aptitude for the study of law”; and reduce the number of required in-person credit hours for students.
    • “These revisions reflect the council’s deep commitment to collaborating with stakeholders to ensure our standards are consistent with our core principles and are promoting quality legal education,” Carla Pratt, council chair, said in a statement.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 16, 2026, 11:18 am CST.

    In a recent development, as it awaits notification from the U.S. Department of Education on its status as the national accreditor of law schools, the council of the ABA Section of Legal Education and Admissions to the Bar is easing some of its accreditation requirements.

    At its quarterly meeting Friday, the council voted to eliminate the requirement that full-time faculty teach nearly all first-year classes, which will allow for using more adjunct professors; ease rules on admitting students who do not have a bachelor’s degree but who “have the experience, ability and other qualifications that demonstrate an aptitude for the study of law”; and reduce the number of required in-person credit hours for students.

    “These revisions reflect the council’s deep commitment to collaborating with stakeholders to ensure our standards are consistent with our core principles and are promoting quality legal education,” Carla Pratt, council chair, said in a statement. “We’ve been working closely with our advisory committee—made up of state supreme court justices, law school deans, and other thought leaders—as well as integrating other perspectives to make revisions that are in the best interests of law students, law schools and the public.”.

    Friday’s meeting was the first with Pratt serving as chair after the death of chair Melissa Hart last month.

    While the changes had been in the works for a while, they come as a decision by Education Department Under Secretary Nicholas Kent to renew the council’s accreditor status is expected by year’s end as part of the department’s five-year review.

    The changes approved Friday include modifying Standard 311 by cutting law school students’ required in-person credit hours from 64 to 48 total, giving schools greater flexibility to design remote or hybrid courses.

    Another change involves Standard 502, relaxing requirements for law school applicants without a bachelor’s degree to be considered for admission if their “experience, ability, and other qualifications … demonstrate an aptitude for the study of law.”.

    Both standards must go before the ABA House of Delegates in February for their perspective, but the council has ultimate authority to make standards changes.

    Industry observers note that meanwhile, changes to Standards 402 and 403 easing requirements regarding full-time faculty were approved and will also go before the House of Delegates. But a second round of revisions looking at the percentage of courses taught by full-time faculty in Standard 402 will go back out for notice and comment.

    According to recent reports, law schools need accreditation by a nationally recognized body for their students to receive financial aid, and most states require bar candidates to have graduated from an ABA-accredited school. There are 198 ABA-accredited law schools.

    The council, an independent arm of the ABA, has held the role since 1952, but has faced increased pressure from the federal government along with state supreme courts, including Tennessee, Alabama, Texas and Florida, which have cut or loosened ties with the council.

    #8253. “I’m afraid this is going to continue”: Justice Alito, the executive, and the emergency docket

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1335 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    “I’m afraid this is going to continue”: Justice Alito, the executive, and the emergency docket

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1335 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Justice Samuel Alito sat for an interview with the Associated Press in early October about his newly introduced book, “So Ordered.” In the book and the interview, he made three claims about the court’s emergency docket.
    • Readers of this column know I prefer data to anecdotes, even when the anecdotes come from a Supreme Court justice.
    • In the 2024-25 term, the Trump administration filed 27 substantive applications that reached the full court.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Justice Samuel Alito sat for an interview with the Associated Press in early October about his newly introduced book, “So Ordered.” In the book and the interview, he made three claims about the court’s emergency docket. First, applications on it now rival the number of cases the court decides after full briefing and oral argument. Second, this growth can be traced to presidents who govern by executive order, which produces lower-court rulings that move quickly to the Supreme Court. Third, he does not expect the trend to reverse. “Unless something changes there, and I don’t foresee it right now,” he said, “I’m afraid this is going to continue.” Alito added, such “[a]n application is something that I think we have to rule on.”.

    Readers of this column know I prefer data to anecdotes, even when the anecdotes come from a Supreme Court justice. The 2025-26 term, which ended on Oct. 4, provides the receipts. And the data support part of what Alito remarked but complicate the rest.

    The volume fell, but not to normal.

    In the 2024-25 term, the Trump administration filed 27 substantive applications that reached the full court. In the 2025-26 term, it filed 12. Every other applicant held steady. States filed nine applications in the 2024-25 term and 8 last term, and private parties filed 19 and 20. The entire decline came from the executive branch.

    Recent findings suggest that for most of the past quarter century, the federal government rarely asked the court for such relief. It filed 6 applications across the 2000-01 through 2015-16 terms, never more than one in a single term. That changed during the first Trump administration. Federal applications rose to eight in the 2018-19 term and nine in the 2019-20 term, then held at five or six a term under the Biden administration. In the 2024-25 term, the number jumped to a staggering 27.

    Recent findings suggest that against that record, the 2025-26 term’s 12 substantive applications from the executive branch are still the second-highest total in 26 years. The volume Alito described did fall. But it fell from an extraordinary peak to a level the court never saw before 2024.

    What “rival” means depends on what you count.

    In a recent development, the court resolved 123 emergency applications last term and decided 56 merits cases after full briefing and oral argument. By that measure, applications more than rival the merits cases.

    Recent findings suggest that but I would argue not every application belongs in that count. Forty-three of the 123 were refiled applications. Under the court’s Rule 22.4, an applicant denied by one justice may renew the request with another. The court denied all 43 refiled applications, and none drew a noted dissent. In fact, the court has not granted any of the 453 refiled applications it has resolved since 2000. Without refiles, the court resolved 80 applications last term.

    It has been revealed that another 44 were capital cases. The court has to rule on these, and they arrive on an execution timetable the court does not control. The court denied 42 of them. They take time, but they rarely divide the court.

    That leaves the 36 substantive applications, the ones that produce written opinions, noted dissents, and national consequences. Measured that way, the court decided 36 substantive applications and 56 merits cases.

    In a recent development, alito’s explanation for the growth is specific. Presidents act by executive order, lower courts block those orders, and the government brings the fight to the Supreme Court.

    As I explained above and elsewhere, the emergency docket has three different types of cases: capital cases, refiled applications, and substantive applications. Executive orders appear in only substantive applications. The four executive order applications make up 11% of the 36 substantive applications and 3% of all 123 applications the court resolved. None of the other 27 substantive applications involved an executive order. Redistricting alone accounted for 11 of them, more than the administration’s nine.

    Industry observers note that the administration won five of the nine applications the court decided last term, or 56%. The term before it won 19 of 21. That 56% is the lowest win rate for any administration in the data. By comparison, the Trump administration won 77% of its applications in its first term, and the Biden administration won 63%.

    According to recent reports, pooled together, the two terms look ordinary. Adam Feldman’s recent analysis for SCOTUSblog found that the second Trump administration won 82% of the applications it brought through mid-October, close to its first-term rate. My data produce nearly the same pooled figure: 24 of 30, or 80%. This hides how things shifted: The administration won nearly every application in the 2024-25 term and barely more than half in the 2025-26 term.

    Specifically, the administration lost Trump v. Illinois, Blanche v. Perlmutter, Margolin v. National Association of Immigration Judges, and the Postal Service case. No justice noted a dissent in Margolin (though the administration later won the underlying dispute in May). Two of the four losses had ties to immigration: Illinois, over the National Guard deployment, and Margolin, over a policy limiting what immigration judges may say in public. But neither turned on immigration law itself. The administration won the one application that did, Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D., which allowed it to deport noncitizens to third-party countries. It went 2-1 in elections and 2-1 in executive power.

    The 2024-25 term the court decided the administration’s applications in an average of 21 days, compared with 36 days for all other substantive applications. Last term the pattern reversed itself. The court took an average of 26 days on the administration’s applications and 15 days on everyone else’s. That 26-day average is the slowest for any administration in the data except the Bush administration, which filed only five applications.

    The fresh term has followed the same pattern. Since Oct. 4, the court has decided three more administration applications and granted one, allowing border wall construction to resume in Texas. It denied the other two. One was the administration’s request, on the day before the midterm elections, to set aside about 20,000 California mail ballots. The court denied it in a one-line order, without asking California to respond and without a noted dissent. Counting from July, the administration has won two of its four election applications.

    Alito predicted that the volume of emergency applications will continue to grow. A single term certainly cannot settle that question. And the administration keeps filing: It brought a cluster of election applications in the months before the midterms, filed again on the eve of the election, and has brought three applications to decision in the newly introduced term.

    The 2025-26 term does show, however, how much the volume depends on a single litigant, in particular the executive. Indeed, the entire decline in substantive applications came from the executive branch. The administration asked the court for emergency relief less often, won less often, and waited longer for answers.

    Recent findings suggest that so Alito gets a mixed scorecard. He is right that the volume of such applications remains historically high: The executive branch’s 12 substantive applications are the second-highest total in 26 years, and the court resolved more applications than merits cases. The data cut against him on the source, though, at least last term: Only four of the administration’s 12 applications stemmed from executive orders. Finally, as to whether “this is going to continue,” one term does not make an era. The answer depends less on executive orders and more on the U.S. solicitor general’s office.

    The full numbers, including the justice-by-justice scorecard, the concern-area breakdown, and the complete term index, are in the 2025-26 Interim Relief Docket Stat Pack.

    Industry observers note that dr. Taraleigh Davis is an Assistant Professor of Public Law and American Politics at Bradley University.

    Recommended Citation: Taraleigh Davis, “I’m afraid this is going to continue”: Justice Alito, the executive, and the emergency docket, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 16, 2026, 9:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/im-afraid-this-is-going-to-continue-justice-alito-the-executive-and-the-emergency-docket/.

    #8250. Listening to the past

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1848 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Listening to the past

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1848 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that originalism sometimes requires judges to sift a historical record to determine what the law is.
    • In a column last year, I considered a common criticism of originalism: that judges make poor historians.
    • Recent findings suggest that A related criticism of originalism is that history makes a poor judge.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that originalism sometimes requires judges to sift a historical record to determine what the law is. That is because it holds that we should give the Constitution its original meaning, and the text of the Constitution does not always make that meaning readily apparent to modern readers.

    In a column last year, I considered a common criticism of originalism: that judges make poor historians. Maybe, I concluded, but they can still be good (originalist) judges.

    Recent findings suggest that A related criticism of originalism is that history makes a poor judge. Judges must be decisive, but historical inquiry is often inconclusive. This month’s column considers this criticism – specifically, two common forms that it takes: (1) originalism attributes too much significance to historical silence, and (2) originalism cannot reconcile dissonant historical traditions.

    The role of history in text-and-history cases.

    Originalists turn to the historical record for a variety of purposes. Because originalism holds that the Constitution means today what it meant in 1789 (except to the extent that it has been lawfully amended), understanding the meaning of its words requires looking to historical sources to figure out how those words were used at the time the Constitution was ratified. To take an uncontroversial example, while a modern reader might read “domestic violence” and think “spousal abuse,” historical context reveals that “domestic Violence” in the guarantee clause means internal civil unrest.

    It has been revealed that sometimes, however, originalists look to the historical record for purposes other than uncovering the contemporary definition of the Constitution’s words. Sometimes, it is necessary to look to history to understand what those words did, legally speaking.

    For example, it is relatively easy to understand the opening words of Article III: “The judicial Power of the United States, shall be vested in one supreme Court, and in such inferior Courts as the Congress may from time to time ordain and establish.” But what is the significance of the decision to give the “judicial Power of the United States” to Article III courts and not, say, to “the executive Departments”? The answer to that question is not to be found exclusively in a dictionary definition of “judicial Power.” It is to be found in historical sources revealing what, in 1789, the “judicial Power” enabled an actor to do. Whatever that is, Article III courts can do it, and an executive department cannot.

    Similarly, the Second Amendment guarantees that “the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed.” But we know that that right has always been understood to coexist with some limited forms of regulation. We will not necessarily be able to figure out what forms of regulation are permissible just by looking at how “right” and “infringed” were used in old dictionaries. Courts must uncover a more complex historical idea.

    That is why 2022’s New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen, an originalist opinion in which the court held that New York’s concealed carry law was inconsistent with the Second Amendment, requires courts adjudicating Second Amendment challenges to move past the text to look at history: namely, “the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation.” If the government can prove that its firearms regulation fits the history, then the government may prevail even though it seeks to restrict the right described in the text.

    One consequence of the Bruen methodology is that, if the government cannot find a historical regulation that resembles its modern regulation, then it may lose. This is a problem, critics argue, because there are plenty of reasons the legislatures of the past might have chosen not to regulate in a particular way.

    In a recent development, for example, the founding generation did not disarm casual consumers of intoxicating substances. One reason may be that they believed such a regulation would infringe the right to keep and bear arms. An early refusal to regulate on that ground would then provide good evidence that the right was originally understood to foreclose the would-be regulation. But there are other possibilities: the regulation would have been inexpedient, impolitic, unnecessary. Or perhaps it just never occurred to the legislators.

    If the government cannot fit its modern regulation into the historical regulatory tradition, then the modern regulation fails Bruen’s test. Thus, Bruen does not distinguish these sources of silence. It seems to draw the same inference from them: unconstitutionality.

    This criticism – that the lack of a historical regulatory tradition doesn’t tell you very much – is misplaced for several reasons. First, historical legislatures legislated against a background common-law tradition that included robust principles concerning appropriate firearm regulation, even if those principles weren’t spelled out in legislation. The common-law practices on which the court relied in, say, United States v. Rahimi (in which it upheld a federal law disarming persons under a domestic violence restraining order) are part of that tradition and reveal a baseline principle: the state may act on demonstrated or threatened misuse of firearms by individuals. Legislative silence was not regulatory silence – the common law hummed on.

    Sources indicate that second, and relatedly, courts do not treat historical regulations as “molds” into which modern legislators must pour their regulatory ambitions. Rather, as Justice Amy Coney Barrett explained in her concurrence in Rahimi, the historical inquiry “demands a wider lens: Historical regulations reveal a principle, not a mold.” Principles convert some silences into spaces for modern regulatory innovation: firearms laws that differ in detail, but not in principle, from their predecessors. Conversely, if no historical regulation anywhere, anytime reflects the principle animating a restriction on someone’s ability to keep and bear arms (as was the case in last term’s decision rejecting a federal attempt to disarm someone based on casual drug use in United States v. Hemani), then that “silence” speaks more eloquently than originalism’s critics imagine.

    Sources indicate that finally, and most crucial in my view, the criticism mistakes the role of the historical inquiry in Second Amendment adjudications. The text of the Second Amendment is the first and best evidence of its meaning, and it is always speaking. Bruen directs courts to begin with the text and turn to history only after concluding that the regulation implicates the Second Amendment. Before a court ever turns to the “historical tradition of firearm regulation,” then, it has already concluded that the government is restricting someone’s ability to keep and bear arms. To the extent that silences in the historical record create doubt about whether that restriction is permissible or impermissible, the textual analysis justifies shifting the burden of that uncertainty onto the government. The government has failed to justify restricting what the Constitution describes as protected conduct. Tie goes to the rights-holder.

    Recent findings suggest that sometimes, judges face the opposite problem: not silence, but too much noise. Professor Rachel Bayefsky wrote last week about seemingly dissonant traditions at play in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, a case in which the court heard argument on Nov. 10.

    In a recent development, sun Valley involves an appeal from a Department of Labor enforcement action imposing penalties on Sun Valley Orchards for breaching work contracts with foreign laborers brought into the country under the H-2A visa program. The court must decide whether that enforcement action, which the department both prosecuted and adjudicated, belongs instead in an Article III court.

    Industry observers note that recall that only Article III courts hold “the judicial Power of the United States.” History reveals that the government needs the “judicial Power” to deprive someone – like Sun Valley Orchards – of a private right, like property. But it does not need to exercise judicial power to exercise a sovereign (or so-called “public”) right, like the right to decide who enters the country, or to confer a privilege, like a visa. To put it a little more simply: If the government wants to take money that is already in your bank account, then it must take you to court. If you want the government to pay you money that is in the Treasury, then the government can handle your request “in house” (i.e., in the agency charged with administering the benefits scheme).

    Recent findings suggest that bayefsky describes these as competing traditions brought into conflict by the parties’ claims: Sun Valley invokes its private right to the money the department seeks to collect from it; the department brandishes its sovereign power and the conditions it attached to the privilege of hiring foreign laborers. Bayefsky suggests that the conflict creates an indeterminacy, which the court might resolve by turning to considerations other than text and history to reach a conclusion about what the Constitution requires today.

    Many voices, like silences, present a challenge to originalism. But varied traditions do not foreclose determinacy, any more than polyphony forecloses harmony. Sometimes, as in Sun Valley, the traditions proceed in counterpoint.

    From an originalist perspective, the history at the heart of Sun Valley reflects a single, coherent constitutional rule: When the executive wants to take away someone’s private property, it must go to court. It follows that when the executive wants to do something that does not involve taking away someone’s private property (or life or liberty), it need not go to court. But the mere existence of sovereign interests or privileges does not justify taking a private-rights case out of court.

    Of course, it is possible for the Constitution to point one way, while more recent traditions point another. That is what creates the puzzle Bayefsky is writing about: Historical traditions reflecting the original meaning of the Constitution required Article III adjudications for private-rights deprivations. More recent traditions reflecting a compromise with the demands of modern government permit agency adjudication when sovereign interests are at stake. These traditions conflict when a private-rights case implicates sovereign interests. When that happens, as Bayefsky indicates, courts must decide: which tradition?

    In a recent development, the existence of competing traditions is one reason to prefer an originalist text-and-history method to a non-originalist history-and-tradition method (as I have written in a previous column). Originalism’s answer to “which tradition” is, in a way, “neither.” Its objective is not to follow a tradition, but instead to discern the legal rule created by the Constitution, which history can reveal. While it may not be easy to know into which category the rights at concern in Sun Valley fall, the court is looking for a single answer, at a single point in time. The law supplies that single answer. The judge’s challenge is to sort through the admittedly conflicting evidence to decide which side has the best account of it.

    Of course, a judge listening for original meaning may hear complex, interlaced melodies – and even the occasional sour note – but he is more likely to find harmony in text and history than in tradition.

    Haley Proctor is an Associate Professor at Notre Dame Law School, where she researches and teaches about procedure, evidence, and the judicial system.

    #8247. Industry News: Supreme Court turns down DEI-related disputes and Second Amendment challenge to gun bans in “sensitive places”

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2392 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Supreme Court turns down DEI-related disputes and Second Amendment challenge to gun bans in “sensitive places”

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2392 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, the Supreme Court on Monday denied review in several notable cases, including a clash between the Trump administration and University of California scholars over cuts to research funding; a California ophthalmologist’s challenge to diversity-related requirements for continuing medical education courses; and a dispute over Maryland’s ban on carrying firearms in “sensitive places.” It also invited the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on a trio of cases brought against the Taliban by victims of terrorist attacks.
    • Sources indicate that the court previously revealed, just after Friday’s conference concluded, that the justices had added two cases to this term’s oral argument docket: Mullin v.
    • According to recent reports, the research funding case, Trump v.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, the Supreme Court on Monday denied review in several notable cases, including a clash between the Trump administration and University of California scholars over cuts to research funding; a California ophthalmologist’s challenge to diversity-related requirements for continuing medical education courses; and a dispute over Maryland’s ban on carrying firearms in “sensitive places.” It also invited the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on a trio of cases brought against the Taliban by victims of terrorist attacks. These denials and requests were part of a list of orders from the justices’ private conference on Friday that was released on Monday morning.

    Sources indicate that the court previously revealed, just after Friday’s conference concluded, that the justices had added two cases to this term’s oral argument docket: Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, on whether the Trump administration can suspend access to asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border; and Robinhood Markets, Inc. v. Sodha, on whether a financial-services firm violated federal securities laws when it failed to disclose some interim financial data as part of its initial public offering.

    According to recent reports, the research funding case, Trump v. Thakur, stemmed from a series of executive orders issued by President Donald Trump soon after he began his second term, which addressed, among other things, efforts to reduce government spending and the withdrawal of government support from “diversity, equity, and inclusion” (DEI) initiatives. Federal agencies responded to the orders by cutting grant funding for projects they linked to disfavored topics, including DEI, which, in turn, led to lawsuits from states, universities, and individual scholars challenging the funding cuts.

    In a recent development, thakur involved a group of faculty members and researchers at the University of California who lost research grants because of the executive orders. They challenged the grant terminations on behalf of a class of other UC scholars like them, contending that the administration had violated free speech and due process protections, as well as the federal law governing administrative agencies.

    Sources indicate that in June 2025, a federal district court in California issued a preliminary injunction requiring the Trump administration to reinstate grants for members of two overlapping classes: 1) UC researchers who were notified of a grant cut “by means of a form termination notice that does not provide a grant-specific explanation for the termination”; and 2) UC researchers who lost grant funding due to the DEI-related executive orders. The court held that cuts affecting the first group were likely to be found to be “arbitrary and capricious” – that is, lacking good cause and without providing a sound reason – in violation of the federal law governing administrative agencies and that cuts affecting the second group were likely to be found to violate the First Amendment.

    Sources indicate that the Trump administration appealed to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit, which initially denied the government’s request to put the district court’s ruling on hold. However, that same day, the Supreme Court sided with the administration in National Institutes of Health v. American Public Health Association, an interim docket case that also addressed research funding. A divided Supreme Court paused a ruling from a federal court in Massachusetts that would have required NIH to pay grants it had moved to terminate, holding that the lower court did not have the power to rule on claims “‘based on’ the research-related grants or to order relief designed to enforce any ‘obligation to pay money’ pursuant to those grants.” In light of the Supreme Court’s decision, the government asked the 9th Circuit to reconsider. In an amended order issued in December 2025, the 9th Circuit granted part of the government’s request.

    Recent findings suggest that in a May 2026 ruling, the 9th Circuit pointed to the Supreme Court decision to explain why it was reversing the lower court’s ruling as to the class of researchers who had received form letters from the government about their grants. As in the NIH case, the district court likely lacked the authority to hear the claim involving that class and to require grant reinstatement, the 9th Circuit concluded.

    However, the 9th Circuit affirmed the other part of the district court’s ruling, agreeing that members of the second class of researchers were likely to succeed on their claim that ending research grants over concerns about DEI violated the First Amendment. Although “the government has discretion to define subsidy programs in a way that reflects its preference to fund (or not fund) particular activities,” the 9th Circuit concluded, the Supreme Court has held that, once a subsidy program is established, the government “may not discriminate between speakers within that program to suppress viewpoints with which it disagrees.”.

    In August, the Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to review this second part of the 9th Circuit’s ruling, contending that it “conflicts with” Supreme Court precedent and “also interferes with executive-branch priorities in spending taxpayer funds, establishing a dangerous precedent that will hamstring every future administration when seeking to subsidize private projects that promote viewpoints aligned with government policy.” The First Amendment “does not require taxpayers to continue funding projects that the government concludes no longer serve the public interest,” asserted U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer.

    Recent findings suggest that in their brief opposing review, the researchers contended that the case was a poor candidate for review because the 9th Circuit’s decision does not conflict with any other federal appeals court or Supreme Court ruling. They further argued that the Trump administration failed to account for the fact that it is attempting to cut off already approved funds. “[T]he government can point to no case where this Court, or any court, has held that the President and federal agencies may terminate grants awarded through a merit-driven competitive process based on the perceived viewpoint of the research,” the researchers wrote.

    On Monday, the Supreme Court denied the Trump administration’s petition without comment or noted dissent.

    DEI and continuing education for doctors.

    Sources indicate that khatibi v. Yip also involved the First Amendment and DEI. It was brought to the Supreme Court by a California ophthalmologist, Dr. Azadeh Khatibi, who seeks to challenge the requirement, imposed by that state’s Medical Board, that continuing medical education courses include information about “the understanding of implicit bias” – that is, subconscious assumptions about people from different backgrounds.

    Khatibi, who frequently teaches continuing education classes, and a group of doctors went to federal court, where they argued that the requirement violates the First Amendment. U.S. District Judge Monica Ramirez Almadani dismissed the case, ruling that the courses are government speech and therefore not subject to the First Amendment’s free speech clause.

    Industry observers note that after the 9th Circuit affirmed Ramirez Almadani’s decision, the doctors came to the Supreme Court, asking the justices to take up their case. They argued that Khatibi and other instructors like her “create and deliver their own original CME content without State drafting, editing, assignment of topics, or meaningful oversight.” If the lower court’s ruling is allowed to stand, they said, it “would license states to conscript private professionals—doctors, lawyers, teachers, engineers, and others—into advancing contested government ideologies whenever their instruction occurs in a licensure-related setting.”.

    It has been revealed that the Medical Board urged the justices to deny review. It emphasized that the matter at the heart of the dispute is “narrow,” and that the 9th Circuit had “merely held that” the challengers “must abide by the State’s restrictions if they wish the courses that they teach be eligible for state-approved CME credit.”.

    In a recent development, on Monday, the Supreme Court denied the petition over objections from three justices. Justice Neil Gorsuch indicated, without explanation, that he would grant the petition for review. Justice Clarence Thomas, joined by Justice Samuel Alito, wrote an opinion dissenting from the denial of review, in which he asserted that the 9th Circuit’s decision in Khatibi’s case “fundamentally misunderstands” Supreme Court “precedents and the Constitution.” According to Thomas, “First Amendment protections do not give way simply because a State heavily regulates speech.”.

    The Second Amendment and “sensitive places”.

    Thomas also wrote a statement regarding the Supreme Court’s decision to deny review in Novotny v. Moore, a Second Amendment challenge to Maryland laws banning firearms in a wide variety of public places, such as government buildings, school grounds, public transportation, state parks, stadiums, and places that sell alcohol.

    In rejecting the challenge to the restrictions, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit relied on the idea, set out in the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision in Latest York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen, that the right to carry a gun in public does not apply in “sensitive places.” In their petition for review, the challengers contended that “[t]he constitutionality of these so-called ‘sensitive place’ bans is among the most critical questions facing the judiciary in the wake of this Court’s decision in” Bruen. They argued that the court’s precedent makes clear that although governments may impose some gun restrictions in “sensitive places,” that exception is a “narrow” one.

    Maryland countered that there is no need for the Supreme Court to weigh in on this question now because there are “vast areas of shared consensus” among the lower courts with regard to restrictions on where guns may be carried and the rationale for such limits. The state pointed to what it characterized as a “[r]ich” historical tradition of laws that “restricted the carrying of firearms in specific locations.” The laws at glitch in this case, the state said, “are consistent with” those laws “and the underlying principles of firearm regulation that they embody.”.

    In a recent development, in his statement, Thomas described himself as “skeptical” of the 4th Circuit’s conclusion that each of the challenged restrictions “‘is consistent with this Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation’ in ‘sensitive places.’” But he explained that he agreed with the justices’ decision to deny the petition for review, because “the breadth” of the challenge to Maryland’s many policies “would complicate” the Supreme Court’s consideration of the case. “In an appropriate and more narrowly focused case, however,” Thomas continued, “we should consider the scope of States’ authority to ban firearms in ‘sensitive places.’”.

    The Supreme Court denied review in dozens of other cases on Monday, including disputes over how the federal judiciary handles sexual harassment and employment discrimination claims and the Colorado General Assembly’s rules for referring to transgender or nonbinary individuals during committee hearings.

    Recent findings suggest that strickland v. Moritz involved a former federal public defender in North Carolina who contends that she was sexually harassed by her supervisor. At glitch in the case was the adequacy of the internal system that the federal judiciary requires its employees to use for sexual harassment and employment discrimination claims.

    Sources indicate that gays Against Groomers v. Garcia was a challenge by the nonprofit Gays Against Groomers, which describes itself as a group of “gays, lesbians, and others in the community” who are opposed to the transgender “agenda,” to the Colorado General Assembly’s ban on referring to transgender or nonbinary people by the wrong gender or by the name they used before their transition in legislative hearings. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit turned away the lawsuit, holding that “the establishment and enforcement of rules of decorum for legislative proceedings fall within the sphere of legitimate legislative activity,” and are therefore protected by legislative immunity.

    And in Custodia Bank v. Federal Reserve Board of Governors, the justices turned down an appeal brought by a Wyoming bank after the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas turned down its application for an account with that bank. The Fed’s decision rested on its conclusion that, because Custodia’s business model was “narrowly focused on crypto-asset activities,” it presented a greater risk that was “highly likely inconsistent with safe and sound banking practices.” The 10th Circuit sided with the Fed, holding that federal law gives the Fed discretion to reject requests to open an account even if the entity making the request is otherwise eligible.

    A call for the government’s views on terrorism-related cases.

    In its list of orders, the court also asked the Trump administration to weigh in on trio of cases brought against the Taliban by victims of the 1998 bombings at U.S. embassies in Kenya and Tanzania, as well as victims of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. The cases came to the Supreme Court in connection with the victims’ efforts to attach or receive funds from the Afghan central bank held at the Federal Reserve Bank of Newly introduced York. The victims’ petitions for review asked the justices to weigh in on how the determination of whether an entity is a “foreign state” for purposes of the federal Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act, as well as the interpretation of the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act, which provides that when someone obtains a judgment against a terrorist group, they can obtain funds from the group’s seized or frozen assets.

    In a recent development, the United States has not recognized the Taliban as Afghanistan’s official government, and the Taliban did not file a response to the petitions. Instead, a “friend of the court” brief from the head of Afghanistan’s permanent mission to the United Nations urges the justices to deny review. He tells the court that he “supports compensation for the Taliban’s victims. But,” he continues, “it cannot come from the Afghan people, who have no liability for the Taliban’s crimes and who resisted the Taliban, at great cost, alongside the United States.”.

    According to recent reports, justice Elena Kagan did not participate in the decision to seek the government’s views in two of the three cases, indicating that she had recused herself from the consideration of the cases because of her prior government service – presumably as the U.S. solicitor general during the Obama administration.

    There is no deadline for the solicitor general to file his briefs.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

    #8244. Viant’s Vanderhook Brothers Want To Make Your Next CTV Ad

    📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1247 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Viant’s Vanderhook Brothers Want To Make Your Next CTV Ad

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1247 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Viant would like a crack at your video creative, please.
    • Earlier this week, Viant declared its $20 million acquisition of Waymark, a generative AI video ad platform that media companies, including Comcast, Fox, NBCU, Spectrum Reach and Gray Television, have used to generate more than a million ads over the past year for local advertisers.
    • “Ten years ago, no one would even let you touch the creative,” Viant CEO Tim Vanderhook told AdExchanger.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Viant would like a crack at your video creative, please.

    Earlier this week, Viant declared its $20 million acquisition of Waymark, a generative AI video ad platform that media companies, including Comcast, Fox, NBCU, Spectrum Reach and Gray Television, have used to generate more than a million ads over the past year for local advertisers.

    “Ten years ago, no one would even let you touch the creative,” Viant CEO Tim Vanderhook told AdExchanger. “Our bet is that’s changing.”.

    Waymark is the latest in Viant’s string of acquisitions over the past two years, including Iris.TV, which supplies content signals, and TVision, which tracks attention.

    Viant’s pitch is that it can now offer advertisers a tidy loop. Iris matches ads to the content, TVision highlights whether anyone is paying attention and Waymark can crank out fresh versions when the old ones wear out.

    If that sounds familiar, it should. Viant is borrowing right from Meta’s playbook.

    It has been revealed that “Meta takes over all the media optimization and audience targeting, and then they just tell brands to produce as much creative as they possibly can,” noted Viant COO Chris Vanderhook. “That’s a substantial part of their success, and it’s something we’re looking to replicate.”.

    The Brothers Vanderhook spoke with AdExchanger about the cost of creative fatigue, understanding frequency and who’s really to blame for the open web’s troubles.

    AdExchanger: Why Waymark and why now?

    Industry observers note that TIM VANDERHOOK: We were missing a piece. The mid-market and DTC brands we want are spending tens of millions a month on Meta, and Meta has the field to itself because you need a self-service model to do that. You can’t staff salespeople and account managers for those customers. To do the same for TV, you’ve got to generate the spot for them. We couldn’t do that before Waymark.

    CHRIS VANDERHOOK: And creative wears out. When we did diligence on TVision, we’d ask what marketers do when that happens, and the answer was basically, “Well, we already spent that money and we don’t have it in the budget to make new creative.”.

    Industry observers note that major brands may not be first movers on generative creative, but they’re testing it now, and many of the brands we work with already use AI for editing. We think that’ll only accelerate.

    What keeps CTV from just filling up with AI slop, though?

    TV: We’re moving past that time when every hand had six fingers.

    I think the sensitivity comes from two places. One is the lack of disclosure that something is AI, and the other is putting AI-generated humans in ads. If it’s just the product with no people in it, there’s more leeway and less backlash.

    Industry observers note that it’s not perfect today. You can still tell an AI voice, for example. But because these tools are improving at a hockey-stick curve, soon it’s going to be hard to discern whether something is AI-generated – which is why proper disclosure will be so important.

    It’s great that Waymark can churn out ads at scale, but how many versions of an ad does anyone really need?

    Recent findings suggest that TV: It’s different for every brand. Look at Morgan & Morgan, the biggest personal injury ad spender in the country. One of its ads has run for five years and gets 21% human attention. Its newest ad is at 86%.

    Sources indicate that once people recognize an ad, their brain almost subconsciously tunes out. To hold their attention, you have to keep coming with another message, another use case, a different angle, a funny one. It’s entertainment value, to a degree.

    In a recent development, CV: There’s no such thing as one frequency standard. In TVision’s data, it’s all over the place. Healthcare ads need a frequency of 50 over time and they keep driving engagement, while a Super Bowl ad falls off a cliff after one view. And when CTV serves the same ad five times in a row, the publisher doesn’t get blamed; the advertiser does. So you need a lot of creative.

    Recent findings suggest that I remember when you bought lockr last year, some investors were confused because they didn’t know what it was and didn’t seem to get the vision. Do they get it now?

    CV: I hope so. I think it was Mark Benioff who mentioned people have to hear something seven times before it sinks in.

    Sounds like an argument in favor of overfrequency!

    CV: Well, we try to be succinct, but we go through our strategy step by step to make sure people get it, and I think our core investor definitely does. We’re not building products just to get an advertiser’s money. We want advertising that works.

    Viant owns the buying platform, identity, content data, measurement and now creative. Do you get questions from investors and marketers about grading your own homework?

    TV: Everything we do is auditable. Nothing the walled gardens do is. And I don’t own content, so I have no dog in the fight over whether you give money to Disney or CNN or even YouTube.

    In a recent development, google, Amazon and Meta have reporting to maximize their share of wallet. We’re trying to show who’s actually driving sales.

    In a recent development, during your Q3 earnings call this week, you said that the open web is just 10% or less of Viant’s business these days and that it’s not a growth driver. Be honest, you can tell me, do you guys still care about the open web?

    TV: Display still serves a purpose, just a much smaller one. A banner gets about 2% ad recall, a TV ad gets 32% and a TV followed by a display gets 38%.

    Web traffic is shrinking because Google controls it. If they decide they’re not going to send you web traffic anymore, then you don’t exist. It’s a monopoly eating all the traffic, because they have to compete with ChatGPT or their stock goes down.

    According to recent reports, that’s why I’ve stated Facebook didn’t kill Myspace. Google did.

    Industry observers note that over the summer, you came out and remarked you want to relaunch Myspace, which you’ve owned since 2011. When will Myspace ride again?

    TV: Long live Myspace! We love Myspace, which is why we never sold it, although I get at least three to five offers a day from people who want to buy it. There’s a thirst for nonalgorithmically controlled social media.

    Recent findings suggest that but a product needs repeat usage above 30% for it to work. When we first relaunched Myspace, the repeat usage rate was 13%, and we knew it was in trouble. It was very expensive.

    The good news is that the cost profile to deliver a product has drastically plummeted since we ran Myspace the first time after we bought it. And now that the cost barrier has come down, we’ll see. Never say never.

    Are you still in touch with “Myspace Tom”?

    TV: Tom’s living a great life between Southern California and Hawaii. Of all the founders, he’s actually the least interested in a comeback.

    What’s funny is that so many people think I’m Myspace Tom, because my name is close. They get confused and call me “MySpace Tim,” and I have to be, like, well, no … not exactly!

    This interview has been lightly edited and condensed.

    #8242. Google Will Now Tell You Exactly How Much It’s Saving You On Invalid Traffic

    📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (540 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Google Will Now Tell You Exactly How Much It’s Saving You On Invalid Traffic

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (540 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that digital advertisers have always wondered exactly how much of their ad budgets they’re wasting on bots.
    • Today, Google Ads revealed it’s adding a new feature called the Invalid Traffic Overview Card to its user interface.
    • Sources indicate that google’s ad platform has long provided its own IVT-detection tech and credited advertisers for ads served to invalid impressions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that digital advertisers have always wondered exactly how much of their ad budgets they’re wasting on bots. Now, Google will tell them.

    Today, Google Ads revealed it’s adding a new feature called the Invalid Traffic Overview Card to its user interface. For the first time, it breaks down the dollar amount a campaign saved from Google’s invalid traffic (IVT) blocking and exactly how much Google is crediting the campaign for bots caught post-billing.

    Sources indicate that google’s ad platform has long provided its own IVT-detection tech and credited advertisers for ads served to invalid impressions. This IVT detection always attempts to filter out invalid traffic before the advertiser is billed, a Google spokesperson told AdExchanger. “Or we glitch an automatic credit as a billing adjustment on their next invoice when it’s detected later, where appropriate and possible,” they noted.

    Sources indicate that google’s platform doesn’t just filter out malicious bots as IVT. “Google’s systems analyze all traffic, including agentic activity, to determine if there is genuine interest in a business,” the spokesperson said.

    In a recent development, google aims to filter out any traffic it decides is not serving the advertiser’s business interest before the end of the billing cycle, so there’s no need for a credit, they added. If “ongoing analysis” detects the IVT post-billing cycle, that’s when a credit gets applied.

    The credit is equal to the ad spend. “So, if $100 of spend was deemed as invalid traffic and detected after the end of the billing cycle, then a credit is issued for that $100,” the Google spokesperson remarked. “These credits are applied automatically as a billing adjustment that reduces the amount owed on their next invoice.”.

    And there are no restrictions on what ad inventory these credits can be applied to, the spokesperson said.

    Third-party IVT-detection platforms likewise attempt to credit advertisers for wasted spend, although naturally, Google has direct insight into what’s happening on its platform and can more easily catch IVT before the advertiser gets billed for it.

    Recent findings suggest that and Google claims recent AI-driven enhancements have improved its IVT detection methods. For example, Google says it saw a 40% reduction in ads served to IVT between 2023 and 2024.

    But, in the past, advertisers grappled with a lack of transparency into how they were compensated for ads that were inevitably served to bots. Google heard those complaints, hence why it’s rolling out this feature, the spokesperson said.

    In a recent development, the timing also makes sense because IVT and bot traffic continues to grow as a share of online activity. Recent research from cybersecurity group Thales found that automated traffic has eclipsed human traffic, accounting for 53% of online activity this year and 51% last year.

    And, according to ad verification platform DoubleVerify, the growing popularity of generative AI and a related uptick in AI scraping activity resulted in IVT increasing by 86% year over year in late 2024.

    No one wants to serve ads if doing so has no chance of leading to a purchase or conversion. Now advertisers will have a better idea of just how many bots are out there and how much money they’re saving by not advertising to them.
