    #8239. Latest Update: The Many Ways AI Can Influence A Purchase; ‘Premium’ TV Is So Fetch

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (847 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: The Many Ways AI Can Influence A Purchase; ‘Premium’ TV Is So Fetch

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (847 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It’s early days for agentic search marketing, and the industry hasn’t figured out how to attribute purchases to AI agents.
    • Right now, more than 90% of AI-driven sales are miscredited as branded search, direct traffic or retail media, according to Similarweb.
    • The IAB has proposed a solution: The AI-Era Attribution Blueprint.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It’s early days for agentic search marketing, and the industry hasn’t figured out how to attribute purchases to AI agents.

    Right now, more than 90% of AI-driven sales are miscredited as branded search, direct traffic or retail media, according to Similarweb.

    The IAB has proposed a solution: The AI-Era Attribution Blueprint. It establishes three different types of AI-attributable conversion: human-owned, AI-assisted or AI-executed.

    A human-owned conversion is when AI didn’t substantively create the purchase intent, influence the product decision or carry out the purchase; however, an AI assistant may still have been involved in the decision-making process.

    In a recent development, AI-assisted conversions involve the AI narrowing down and suggesting options. The IAB proposes two sub-types: “AI-influenced” conversions in which the AI “shapes intent” but a human makes the final choice, and “AI-recommended” conversions in which the AI “shapes the choice itself.”.

    And AI-executed conversions involve a human giving an agent permission to purchase an item. There are two sub-types of AI-executed conversions, too: one in which the human has told the AI specifically what to buy and one in which the AI makes the selection.

    If all that sounds a bit ambiguous and not exactly suited to how programmatic measurement works, well, you’re right.

    But the IAB’s aim at this stage is just to describe how these AI experiences play out in practice, stated Caroline Giegerich, IAB’s VP of AI, during a webinar on agentic advertising on Monday.

    “We define this based on what’s actually happening,” she said, “not what we can measure, per se, today.”.

    Speaking of the IAB, the organization hosted its “I Want My CTV” event in New York City yesterday.

    Among the topics discussed: What’s the deal with “premium” TV, anyway? Does that term even mean anything anymore?

    It has been revealed that “Premium” could mean any professionally produced content with engaged audiences, said FreeWheel product chief David Dworin during the opening panel at the event. But, he added, the “premium” classification is ultimately less important than finding content – or, more accurately, audiences – that fulfill the buyer’s performance goals.

    Sources indicate that not that “performance” doesn’t come with its own baggage as a streaming TV ad term these days. But, as Roku Product Innovation Leader Curt Larson put it, every marketer is a performance marketer, even those who focus on TV.

    “You’re not spending money for the sake of spending money,” noted Larson. “You’re spending money to create some sort of outcome. And when that outcome is far in the future or very difficult to measure, you call yourself a brand marketer.”.

    In practice, however, media buyers still need to balance directly attributable performance with things like scale and cost, which also impacts what kind of premium inventory is feasible for them to buy.

    In a recent development, “You need premium, first-impression, low-session, very visible placements,” said PMG Head of Video Mike Treon. “But you also need that efficiency to really balance it.”.

    A sweeping new set of Claude usage policies went into effect on Friday.

    Anthropic first announced the changes a month ago, but it’s worth calling out a few updates.

    Sources indicate that one section forbids people being “abusive or cruel toward our models,” a requirement that was widely panned online. So if you’re going to deride some stupid chatbot, save it for Alexa. And so help you if Claude catches you foul-mouthing its predecessor Clippy (just kidding).

    Protecting chatbots’ feelings aside, other parts of the upcoming usage policy may make actual differences.

    Anthropic now promises to remove state or commercial media outlets that use Claude to fabricate social accounts and news sites or to run other influence operations.

    It has been revealed that using Claude to amplify a message while obscuring the person or organization behind that message is also verboten. Misrepresenting sponsored content as organic is another no-no, as is using Claude to game AI search engines in general.

    Sources indicate that the main focus of the fresh policies is to crack down on political manipulation. Although Anthropic could do Google a major solid, too, if it strikes at the source of the AI slop news and content sites plaguing Google’s search response pages.

    Sources indicate that google is testing moving citations to the very bottom of AI Overviews, which should further reduce website referral traffic. [Search Engine Roundtable].

    According to recent reports, the candy brand Mars has a conundrum: What happens to cash register impulse buys when AI agents do the grocery shopping? [Digiday].

    AI platforms like OpenAI and Anthropic have significant marketing budgets and want to sponsor podcasts. The problem is that listeners tend to revolt when they hear ads from these companies. [Bloomberg].

    Recent findings suggest that after losing “hundreds and hundreds of millions of dollars” over the past few years, The Washington Post’s executive editor Matt Murray notes the paper is on the cusp of breaking even next year. [Adweek].

    Recent findings suggest that jensen Huang confirms his resignation as Nvidia CEO. Colette Kress, the company’s CFO, will serve as interim CEO until Huang’s successor is appointed. [WSJ].

    What does an end-to-end programmatic marketing platform look like these days?

    If you’re Amazon, Google, Meta or (most recently) Viant, your buying platform includes an AI-assisted creative generator.

    In a recent development, viant bought Waymark this week. The deal will allow its marketer clients, especially small and midsize businesses (SMBs), make CTV ads that are better, cheaper and regularly refreshed.

    On today’s podcast, we discuss why time-strapped SMB marketers, who often lag enterprise marketers in tech adoption, have bucked the trend and become early adopters of AI. Business flyers, for example, are increasingly made by AI and promoted on Meta. One can only imagine what happens when SMBs get a hold of Waymark’s tech to generate the mattress warehouse and regional car ads of the future. We’re joking, but also not joking.

    It has been revealed that then, we dissect The Trade Desk’s most recent earnings. Investors rewarded TTD with a 20% rise in stock price for having (almost) stabilizing revenue, which declined just $3 million to $736 million year over year. The Trade Desk touted that its strength in attracting political advertising and healthcare advertising, though it’s notable that the DSP’s rivals don’t play deeply in those highly regulated verticals. Amazon outright bans political advertising (though perhaps because Amazon operates a pharmacy, it’s open to healthcare and pharma ads, albeit with standard caveats), while Google tightly restricts both political and healthcare advertising.

    Industry observers note that as part of its turnaround, it’s possible The Trade Desk may buy another company, which it’s done only sparingly during its run as a DSP (Sincera being a notable exception). CEO Jeff Green signaled his openness to buying a company on the Q3 earnings call. Who knows what startups or established companies might call TTD in response.

    CTV Has Trust Issues

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (788 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Around four months ago, Serge Matta, president of global ad sales at LG Ad Solutions, had a meeting with a large QSR advertiser, and he offered the CMO a guarantee.
    • “We remarked, ‘You only pay us based on incremental visits to your store as defined and measured by your independent third-party measurement provider,’” Matta shared during a session at LUMA’s Digital Media Summit earlier this week, in what felt a little like group therapy for CTV ad tech platforms.
    • The QSR advertiser wasn’t convinced.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Around four months ago, Serge Matta, president of global ad sales at LG Ad Solutions, had a meeting with a large QSR advertiser, and he offered the CMO a guarantee.

    “We remarked, ‘You only pay us based on incremental visits to your store as defined and measured by your independent third-party measurement provider,’” Matta shared during a session at LUMA’s Digital Media Summit earlier this week, in what felt a little like group therapy for CTV ad tech platforms.

    Sounds like a slam dunk, right?

    Not so much. The QSR advertiser wasn’t convinced. “Well, how do I know I can trust them?” he asked.

    “They’re your measurement partner!” Matta recalled thinking, still incredulous in his retelling.

    “That’s when I gave up,” he noted.

    It has been revealed that matta’s tale highlights a frustration that plenty of CTV sellers share. They’ve spent years positioning connected TV as a vehicle for driving outcomes, not just reach and frequency – but getting advertisers to believe it is another matter.

    It has been revealed that “We’re not there yet,” Matta stated. “The promise is there, we’re pitching it, we have it, but we need advertisers to come on board.”.

    Recent findings suggest that ad industry vet – and self-described “recovering marketer” – Lou Paskalis piped up from the audience to venture a theory. It’s partially a perception thing.

    Although there’s been an “inexorable pull down the funnel” toward performance, he stated, marketers still tend to see TV as upper-funnel “hero media,” he said.

    Sources indicate that advertisers also often don’t have the right creative for CTV, and making the creative is too expensive. “There are legacy barriers to taking full advantage,” Paskalis said, “and [CTV is] just not seen as being as performative as programmatic.”.

    But whatever it is that’s holding buyers back, it’s not a lack of measurement options.

    Philip Inghelbrecht, CEO and co-founder of CTV ad platform Tatari, said that around 10 years ago when he started the tech giant, people would look at him cross-eyed when he tried to talk about incrementality.

    But today, there are lots of different independent third-party measurement companies that offer incrementality through a variety of models. It’s a good thing, Inghelbrecht remarked.

    In a recent development, yet, be that as it may, even the offer of a guarantee backed by independent measurement couldn’t close the deal for Matta. And sometimes the skepticism is warranted. There’s no denying that attribution is kind of a mess.

    Every channel, from display to social, tries to take credit for the same conversion, said Scott Young, co-founder and chief product officer of streaming ad insertion platform Transmit.Live.

    To be fair, CTV is no different in that regard, although it does bring something to the table that other channels don’t.

    “You’re getting a higher rate of attention,” Young said. “Yes, you might be paying more for it, but you need exposure and attention in order to actually convert.”.

    But it’s also worth pointing out that this whole debate can sound rather academic to the people who control the budgets, Vinny Rinaldi, VP of client strategy and growth at The Trade Desk, reminded the room.

    Sources indicate that “Not many brands think about all the things that we talk about on a daily basis,” Rinaldi noted, and he knows of what he speaks. Before joining TTD over the summer, Rinaldi spent most of his career on the brand and agency side, including multiple long stints at Hershey’s in media, marketing and strategy roles.

    It has been revealed that marketers care about things like timing, seasonality and sales, not the ad tech plumbing underneath. And that, he argued, is why it makes sense for the DSP, not the publisher, to have the final say on when and where ads run across CTV and everywhere else.

    In a recent development, at Hershey’s, for example, October was like its Super Bowl, but most candy sales wouldn’t happen until the last three or four days of the month in the countdown to Halloween. When he’d buy direct from publishers, however, most of the impressions would run in the first week of October, well before shoppers were thinking about Halloween candy, because the publishers were focused on monetizing their own inventory, not his business problems.

    There would only be a trickle of impressions remaining by the end of the month.

    If pressed, Rinaldi said, “[the publishers] would be like, ‘Well, we delivered in full, what do you mean?”.

    “But I wanted 95% of my spend to be the last week of October,” he mentioned, “because it would have driven a lot more revenue for my company, not somebody else’s.”.

    Earning trust, it turns out, takes more than just a third-party measurement partner.

    #8233. Liftoff Sees Substantial Wins Ahead For Mobile As AI Pushes Budgets Into Apps

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1077 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Liftoff Sees Substantial Wins Ahead For Mobile As AI Pushes Budgets Into Apps

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1077 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The mobile growth marketing platform reported its second-ever quarterly earnings on Thursday after the market closed.
    • Sources indicate that liftoff earned $237.5 million in Q3 2026, up from $179.5 million during the same period last year.
    • Liftoff is pitching itself to Wall Street as riding two tailwinds.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The mobile growth marketing platform reported its second-ever quarterly earnings on Thursday after the market closed. Shares were up by almost 25% overnight after the firm exceeded its revenue target and projected an optimistic profit margin outlook moving forward.

    Sources indicate that liftoff earned $237.5 million in Q3 2026, up from $179.5 million during the same period last year. And Liftoff delivered what investors really like to see: It earned $86.7 million in profit in the quarter, after taking a $5.7 million loss in Q3 a year ago.

    Liftoff is pitching itself to Wall Street as riding two tailwinds.

    There’s the overall growth of the mobile economy, to which the tech giant’s growth is pegged; that growth is being boosted by an influx of AI-generated apps.

    And, secondly, there are the outsized revenue gains Liftoff earns through AI advancement compared to the relatively low investment the company must shell out for AI and data infrastructure.

    LLMs are great at coding apps and are thus “lowering the barrier” for companies or individuals to churn out a serviceable app, Liftoff CEO Jeremy Bondy told investors. “In the first half of this year alone, new apps released in the Apple App Store doubled versus the prior year to roughly 560,000.”.

    Each of these upcoming apps has its own demand for new owners. “For Liftoff, that means more demand for user acquisition,” Bondy stated.

    AI products are also separately “changing where search and discovery starts” for consumers, he noted.

    For one thing, that means “answering more questions without sending people to a website,” Bondy said. And that latest dynamic – where the open web is no longer a reliable traffic and user acquisition vehicle – incentivizes businesses to invest more into their own apps, where they still can “build direct relationships with their customers,” he added.

    AI search isn’t the only thing putting pressure on the open web when it comes to user acquisition. Apple’s iOS 27 machinations are also a drag on cross-site user tracking.

    AppLovin, which reported earnings a week ago, said that Apple’s obscure initiative to stamp out web tracking for all iOS devices will shift marketing budgets from the mobile web to mobile apps.

    Recent findings suggest that and Bondy added some color, arguing that the mobile app advertising market is “drastically under-monetized” right now at about seven cents per hour, in terms of average earnings per attention time. That’s less than a sixth of what TV earns. Which means plenty of room for growth.

    Speaking of growth opportunities, there is also the fact that mobile marketing gains have, to date, mostly accrued to mobile gaming apps, Bondy said.

    Sources indicate that gaming is a category dominated by AppLovin, which is about 40x times bigger than Liftoff, in terms of the market cap. But more than half of Liftoff’s business is outside gaming, according to Bondy.

    Gaming apps are a valuable source of data, though, in regard to whether someone will actually fork over money when they’re using an app (rather than just being blasted by ads without making a purchase).

    In a recent development, “Someone who spends money in a game is also a potential high-value customer for a retailer, a social media app or a streaming service,” he remarked. And those are the categories in which Liftoff is positioned to grow, he said, as AppLovin has in the gaming space.

    However, those nongaming apps are more prone to seasonal fluctuations than gaming apps. Which can be a good or bad thing, depending on how revenue is currently ebbing and flowing.

    In a recent development, for instance, Liftoff rode the momentum from the FIFA World Cup and is seeing a similar surge for the NFL season, as advertisers are investing more in live sports. But it’s like surfing waves as they come, rather than riding a predictable cycle of consumer engagement ups and downs.

    But Bondy noted that Liftoff has been able to convert periodic or event-based customers (like a marketer investing in promoting their app around the World Cup) into steadier, higher-spending accounts.

    Liftoff had 396 customers who spent more than $100,000 in the past 12 months, Bondy stated. That’s up from 362 customers at the same time last year.

    Another key factor from the investor perspective is that Liftoff benefits from the AI revolution without having to financially support it.

    It has been revealed that bondy noted Liftoff has been able to greatly refine its ad targeting and personalization on the back of AI advances. The models are better at identifying a big spender from a retailer app, which makes that user a more valuable target in a gaming app, for example.

    It has been revealed that the models also now have greater longitudinal data, so they’re better at understanding long-term trends and how ROI develops over a year or more. However, the campaign returns from the week immediately after the budgets are spent are still the most important data for the model’s decision-making, Bondy remarked.

    Meanwhile, he added, Liftoff’s profit margin expansion in the past year was propelled by the tech giant’s relatively low cost of infrastructure and AI services. The company’s entire capital expenditures (which encompass AI and data infrastructure costs) for Q3 was $14 million, or approximately 6% of revenue.

    In contrast, some companies that Liftoff competes with in mobile performance marketing (namely, Meta and Google) have committed hundreds of billions of dollars to their capex expenses.

    “As a reminder, our business is capital light,” Bondy told investors yesterday – and he periodically reminded them of this fact throughout the call.

    According to recent reports, bondy also reminded investors that Liftoff will be discontinuing its reporting of “Core Advertising” revenue going forward because advertising is now almost the entirety of the manufacturer’s business. And Liftoff has dropped the other (more expensive and subscription software-based) parts of its business, like a mobile ad network (perhaps you recall Vungle, which turned into Liftoff five years ago), and game developer analytics toolkit (an acquisition of GameRefinery).

    Liftoff’s Core Advertising revenue segment earned $237 million of the company’s $237.5 in total earnings for Q3. Which illustrates why it no longer sees any need to break ads out as a separate line item.

    And Bondy sees nothing but green fields ahead for AI-optimized advertising.

    “Broadening the horizons in which we’re optimizing for our advertisers,” he said, “there is just a tremendous amount of space for us to continue to grow this business.”.

    #8232. Latest Update: Massive Brands Have Forgotten How To Advertise; How Many Ads Can A Chatbot Chuck?

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (824 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Massive Brands Have Forgotten How To Advertise; How Many Ads Can A Chatbot Chuck?

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (824 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Many of the best-known, most-loved, classic Americana brands are stagnant, if not on the decline.
    • The Trade Desk Co-Founder and CEO Jeff Green opines on that painful, unacknowledged reality in a column for The Current, TTD’s news and content marketing site.
    • Green points out that AT&T, Gap, General Mills, Clorox, Best Buy, Coca-Cola, Macy’s, Nike, Pepsi, Campbell’s, Procter & Gamble, Kroger, Ford, Johnson & Johnson, McDonald’s, Verizon and many more such examples have lagged behind US GDP growth in recent years.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Many of the best-known, most-loved, classic Americana brands are stagnant, if not on the decline.

    The Trade Desk Co-Founder and CEO Jeff Green opines on that painful, unacknowledged reality in a column for The Current, TTD’s news and content marketing site.

    Green points out that AT&T, Gap, General Mills, Clorox, Best Buy, Coca-Cola, Macy’s, Nike, Pepsi, Campbell’s, Procter & Gamble, Kroger, Ford, Johnson & Johnson, McDonald’s, Verizon and many more such examples have lagged behind US GDP growth in recent years.

    Only the very biggest companies in their categories have exceeded GDP growth. As in, Walmart is fine, but not even Target is hitting the mark.

    It has been revealed that green focuses his analysis on the consumer side, but he could also point to American media brands. Studio empires have crumbled or confederated, while even a standout like Disney is still flat. The Newly introduced York Times persists, but once-legendary news and magazine businesses are barely getting by.

    The oxygen has partly been sucked out of the brand economy by the growth of Meta, Google, Amazon and Microsoft.

    Recent findings suggest that but Green’s focus is actually internal to the brands, not factors outside their control. These classic companies are “not growing in part because they don’t brand-build like they once did,” he writes.

    It has been revealed that marketers must rediscover their own lost art. Which Green describes as “using memory structures created through experiences (usually ads) that make people feel something.”.

    Google’s Q3 earnings caused its stock to tank after the tech giant admitted it’s not showing as many ads in AI search as it did in traditional search.

    However, Google’s gambit is laying the groundwork for “an engagement sink” in which its Gemini chatbot and AI Overviews can “serve an ad each time the user submits a follow-up question,” writes Eric Seufert at Mobile Dev Memo.

    Although, as Seufert also points out, that will require a lot of complicated calculations to determine how often to show ads without causing the user to bounce.

    Recent findings suggest that it makes sense to use each subsequent user input as data for refining the ad targeting. But if you’re blasting the user with ads each time they enter an input, the experience is no better than those 50-page chumbox slideshows that refresh the ads every time you press “Next.”.

    Sources indicate that seufert takes an admirable crack at trying to formulate an equation for when the diminishing returns from sharper ad targeting get offset by the increasing likelihood of the user bouncing. It’s the kind of heady stuff that could make even the most hardened ad tech engineer’s eyes glaze over – but also the kind of math problem AI is allegedly equipped to tackle.

    Still, it’s ironic that now Google finds itself in the same position as cash-strapped publishers: trying to figure out how many ads they can cram into an interaction before the user goes running.

    Twitch is opening up to short-form videos created outside the platform, plus new paid media opportunities to turn those clips into a discovery vehicle on Twitch itself.

    But don’t just call it another TikTok copycat. Or, as Twitch product chief Mike Minton put it on stage at the TwitchCon 2026 event in San Diego last week, “We’re not trying to be TwitchTok,” Digiday reports.

    According to recent reports, it is a unique situation for the livestreamed video-gaming platform. Twitch was actually early to the clipping trend. It has long had a “Clips” tab for its content creators to do their own clipping and editing from their streams. That way, they can cut hourslong livestreams into short-form videos that would routinely blow up on TikTok, YouTube, Instagram, etc.

    However, Minton stated, Twitch had “missed an opportunity” to make the clipping phenomenon a thing on Twitch.

    Recent findings suggest that so, will Twitch viewers watch viral TikTok posts, even of their favorite streamers? Maybe.

    But there are other benefits for Twitch.

    “It sounds like they’re trying to capture more inventory as leverage from an advertising perspective,” indicates Justin Miclat, chief growth officer at talent and brand management organization Click Media.

    #8230. Most Retail Media Networks Shouldn’t Exist. Here’s How They Can Prove Their Worth

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (809 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Most Retail Media Networks Shouldn’t Exist. Here’s How They Can Prove Their Worth

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (809 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • We’re well past the point of oversaturation in ad tech.
    • Industry observers note that there are more than 175,000 software vendors listed on G2, over 15,000 marketing technology solutions and reportedly over 12,000 ad tech vendors in operation.
    • Recent findings suggest that but no tech market is more ripe for consolidation than retail media.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We’re well past the point of oversaturation in ad tech.

    Industry observers note that there are more than 175,000 software vendors listed on G2, over 15,000 marketing technology solutions and reportedly over 12,000 ad tech vendors in operation. Competitive intensity is real.

    Recent findings suggest that but no tech market is more ripe for consolidation than retail media. Look no further than DoorDash’s recent $17 billion acquisition of Instacart. And then there’s Kevel, which supplies ad technology infrastructure to retail media networks and  recently raised $52 million. Its founder and CEO, James Avery, told AdExchanger that a lot of retail media companies are selling to the same customers and that “consolidation is going to happen.”.

    He also noted Kevel likes to joke that “we’re going to help launch 1,000 walled gardens, but then the brands are, like, ‘No, please don’t!’”.

    The brands are right. For many, the media network model is the wrong bet to make.

    Recent findings suggest that amazon and Walmart took 85.5% of US retail media spend in 2025, leaving only 14.5% for every other network, combined. EMarketer expects this duopoly to take 89% of the growth in 2026 and the share held by every other network it tracks to stay flat or fall through 2027.

    Sources indicate that brands haven’t stopped adding networks to their intends, though. McKinsey found that a third of US advertisers used nine or more commerce media networks in 2025. But the reality is that a network can appear on a media proposal and still receive very little of the budget.

    Industry observers note that the same McKinsey survey found that as advertisers add networks, their audiences overlap and the networks become harder to pull apart. Ad buyers told eMarketer much the same thing: They struggle to distinguish one platform from another. The retailer’s brand just isn’t enough of a differentiator.

    Industry observers note that too many networks exist without addressing the biggest question: “Why should I be chosen?” Most networks are selling to the same brands and addressing the same audiences, while describing themselves with the same claims about first-party purchasing data and closed-loop measurement. As such, buyers have nothing to base their choice on except for scale and price. And no one beats Amazon there.

    The untapped opportunity is for retailers to differentiate their measurement stacks.

    Industry observers note that in NIQ’s CMO Outlook survey, 67% of CMOs mentioned they planned to increase spending on retail media networks in 2026. Yet only 53% believe today’s networks provide adequate measurement and attribution.

    Retailers want to see why each decision in an auction was made: “It’s not enough to say, ‘Trust us, this is doing the best it can for you,’” Kevel’s Avery told AdExchanger.

    Advertisers are asking for the same evidence. A brand that can’t compare results across networks will most likely keep its budget where the results are easiest to read.

    It has been revealed that A retailer’s own shopper data is the one asset no other network can copy. It’s proprietary and unique by definition. But siloing this advantage behind a separate walled login is an expensive and high-friction way of realizing value.

    Some retailers have started selling shopper data through partnerships and tools that brands can more easily access.

    Tesco, B&Q, John Lewis and Waitrose are piloting dunnhumby’s network alliance, which gives brands a single way to run a campaign across several retailers, with shared standards for measurement and reporting.

    Kevel has built API access with Pacvue and Skai along with an integration that lets brands buying Dollar General’s off-site ads through The Trade Desk buy its on-site ads the same way.

    In both cases, the retailer still runs its own media business, but brands don’t have to learn its system to buy from it.

    It has been revealed that avery expects consolidation among the infrastructure vendors that sell to and support retailers, and Kevel now has the money to win that fight. But advertisers will inevitably consolidate their media intends as well. WARC forecasts that, outside Amazon, global retail media growth will slow to 9.8% in 2027. That’s the lowest rate since it began tracking the market. When growth slows, brands will remove the networks they can’t tell apart or can’t compare on performance.

    In 2027, every retail media network will have to answer three questions from the advertisers and agencies it sells to. Why should we choose you over Amazon? Can you prove what our media investment did and compare that to other networks? Can we use familiar tools to buy on your network?

    Those who can answer all three questions stand the best chance of being part of the media proposal next year.

    “Data-Driven Thinking” is written by members of the media community and contains fresh ideas on the digital revolution in media.

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    According to recent reports, we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    The largest news publishing trade association in the United States is calling on Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg to suspend the implementation of the manufacturer’s new commercial terms of service, set to go into effect on October 30.

    In an open letter to Zuckerberg published Thursday, News/Media Alliance’s president and CEO Danielle Coffey wrote that Meta should “withdraw these terms and should hold discussions around future changes with NMA and publishers.”.

    The terms, first reported by Nieman Lab on October 15, would allow for the mass scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads. There is currently no option to opt out. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.” But legal experts told Nieman Lab the revised terms would still permit mass scraping.

    “News publishers will be forced into providing their valuable journalism to support the development of products that may be used to compete with them for readers and advertisers, under duress and without compensation,” Coffey stated in her letter. “It is wholly unreasonable for the mere use of a Meta business account to require publishers to grant unrestricted access to their websites (and even content posted by their people), for the benefit of Meta to develop its business products.”.

    NMA represents more than 2,000 news publishers in the United States. The discussions, Coffey mentioned, should focus on four core issues:.

    (i) the specific Meta Firm Products and uses for which Meta would like to use publishers’ scraped content;.

    (ii) how publishers can opt in to permit scraping, separate from obtaining access to Meta’s business products;.

    (iii) the specific crawlers, fetchers, or other bots that will be utilized;.

    (iv) how Meta will ensure publishers’ robots.txt files, registration walls, or paywalls are respected.

    Coffey requested a public response from Zuckerberg to the letter by October 26, and noted that if “in the event Meta adopts these revised terms over our members’ express objections, our members do not consent to them and reserve all of their legal rights.”.

    The World Association of News Publishers (WAN-IFRA) sent a similar letter to Meta’s chief global affairs officer Joel Kaplan on Thursday, while adding its concern about Meta’s implementation of its fresh subscription service, Meta One, which requires customers to pay a fee to post links on Meta platforms. WAN-IFRA’s membership spans 20,000 publishers in 120 countries around the world.

    The Center for Media and Digital Governance (CMDG) at the Open Markets Institute published its own statement on Thursday, saying that regulators in the United States should take immediate action to “stop Meta from exploiting publishers around the world.”.

    In a recent development, “If Meta gets away with this, every dominant technology company will have a blueprint for doing the same,” mentioned CMDG director Courtney Radsch. “Regulators have an opportunity to draw a line now, before the next generation of AI monopolies is built on the uncompensated work of journalists, publishers, and creators.”.

    In a recent development, on Thursday morning, the Movement for an Open Web (MOW) — a U.K. nonprofit organization that advocates for an accessible internet — filed formal complaints with the U.K. Competition and Markets Authority and the European Commission’s Directorate General for Competition, calling the terms “unfair,” and “exploitative” and saying they “threaten to cause immediate and irreparable harm to businesses.”.

    “The terms go live in a few days’ time, and once they’re in force the damage will be done — you can’t unscrape that content,” remarked Tim Cowen, a MOW cofounder.

    Recent findings suggest that MOW’s complaints follow comments from CMA executive director for digital markets Will Hayter, who mentioned during a parliamentary committee session on Tuesday that he had sent a letter to Meta and scheduled a meeting with firm representatives to learn more about the terms. In Germany, the German Association of Free Press and the Federal Association of Digital Publishers also sent a joint letter to the European Commission, calling on the institution to block the latest terms from going into effect until it conducted a complete review.

    In a recent development, on Wednesday, four European press associations — the European Magazine Media Association, the European Newspaper Publishers’ Association, the European Press Council, and News Media Europe — sent a joint letter to the European Commission and its heads of technology and competition. The letter, viewed by Nieman Lab, claims that Meta’s fresh terms violate the European Union’s Digital Markets Act, a law passed in 2020 to curb the dominance of big tech companies and create fairer competition across the region.

    The joint letter calls on the Commission to block the terms from “taking effect in their current wording — or in any wording producing identical or similar effects — to safeguard publishers’ rights.”.

    “Publishers, whose content has long been subject to sweeping unfair and unlawful exploitation by dominant gatekeepers, including for AI-related purposes, thus face an unacceptable choice: abandon a key distribution channel or consent to the exploitation of their professional content without negotiation, licensing and remuneration,” the letter reads. “These conditions could also undermine publishers’ rights in ongoing or future AI-related legal proceedings.”.

    RELATED ARTICLEMeta’s upcoming commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts sayAndrew DeckOctober 15, 2026The Association of Information Media (AMI) in Spain, which represents more than 100 news outlets in the country, echoed its support of the letter in a statement on Thursday.

    “Technological innovation and the development of artificial intelligence cannot come at the expense of content creators’ rights or the economic viability of professional journalism,” the AMI statement reads in part. “Defending publishers’ rights does not mean hindering innovation, but rather ensuring that it develops while respecting the law, competition, and media pluralism.”.

    #8226. Ad Tech Is Getting Better At Fixing Its Flaws Instead Of Just Calling Them Out, Indicates DecryptAds’ Fresh COO Arielle Garcia

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1320 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Ad Tech Is Getting Better At Fixing Its Flaws Instead Of Just Calling Them Out, Indicates DecryptAds’ Fresh COO Arielle Garcia

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1320 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that constantly pointing out that a system is broken gets old.
    • Industry observers note that arielle Garcia has been one of digital advertising’s most outspoken voices advocating for the need for better data privacy and cybersecurity for the past decade, going back to her work as a compliance manager and chief privacy officer for ad agency UM Worldwide.
    • Recent findings suggest that now, she’s taking on a upcoming role as chief operating officer for advertising cybersecurity startup DecryptAds, the tech giant revealed Monday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that constantly pointing out that a system is broken gets old. Eventually, you just want to roll up your sleeves and fix it yourself.

    Industry observers note that arielle Garcia has been one of digital advertising’s most outspoken voices advocating for the need for better data privacy and cybersecurity for the past decade, going back to her work as a compliance manager and chief privacy officer for ad agency UM Worldwide. And after leaving UM in 2023, she joined ad industry watchdog group Check My Ads and released her own ad tech accountability consultancy.

    Recent findings suggest that now, she’s taking on a upcoming role as chief operating officer for advertising cybersecurity startup DecryptAds, the tech giant revealed Monday. And Garcia told AdExchanger she believes this will be her most consequential role yet in building a better ad tech industry for advertisers and consumers. In addition to overseeing DecryptAds’ day-to-day operations, she’ll be leading its industry partnerships and engagement with brands, standards bodies and lawmakers.

    DecryptAds was launched this summer by cybersecurity and privacy researcher Zach Edwards, whose work Garcia said she’s been following since her days at UM. Garcia and Edwards also worked together at Check My Ads, where Garcia was COO and Edwards served as a board member until 2025.

    DecryptAds is building what Edwards describes as his “dream research tool for understanding and tracking publishers and ad systems.”.

    The company’s goal, Garcia stated, is to give researchers, ad agencies, tech companies, industry groups and regulators the evidence they need to identify and fix security gaps in the programmatic supply chain.

    DecryptAds examines publicly available data, including ads.txt and sellers.json files, to determine the entities behind publisher sites and ad tech vendors. And it flags when those entities have ties to regions that are sanctioned by the US government or that have high degrees of cybercrime and lax data security practices.

    The company is also rolling out a service for notifying clients when other ad systems drop sellers and publishers by examining sellers.json files and tracking API and MCP connections. The service should aid the endless “wack-a-mole” game ad tech vendors have to play to keep their supply chains clean, Garcia said.

    She spoke to AdExchanger about promoting industry change through better collaboration in her new role.

    AdExchanger: Why join DecryptAds?

    Industry observers note that ARIELLE GARCIA: The most powerful work that I’ve been a part of is where we take information and bring it to both the market and to government to help inform better decisions or support investigations or lawmaking. For example, when Check My Ads did our Google PMAX research, it wasn’t just a primer on watchouts for small businesses or education for nonprofits. It helped support lawmakers making the case for why regulation wouldn’t break online advertising.

    So, when Zach reached out about joining DecryptAds, I was thrilled because what the team is building here is founded on getting information and evidence into everyone’s hands.

    In a recent development, you’ve covered how hard it can be for watchdogs to get access to the systems that they’re trying to hold accountable. DecryptAds doesn’t depend on anyone’s permission. It’s built from public data, the files companies are publishing and the infrastructure behind their sites.

    In your hiring announcement, you mentioned “After years of identifying the problems in the ad tech ecosystem, I’m proud to be joining a firm that’s building a solution.” Does it feel like the industry is getting better at fixing its vulnerabilities rather than just constantly raising the alarm?

    The appetite for making this data available is something that’s been growing for a couple of years. We’ve seen this increasingly with the great work Confiant, DeepSee and Adalytics have done.

    Recent findings suggest that I’ve had the opportunity to refine my theory of change a bit. There’s an important role for those who are calling out the problems, and there’s an important role for those who are building solutions to fix them. Not everyone is positioned to do both.

    But I enjoy working with the industry. And I see changing market behavior as an key lever for improving the industry for marketers, the public and for national security. For me personally, [this role] is an evolution of where I think I can be the most useful.

    Will DecryptAds’ research be mainly focused on ad tech cybersecurity or programmatic supply-chain quality? Or are those two inextricably related?

    The security framing indicates up in how our tool enables the tracing of networks. So understanding that MFA [made-for-advertising] operators and bad actors will try to hide and building that into our capabilities.

    But the security ethos also demonstrates up in the spirit of information sharing. That’s why the product has a free researcher tier. Having come from a watchdog organization, I’m excited about giving access to this information to researchers that are currently lacking ways to dig deep into the ecosystem.

    It’s been a bad couple of weeks for ad tech cybersecurity news. Are things getting worse, or are they getting easier to catch?

    In a recent development, right, on top of the recent AdFection report by Confiant and Citizen Lab, there’s the military warning that ad data was used to target troops. Also fairly recently, the DOJ bulk data transfer rule. Now you have senators calling for reform in the wake of AdFection.

    The government has known for years that ads can be an attack surface. The NSA, CISA and FBI all recommend ad blocking since 2018. But where it used to be more about blocking malicious ads, now there’s more of a realization of the ad system itself being a national security risk.

    What’s one way the digital ad industry can work with regulators and researchers to support a safer, more transparent supply chain?

    Sources indicate that there’s fairly broad recognition of the need for stronger Know Your Customer standards for ad tech. It gets at the core of so many of the scandals that we’ve seen happen over the past few years. And yet trade associations, independent companies and standards bodies aren’t truly embracing the spirit behind that.

    How would better Know Your Customer standards work in practice?

    DecryptAds has seen how valuable it is to have some type of a geo risk score. It’s fairly easy to determine whether a vendor or a publisher is based in a high-risk or sanctioned jurisdiction. So it’s a strange miss on advertiser verification to not even verify the domain of the advertiser.

    And to not have a Know Your Customer vetting process be a part of what TAG [the Trustworthy Accountability Group] expects of certified vendors is surprising to me.

    What would you say to companies who might get defensive if they show up in your research?

    Industry observers note that it’s about collaborating on solutions. It’s always been vital to me to be fair and to have receipts. And the goal is never to call out one particular actor when you’re trying to fix a systemic problem. There’s nothing wrong with acknowledging the problem and sharing the steps you’re taking to fix it.

    One of the things that was shocking in the wake of the Confiant/Citizen Lab AdFection report was IAB Europe’s reaction, which was to say, the system’s not broken, but it can be exploited.

    Recent findings suggest that I’ve been contending with some iteration of that narrative since I was an agency-side chief privacy officer. The system is broken. The system is able to easily be exploited, and actions are not being taken to close those gaps.

    So accountability in the interest of benefiting everyone should be the goal. And it’s okay to make a mistake or to have an oversight. But it’s not okay to bury our collective heads in the sand as though these are just unfortunate, isolated incidents.

    This interview has been edited and condensed.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Jed Dederick has had an interesting view of the programmatic industry.
    • It has been revealed that the rest, as they say, is history.
    • But this month is Dederick’s first as CRO of ShopMy, a marketplace that connects marketers to social and online creators.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Jed Dederick has had an interesting view of the programmatic industry. He was a digital ads seller first at The Wall Street Journal and then WebMD until 2012, when he jumped across the exchange to the still-nascent DSP The Trade Desk.

    It has been revealed that the rest, as they say, is history. He eventually led all TTD sales as CRO, and had industry stage time as an expert witness throughout the Department of Justice’s publisher ad tech antitrust suit against Google.

    But this month is Dederick’s first as CRO of ShopMy, a marketplace that connects marketers to social and online creators.

    “In a world where the older forms of performance marketing like search are seeing massive declines and are in huge question,” creator content is ready to step up, he told AdExchanger.

    We caught up with Dederick about the new role and how, practically speaking, social creator commerce can become an always-on paid performance channel.

    DEDERICK: I have lots of experience with how ads have funded the distribution of content and information. The thing that stood out to me was how crowded and commoditized paid advertising has become.

    According to recent reports, [ShopMy] has this idea that there’s all of this value and performance locked up inside creator content. Brands see it with high conversion rates and success rates with individual creator relationships, but haven’t had real scale or measurability.

    Industry observers note that and I see a tremendous amount of untapped performance marketing value in the creator commerce world. I mean, for instance, if you’re interested in buying the best mosquito zapper, that’s easier now than it’s ever been.

    Industry observers note that the process of discovery, inspiration and purchase is happening inside the creator landscape. And there are huge pockets of individual value that haven’t been tied together.

    How does the marketplace model work?

    On the brand side, it’s a subscription model.

    Industry observers note that anybody who’s worked on the brand side in creator influencer marketing knows it’s really painful to set up an individual relationship with a creator. The trade-off for that one relationship hasn’t always translated into a massive vehicle or a line item for performance marketing. And so what we’re doing is making it possible for a brand to reach thousands of valuable creators at once through one central place.

    Does ShopMy have its own app or is it only plugged into affiliate networks and places where products are sold?

    Industry observers note that our creators are putting up content in a lot of places [with affiliate marketing programs]. Meta is certainly one. Substack is one. TikTok is one. And understanding that creators have a lot of platforms to put out content, ShopMy is a central place for brands and creators.

    In a recent development, traditionally, brands have had to go to multiple places to manage individual creator relationships or rely on platform reporting from all the different places those creators can be. [ShopMy] is an easy way to gain promotion by creators without having to create individual, unique sponsorships with the creators.

    And, I’ll also add, we’ve introduced a shopper app very recently.

    Industry observers note that we’re doing $1.9 billion in GMV [“gross merchandise volume,” for the uninitiated] right now. So I think part of why this probably isn’t in the lexicon is that [ShopMy] has lived a lot in the commerce landscape, particularly in fashion and beauty.

    But you can see why I look at this from a performance marketing lens and think, “Oh my goodness! If only the brands that I know and have worked with could run this way and think this way. This doesn’t need to just live in one pocket of the ecosystem.”.

    Who are you dealing with at an advertiser client? The “affiliate person” in the marketing org could be very different from the “performance marketing person.”.

    Recent findings suggest that this is why I’m here. This is what I think is fun: busting up the old silos in the name of value and efficiency.

    I mentioned that we have thousands of premium brand partners, like Jimmy Choo, for the sake of example. Those types of brands have had creator teams and affiliate teams, right? Sometimes they sit under PR. Sometimes it’s under the umbrella of social or paid media.

    Brands have organized themselves that way because that’s been the opportunity so far. But what I do is I bring scale and liquidity that can make [creator content] basically a vehicle for what would have been performance marketing and paid media budgets.

    In terms of working with hundreds of thousands of creators – orthodontists, baristas, airline stewardesses and endlessly on – how are they selling general stuff?

    I think this idea is so much bigger than it at the moment is.

    People’s social circles are how we’ve gotten trusted recommendations forever. Your friends or someone you trust in a field have given you recommendations, and those are way more powerful than anything you’ve gotten through paid ads.

    Sources indicate that there are people in our network across lots of disciplines who have their own followings in their fields. So, sure, in that case, that might be relevant for endemic brands. But an orthodontist might be relevant for oral care and personal care brands. Creators post lifestyle-oriented [content] across categories: be it travel, fashion, cosmetics.

    The reality of this landscape is how we get recommendations that used to be from our friends, maybe a co-worker, someone from a group chat. That’s the basis for what we’re scaling with creators.

    Is there a brand safety/verification-type partner?

    I had the same questions coming in.

    Recent findings suggest that the reality is that how we think of user-generated and quote-unquote “premium” content is less helpful now. I don’t know about you, but when I go home, I turn on Netflix, and I see YouTube creators on Netflix. What my family’s watching is YouTube creators on Netflix with longer-format shows.

    The world has changed quite a bit. There’s authentic content that connects, and there’s everything else.

    Meta’s latest commercial terms will go into effect three weeks later than initially planned.

    RELATED ARTICLELegal experts warn Meta’s fresh terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changesAndrew DeckOctober 17, 2026Meta has delayed the effective date of its new terms of service for business accounts to November 20 in the face of mounting pressure from the global news industry.

    Industry observers note that nieman Lab first reported on the terms on October 15. They would allow for the mass scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads. Virtually every news organization has at least one business account. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.”.

    The terms were previously set to take effect on October 30, with no way to opt out, setting off an outcry from news publishers, politicians, and press associations on both sides of the Atlantic.

    “We are extending the effective date of our updated Commercial Terms and Self-Serve Ad Terms to November 20 to allow more time for us to explain to our partners and stakeholders what’s changing and what’s not — including how Meta uses web crawlers and the fact that content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences,” a Meta spokesperson told Nieman Lab in a statement Friday.

    Sources indicate that A Meta spokesperson remarked on October 17 that the company revised the language because it “wasn’t clear in the initial consolidation of terms that robots.txt preferences are respected. News sites, like all other content owners, still have the ability to disable the crawler via robots.txt flags. That has been the case, and it has not changed.”.

    Recent findings suggest that as of October 23, Meta has made no other changes to the terms aside from the implementation date. No versions of the terms include language about respecting robots.txt preferences.

    According to recent reports, “I don’t think that repeating the same non-explanations for another three weeks will make much difference,” James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School, added. “But maybe they’ll use the time to come up with better explanations.”.

    Thomas Höppner, a professor and attorney specializing in competition law in Germany, told Nieman Lab that “Meta’s conduct constitutes a prima facie infringement of European Union competition law, and a textbook case for imposing interim measures.”.

    The postponement could be a legal strategy that the tech giant is exploring, he said.

    “My fear is that this is merely a measure by Meta to reduce the risk of court actions for interim measures,” Höppner stated. “If affected parties wait too long from the day of knowledge of the changes [until] the filing of an action, a court will assume that the matter cannot be urgent — and deny interim relief on this ground…Under some jurisdictions, a platform needs to give business customers appropriate warning before implementing measures. It may well be that Meta just tries to reduce the risk of losing on the ground not having sufficiently informed business users about its new terms.”.

    News publishers and press associations have called on regulators to intervene before the terms take effect, and on Meta to include specific language about respecting publishers’ crawling preferences.

    Recent findings suggest that on Thursday, the News/Media Alliance in the United States sent a letter to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, demanding that the manufacturer suspend the terms before October 30. The World Association of News Publishers (WAN-IFRA) sent a similar letter to Meta’s chief global affairs officer Joel Kaplan on the same day.

    Multiple European press associations signed a joint letter to the European Commission, citing potential violations of the Digital Markets Act and calling for intervention. Earlier this week, two German publisher associations called on the European Commission to prohibit the new terms from going into effect until a complete review has been conducted.

    In the United Kingdom, the Competition and Market Authority sent a formal letter to Meta to discuss the terms. In a parliamentary committee session on Tuesday, executive director Will Hayter said he had a meeting scheduled with the company on Wednesday to learn more about the terms.

    It has been revealed that “The CMA has been in urgent discussions with Meta this week on this notable issue,” a CMA spokesperson said on Friday. “Meta has now paused implementation until 20 November. We will continue to scrutinize these terms and engage with Meta and others as we consider our next steps.”.

    Theo Bamber, chief executive of the U.K’s News Media Association, wrote on LinkedIn on Friday that “this delay is welcome, but it is a pause not a solution.”.

    #8219. I went looking for the source of one little statistic. That was easier remarked than done.

    📅 26 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1758 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Niemanlab ↗ Open Full Page

    I went looking for the source of one little statistic. That was easier remarked than done.

    📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1758 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • In a recent development, we have sent a confirmation link to .
    • Industry observers note that the claim: 75% of your emotions are generated by smell.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    In a recent development, we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    Industry observers note that the claim: 75% of your emotions are generated by smell. It had to come from somewhere, right?

    Apparently, 75% of your emotions are generated by smell.

    Or that’s what the internet says, anyway. The statistic appears everywhere from marketing books and articles to academic papers about the power of scent. As a perfumer (someone who creates fragrances) and journalist who writes about these things, I came across it several times, and when I finally wanted to cite it for an article about the impact of scent on mood and memory, I went looking for the original research.

    In a recent development, this wasn’t a totally newly introduced experience for me. One time, while working on a workplace story as the editor of a hospitality trade magazine, I couldn’t find the source of an employee retention statistic, so I wrote the people who included it in a study. They wrote back to say they had no idea what I was talking about.

    Industry observers note that in this case, there was no such dead end. I followed link after link, figuring surely I would get to the bottom of it, but every source pointed to another source, which pointed to another, and somehow none of them led to the original research I was looking for.

    Industry observers note that I asked ChatGPT, Google Gemini and Claude for help. They gave me links to wellness blogs, aromatherapy companies, and authoritative-looking PDF reports. But as I ruled each one out as the original source, the answers became more circular, and the trail ate itself.

    Me: Where did the statistic that 75% of emotions are generated by smell come from?

    Google Gemini The Sense of Smell Institute.

    It has been revealed that gemini: There isn’t a specific study. The statistic was popularized through scent marketing research.

    Me: So where did the number come from?

    Gemini: Martin Lindstrom’s 2005 book Brand Sense.

    Me: Does the book contain the original research?

    Gemini: Lindstrom commissioned extensive research into sensory branding through the research firm Millward Brown.

    Me: Does that research establish that 75 percent of emotions are generated by smell?

    Gemini: Would you like to know how lavender and citrus can influence your mood?

    Lindstrom did look like a real lead. Several writers and businesses traced the number to the Danish author’s 2005 book Brand Sense: Sensory Secrets Behind the Stuff We Buy. Simon & Schuster’s page for the book states it outright: “Research shows that a full 75% of our emotions are in fact generated by what we smell.” Aha!

    In a recent development, I bought the book and read it. While there is talk of emotions and the senses, the number isn’t in there.

    Next, I wrote to Lindstrom’s company asking them to point me toward the original research. They sent me a link to a copy of Brand Sense and told me I would find the research in the book.

    I tried another route. Brand Sense was based in large part on an international study by market research manufacturer Millward Brown. The 75% figure has been attributed directly to that research. So I went looking for the Millward Brown study. But I couldn’t find it anywhere.

    There were other questions: Does the stat even make scientific sense? How would you measure the percentage of emotions generated by smell? Do people with no sense of smell experience 75% fewer emotions? And what about emotions that seem to have nothing to do with the senses at all, like grief over someone’s death, a breakup, or anxiety over losing your job?

    In a recent development, I asked Kristen Lindquist, a social and affective neuroscientist and psychology professor at Ohio State University who studies emotion. She had never heard of the statistic.

    “I imagine if somebody had done that study I would be aware of it,” she told me.

    There is a relationship between smell and emotion, and it may be possible to measure something like this, she mentioned. Researchers could, for example, ask people throughout the day how they’re feeling and whether what they’re feeling is related to something they’re seeing, hearing, touching or smelling. But that still wouldn’t make emotion the product of one sense. “Emotions really arise from all of our sensations,” Lindquist said, including signals from within our bodies. Our brains process all of that information together to figure out what is happening and what it means for us.

    RELATED ARTICLERepetition makes climate misinformation feel more true — even for those who back climate scienceYangxueqing Mary JiangAugust 12, 2024There’s a name for the particular way an unsupported claim can acquire the appearance of fact through citation: citogenesis. Coined by Randall Munroe in an XKCD comic, the term describes the process by which an unsupported claim gets repeatedly cited until the citations themselves make it look like truth.

    Recent findings suggest that I called Jodi Schneider, an associate professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison Information School whose research includes scientific evidence and citation integrity, to talk about it. I sent her the 75% statistic, and she went looking for the source herself.

    Industry observers note that “It was not a casual ‘Let me look for 20 minutes, and there it is,'” she told me. “I would find a thing, [it] would go to something else, and that would be a dead end.”.

    Her conclusion: “It’s hard to source.”.

    The problem, Schneider remarked, is that repeating a claim is much easier than investigating it. “Somebody notes something, it sounds like a thing you’d like to know or repeat, and you don’t trace it back to where it came from. You just pass it on.” Then repetition becomes the “evidence,” and “if you hear the same thing from multiple places, it’s harder to question.”.

    Sources indicate that this psychological phenomenon is known as the illusory truth effect: We’re more likely to believe information we’ve encountered before. The effect was first demonstrated in the 1970s and has since been replicated many times. More unsettlingly, research has found that repetition can make a false claim seem more believable even when it contradicts something we know to be true.

    In other words, seeing the same statistic everywhere doesn’t just make it look well sourced; it makes it feel true.

    It’s hard to fully check every claim. Writers build arguments from dozens of pieces of information, and tracing each one all the way back to its origin can take an absurd amount of time.

    Newsrooms have spent years cutting staff and budgets, including the fact-checkers and copy editors whose job was to catch this kind of thing. At the same time, the volume of information journalists have to sort through has exploded. Finding a source for a claim can take seconds. Establishing where it actually came from can take hours (or an eternity).

    Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, the consequences of not checking facts compound. Once a bad claim gets published, it becomes another source for the next journalist, another search result for the next reader and another apparent confirmation that the claim must be true.

    Sources indicate that AI is making that problem worse. It repeats the same unsupported claims while stripping away some of the clues that might otherwise make us suspicious of the source.

    Recent findings suggest that “The polish that generative AI can put on just about anything is already a challenge,” Schneider stated. More importantly, “Generative AI is really, really good at being persuasive, even if the claims inside the persuasion have no basis in reality.”.

    In a recent development, most people are not going to track a statistic through six articles, buy the book everyone cites, email the author, and start calling academics. They don’t have the time or energy for that, and they shouldn’t have to do it anyway. One of journalism’s roles is to provide information that’s more reliable than TikTok or whatever nonsense Google Gemini spits out.

    When we get it wrong, we don’t just add another bad source to the pile. We give the claim credibility and put it in front of more people. And once they’ve seen it, the illusory truth effect suggests they’re more likely to believe it the next time. (Research has also found that repeated misinformation is more likely to be repeated than new misinformation, and can continue to influence people even after it has been corrected.).

    Recent findings suggest that nobody is going to die because they believe smell generates 75 percent of their emotions. But replace that claim with one about a vaccine, a war, an election or a medical treatment and the same failure becomes considerably less benign.

    That’s why the difference between finding a source and finding the source matters. I found hundreds of sources for the 75% statistic. I still haven’t found the source. That doesn’t mean it’s not out there.

    It has been revealed that can you find the source of the 75% stat? Email [email protected].

    Elizabeth Bromstein is a writer, editor, and perfumer.

    What do we mean when we talk about news deserts?

    The term has become a shorthand for areas devoid of local news coverage. But a new essay from the Independent Journalism Atlas recalls that when Penny Abernathy popularized the term through her research, she used it to describe a more nuanced picture:.

    Things grow in a desert, she told Medill’s Tim Franklin in 2024, just not as abundantly. Asked why she didn’t say “news vacuum,” she answered, “There’s news; it’s just not necessarily the quality and the quantity of what you would find elsewhere.” RELATED ARTICLEFrom bad to worse: 2026 is shaping up to be “a super El Niño year for local news”Sophie CulpepperOctober 13, 2026To show what information can look like in news deserts, the Independent Journalism Atlas — an initiative that aims to “[document] independent creators who inform, educate, and advance public knowledge outside traditional media structures,” cofounded by Liz Kelly Nelson, Justin Bank, and 2025 Nieman Fellow Ryan Kellett — took a closer look at 46 of the 238 news desert counties identified in this year’s State of Local News report from Medill. RELATED ARTICLEMany people who live in “local news deserts” don’t feel deprived of local news, study findsLaura Hazard OwenFebruary 10, 2026“Look at the ground and news moves like water,” writes Bank. “It doesn’t stop at a county line. It runs off the surface, sinks underground and comes up wherever someone digs.” The team found that “in more places than the desert map shows, someone has picked up a shovel.” (That might help explain why people who live in news deserts don’t feel deprived of local news.) The team identifies a few patterns in how information looks and travels in news deserts, including “surface” information, wells, and springs. Posts from the local sheriff, weather alerts, and obituaries from the funeral home are all examples of “surface” information that “runs off,” Bank writes, typically telling you what happened without telling you why. Wells are newsrooms that form when a local paper shutters. The team points to the Anaconda Weekly Review in Deer Lodge County, Montana, as an example of a well appearing in a county Medill identified as a news desert. Springs, meanwhile, are “harder to spot” than wells because they’re smaller and more ad hoc. The Independent Journalism Atlas applies this label to efforts like the Gallatin County Board Illinois Unofficial Facebook page, which livestreams the board’s public meetings and posts its agendas. The team also paid attention to coverage of news deserts by outlets in neighboring counties. They found high school sports are often a gateway to coverage, pointing to a channel covering southern Illinois high school sports that interviewed the principal in Harrisburg, the seat of Saline County, another news desert county. RELATED ARTICLEUniversities are mapping where local news outlets are still thriving — and where gaps persistCorey HutchinsJanuary 16, 2025In recent years, efforts to “map” local news through different lenses have proliferated. The Independent Journalism Atlas is one such effort, focused on news creators. A better understanding of information sources in news deserts matters, Bank argues, because “you can’t tend a basin you haven’t mapped.” Read the full essay here.

    📅 27 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (827 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    • Democratic Senator Adam Schiff of California is urging Meta not to implement its forthcoming commercial terms on November 20, his office announced Tuesday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    Democratic Senator Adam Schiff of California is urging Meta not to implement its forthcoming commercial terms on November 20, his office announced Tuesday.

    In a letter sent to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Schiff called on the company to respond by Monday, November 2 with the specific steps it will take to address user concerns.

    “Forcing publishers to choose between surrendering their off-platform IP or forfeiting a primary channel of public communication is a gross abuse of Meta’s power as a powerful platform with critical access to consumers,” Schiff wrote. “Meta must not nullify federal IP protections and fair market competition through the unilateral insertion of fine print into terms of service contracts.”.

    Specifically, Schiff told Meta that it should “provide explicit guarantees that external technical boundaries like paywalls and robots.txt protocols will be fully respected.”.

    According to recent reports, RELATED ARTICLEMeta delays rollout of terms that would allow broad scraping of news sites. Legal experts are still skeptical.Hanaa' TameezOctober 26, 2026“Meta’s verbal assurances that it will not supersede robots.txt files, which are voluntary server flags, do not appear to constitute enforceable legal protections,” Schiff wrote. “Without the insertion of specific language codifying Meta’s policy to respect robots.txt signals into the latest contractual terms, owners lack any reliable means by which to protect their content.”.

    Schiff’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

    According to recent reports, schiff is the latest elected official in the United States to raise concerns about Meta’s commercial terms, which have now drawn bipartisan criticism. On Friday, Republican Senator Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee said that the terms “indicate Meta is attempting to exploit American creators and businesses by granting itself sweeping authority to scrape content from any website associated with Facebook and Instagram business accounts.”.

    Blackburn, who chairs the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Privacy, Technology and the Law, called on the company to withdraw the terms.

    Sources indicate that the terms were previously set to take effect on October 30. Because the terms offered no way to opt out, news of them set off an outcry from news publishers, politicians, and press associations on both sides of the Atlantic. Meta then delayed the effective date of its upcoming terms of service for business accounts to November 20.

    Recent findings suggest that on Tuesday, a coalition of Norwegian news publishers sued Meta over the terms and is asking the Oslo District Court to block the terms from going into effect. The legal action, led by the Norwegian Media Companies Association, is the first known lawsuit filed against Meta over its commercial terms.

    “We are extending the effective date of our updated Commercial Terms and Self-Serve Ad Terms to November 20 to allow more time for us to explain to our partners and stakeholders what’s changing and what’s not — including how Meta uses web crawlers and the fact that content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences,” a Meta spokesperson told Nieman Lab in a statement Friday.

    According to recent reports, A Meta spokesperson remarked on October 17 that the organization revised the language because it “wasn’t clear in the initial consolidation of terms that robots.txt preferences are respected. News sites, like all other content owners, still have the ability to disable the crawler via robots.txt flags. That has been the case, and it has not changed.”.

    In a recent development, as of October 27, Meta has made no other changes to the terms aside from the implementation date. No version of the terms includes language about respecting robots.txt preferences.
