    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    “We’re pausing the changes as we continue to engage with stakeholders and take our time to get this right.”.

    Meta has indefinitely delayed its proposed commercial terms of service, which would have permitted the company to scrape the websites of Meta Business account users.

    On Thursday, the manufacturer took down the preview link to the proposed terms and published an update to its Business Help Center that reads: “We recently shared that we were updating the Meta Commercial Terms, Product Catalog Terms, Self-Serve Ad Terms, and Ad Creative Generative AI Terms. These updates are now paused and will not take effect on November 20, 2026. We are continuing to consult with stakeholders and will provide a further update when we have more to share. In the meantime, our existing terms remain in effect.”.

    It has been revealed that meta — which owns Facebook, Messenger, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads — has repeatedly pushed back the terms’ effective date since Nieman Lab first reported on them on October 15. The terms were first set to take effect on October 30, sparking global outcry among news publishers, politicians, and trade organizations. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.” On October 23, Meta moved the effective date back by three weeks to November 20.

    Last week, Meta pledged to consult news publishers and industry leaders ahead of putting fresh commercial terms into effect.

    “We’ve heard publishers’ feedback on our proposed ads and business terms update. We care deeply about our partners and do not plan to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders,” vice president of communications Andy Stone tweeted on October 28. “We’re committed to getting this right, and as we expect this consultation could extend beyond November 20, in which case we’d delay implementation of the updated terms.”.

    Since then, courts in Norway and Brazil have issued preliminary injunctions to block the terms from taking effect as a result of lawsuits filed by media organizations in both countries. The United Kingdom’s Competition and Markets Authority has opened a formal investigation into Meta, examining whether the firm was “abusing a dominant position by imposing exploitative terms on publishers and advertisers.”.

    According to recent reports, in the United States, the proposed terms stoked bipartisan concern. At the end of October, Sens. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) sent letters to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg asking him to withdraw the terms.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that visits to the world’s top million websites were lower in the third quarter of 2026 than at their early 2022 peak (a decline of 12.2%), based on the data from Similarweb shared by SparkToro.
    • Rand Fishkin, SparkToro’s co-founder and CEO, wrote that the project began with his theory that the biggest sites, largely Big Tech properties, were taking more of the web’s traffic.
    • According to recent reports, the post also reports a 29.2% drop in visits per internet user.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that visits to the world’s top million websites were lower in the third quarter of 2026 than at their early 2022 peak (a decline of 12.2%), based on the data from Similarweb shared by SparkToro. The proportion of visits that go to websites that are not among the top 100 stayed relatively consistent over this time. That means while the total number of visits was down, that proportion still added up to less traffic for non-top-100 sites.

    Rand Fishkin, SparkToro’s co-founder and CEO, wrote that the project began with his theory that the biggest sites, largely Big Tech properties, were taking more of the web’s traffic.

    According to recent reports, the post also reports a 29.2% drop in visits per internet user. This calculation uses user estimates that were revised partway through the period.

    Fishkin asked Similarweb for total visits to the top million sites from its worldwide desktop and mobile web panel, along with a breakdown by site rank.

    In the post’s figures, total visits peaked in Q1 2022 at 2.243 trillion. At the low point in Q1 2026, the total was 1.914 trillion, down 14.7% from the peak. The latest quarter, Q3 2026, came in at 1.970 trillion, 12.2% below the peak.

    The totals on the post’s chart stay roughly level through 2023, then dip in early 2024 and fall again in the first half of 2025.

    Similarweb categorized the top million websites from the number 1-10 to the 100,001st to 1 millionth website by five levels of ranking.

    Industry observers note that the share chart demonstrates roughly a combined 33% and 36% of visits for the #1-10 (top) and #11-100 (next 90) sites during Q4 2021 and Q3 2026 respectively. The percentages for each band below the top 100 were a little lower at the end of the period compared to the beginning.

    Fishkin described growth in the share for the top 100 as small, writing that “stagnation is a more accurate description of the trend.”.

    SparkToro’s per-user number is found by dividing Similarweb’s total visits by DataReportal’s estimated quarterly internet people globally. The table included in the blog post reports 4.95 billion internet users in Q4 2021 and 6.15 billion for Q3 2026. This represents an increase of around 24% during that time. The blog post reports the decline in visits per user at 29.2%.

    The user series jumped from 5.65 billion to 6.04 billion in one quarter (Q3) of 2025. According to DataReportal in their October 2025 report, this jump in the number of customers online was “largely attributable to significant revisions” in the rate of internet use that were officially reported by India and China. They also warned the reader to avoid interpreting this change as if hundreds of millions of new people came online in 90 days.

    The SparkToro post did not include information regarding the change in reporting. Their estimate of 24% user growth compared data prior to and subsequent to the reporting change.

    It has been revealed that similarweb’s panel tracks browser visits on desktop and mobile, but not app use. Fishkin wrote that consolidation by Massive Tech is likely much more common in apps.

    The data is also worldwide, and he wrote that it’s plausible traffic to U.S., U.K. and EU sites declined while regions with growing internet access, such as Asia and Africa, grew. The post doesn’t break out regions or state the panel’s size.

    He did not provide reasons for the decline in visits. Fishkin’s list of possible factors includes app-only use, reliance on search engine results, AI tool utilization, social media platforms and the user behavior changes after the COVID-19 pandemic.

    After initial publication SparkToro updated their article. On Nov. 10, Fishkin stated on X that the prior version of his post “had an incorrect graph/data.” That version’s headline put the decline at 24%, which the URL still demonstrates.

    SparkToro sells audience research software, and Fishkin co-authored the book “Zero Click Marketing.”.

    SparkToro has provided an international benchmark for when a multi-year traffic decline shows up in your reports. The percentage of visits based upon the ranking of the website held close to steady in Similarweb’s browser-based metrics, although the actual number of visits decreased. The headline statistic in the report without reliance on changes in user estimates is the 12.2 percent decline in overall visits.

    This report measures the number of browser visits to the top million websites regardless of where they came from, whereas the zero-click data I reported on back in June measured clicks per U.S. Google search.

    Until a regional breakdown is available, SparkToro’s figures are best viewed as global context for traffic conversations, rather than as a benchmark for any single market. Fishkin also wrote that he plans to compare the findings with other sources and revisit the numbers every year or two.

    Latest Update: The IAB has had enough: It’s calling on platforms to standardize the definition of a “view”

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (716 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tubefilter

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When YouTube changed the way it counts public views this past August, it said its main goal was helping creators get more brand deals, and get paid more for those brand deals.
    • The new counts, it mentioned, would “[give] creators a clearer picture of their overall exposure and [make] it easier to confidently express their true scale and value to brand partners and sponsors!”.
    • In a recent development, but the “clearer picture” that emerged was one of inaccurate inflation.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When YouTube changed the way it counts public views this past August, it said its main goal was helping creators get more brand deals, and get paid more for those brand deals.

    The new counts, it mentioned, would “[give] creators a clearer picture of their overall exposure and [make] it easier to confidently express their true scale and value to brand partners and sponsors!”.

    In a recent development, but the “clearer picture” that emerged was one of inaccurate inflation. Data from Agentio indicated public viewcounts over-reported actual views by 40%; experiments by individual creators like John Green, who compared his backend viewcount of one video to its public-facing count, found similar inaccuracy.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    Now, the Interactive Advertising Bureau has released a report, The Creator Economy’s Next Chapter, that calls for wide standardization of what counts as a “view.”.

    Sources indicate that accurate measurement is the “fault line beneath the creator economy,” the IAB remarked in its report. This overall conclusion came from 53 participating industry leaders who filled out the IAB’s survey, and also from senior industry leader interviews conducted by the IAB’s Creator Economy Board.

    In a recent development, “Measurement also sits inside problems that look like something else. Two sides who disagree on creator pricing both agree they cannot judge whether creators are paid fairly because nobody agrees what creator content is worth,” the IAB wrote. “One in eight respondents traced budget fights with leadership to measurement gaps, and a similar share remarked organizations withhold results because the numbers behind them are not solid enough to publish.”.

    We see why this is a major concern: Brands pay creators based on their reach, so when platforms like YouTube roll out changes that inflate views, marketers end up overpaying.

    It might not sound bad for creators to make a little extra cash, but this situation doesn’t end well for them either. If they secure a brand deal based on inflated views, that sets a high bar for engagement that their sponsored content almost certainly will not clear. This performance gap might result in them losing their relationship with that individual brand, or with an entire agency that represents other vital brands in their niche.

    Industry observers note that it’s not just marketers that told the IAB standardization is needed. “Measurement providers, who see the problem most closely, were unanimous in choosing a common definition of a view as a top priority,” the bureau stated in its report.

    In a recent development, they also have a proposed solution: “Respondents are clear about where to start. Given 11 possible standards, two-thirds (66%) chose a common definition of a view and exposure metrics across platforms,” per the report. “Each platform counts a view differently, and shared reporting format, cross-channel planning, and any comparison with video or television all depend on counting it the same way.”.

    Among the IAB’s respondents, another interesting data point emerged. The majority of entities that produce metrics (like platforms, marketing agencies, and measurement companies) say they are “very confident” in the accuracy of the numbers they provide.

    Meanwhile brands and talent agencies both said they have zero percent confidence in numbers they receive.

    The IAB states to rectify this problem, it plans to work alongside the Media Ratings Council and other “engaged industry bodies” to bring content platforms and measurement providers together so everyone can agree on cross-platform definitions of a view, an impression, reach, and watch time.

    It notes it hopes to secure one to two platform agreements within the first year of this effort.

    If it does that, we might be looking at one of the biggest industry shifts to date, and could end up in a radically different era of social media and content creation.

    35% of respondents said creators’ work split across teams and tools is not working. 33% said brands don’t understand creators’ channels. 31% cited pricing inconsistency, and 25% said agreeing on contract and deal terms is difficult.

    Solutions they suggested include standard T&Cs and contracts for creator x bran deals (66% of respondents), transparency standards for agency fee disclosure (38%), and a unified creator taxonomy (31%).

    You can read the IAB’s full report here.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that as TwitchCon descends upon San Diego, a different hub for video game streaming is celebrating its ascendance.
    • Industry observers note that hatchet (previously known as Stream Hatchet) dispensed its TikTok Live status report as part of a biannual update related to the ByteDance-owned platform.
    • Sources indicate that previous Hatchet reports have characterized Twitch and YouTube Gaming‘s dominant positions within the streaming landscape, but the firm’s latest dispatches have shown that TikTok Live is gaining on its market-leading rivals.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that as TwitchCon descends upon San Diego, a different hub for video game streaming is celebrating its ascendance. TikTok Live is the fastest growing platform in that category, according to a fresh report published by the GameSquare subsidiary Hatchet.

    Industry observers note that hatchet (previously known as Stream Hatchet) dispensed its TikTok Live status report as part of a biannual update related to the ByteDance-owned platform. During the first half of 2026, gaming streams on TikTok Live pulled in 2.5 billion hours of watch time. That traffic gave TikTok Live a 14% share of the game streaming market, pulling it even with the Stake.com-affiliated platform Kick.

    Sources indicate that previous Hatchet reports have characterized Twitch and YouTube Gaming‘s dominant positions within the streaming landscape, but the firm’s latest dispatches have shown that TikTok Live is gaining on its market-leading rivals. While TikTok Live watch time grew 96% year-over-year, Twitch and YouTube Gaming’s respective market shares both went down.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    Through properties like Hatchet, FaZe Clan, and TubeBuddy, GameSquare has made deep inroads in digital gaming communities. “Hatchet’s latest report highlights just how quickly TikTok Live has established itself in gaming live-streaming,” mentioned GameSquare CEO Justin Kenna in a statement. “Nearly doubling its gaming hours watched in a year is a clear signal that audience habits are shifting toward mobile, discovery-driven viewing.”.

    Kenna cited titles like Roblox, Garena Free Fire, and Mobile Legends as three major drivers of TikTok Live’s watch time uptick. Roblox led all games in terms of TikTok Live watch time during the first half of 2026; it generated 631 million hours of TikTok viewership during that period.

    It has been revealed that roblox is a favorite of Gen Alpha gamers, while Free Fire and Mobile Legends appeal to gamers on mobile devices, especially outside of the United States. Those two data points help explain how TikTok Live has managed such a sizable gaming glow-up — it has volume none of its competitors can match. With 1.4 million creators active each day, TikTok Live’s community is nearly twice as significant as Twitch’s.

    Sources indicate that that massive quantity has made TikTok Live a market leader across multiple streaming categories. Its gaming operation, however, is one of its strongest fortes, and rival platforms should be prepared to see more growth from their ByteDance-owned competitor.

    #8154. Breaking: Does The Affiliate Model Survive Checkout Inside AI Mode And Gemini? – Ask An SEO via @sejournal, @rollerblader

    📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1002 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Does The Affiliate Model Survive Checkout Inside AI Mode And Gemini? – Ask An SEO via @sejournal, @rollerblader

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1002 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This week’s Ask an SEO is about affiliate marketing, which is actually one of my favorite topics to cover.
    • It has been revealed that “With Google’s UCP and checkout happening inside Gemini and AI Mode, the shopper never clicks my link.
    • Great question, and yes, affiliate links still matter, so make sure you keep using them.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This week’s Ask an SEO is about affiliate marketing, which is actually one of my favorite topics to cover.

    It has been revealed that “With Google’s UCP and checkout happening inside Gemini and AI Mode, the shopper never clicks my link. Does the affiliate model survive this, and what should I be doing now?”.

    Great question, and yes, affiliate links still matter, so make sure you keep using them. It is similar to Shopify having the Google Direct Checkout UCP. That doesn’t mean you don’t need to keep your Shopify store, but you also want to make sure you are protected with multiple ways to monetize and that you work with brands that focus on more than just links.

    According to recent reports, this is why there is a question. If the person doesn’t make it to the link, do links matter? Yes, and this goes back to the history of links.

    The message displayed was a benefit to them, to let them know that if they logged in, they could add to their cart and check out later when they have more time vs. needing to do everything right now. When they logged in, we could sync up the sale with the original click, and the affiliate would get credit. This led to fingerprinting and many more advanced techniques the networks (like Buy.at at the time) began working on.

    There are also affiliate companies that show ads via streaming TV shows and track the IPs connected to the same connection to track affiliate sales back. They count the IPs against consumer data sent back to the network and get credit for the sale.

    Industry observers note that the reason I mention this is because, clicks don’t always matter, but they do add levels of tracking security for you. There is IP hashing, companies like TV Scientific and AudioHook are using alternative tracking methods, and vanity codes. Just make sure your vanity code doesn’t get leaked to coupon websites, browser extensions, and that AI doesn’t start showing them to traffic you didn’t refer.

    See also: When Attribution Looks More Precise Than The Data Behind It.

    Being afraid of Google taking the order and cutting your link out is a valid concern. But think about TikTok Shop, or retailer apps inside ChatGPT like Walmart’s, which keep the purchase on the platform. These cut your link out completely. The person may read your content then go to TikTok for a review and purchase there.

    You have big brands that allow third parties to sell on their website (i.e., marketplaces), and with some you don’t get commissions for those sales as they’re third party vendors. Your links matter and clicks tracked, but the conversion is not commissionable. In the case of systems like TikTok, use links on your website and upload content to their platform to make money with your vendors that are synced there. You control the situation, don’t stress over a single link on the website.

    In a recent development, for programs that allow third-party sales and don’t pay, select other programs. That is a choice you are knowingly making and you are knowingly sending your traffic there.

    See also: Getting Your Product Into ChatGPT Isn’t The Hard Part, Getting It Through Checkout Is.

    Recent findings suggest that another reason to not stop using affiliate links is that consumers do not trust AI. Keynote speakers at college graduations keep getting booed when they talk about it; younger generations are avoiding brands that use it for creating images; people are starting to engage less with AI ads on social media and convert less when the content and images are clearly AI on a website (blog posts, product pages, etc.).

    When AI is used, there’s no way to know if the store and ad are legit, or if they’re a third-party counterfeit produced overseas. Reviews are also being gamed. Consumers may not trust the AI Overview as much if quality doesn’t improve, and if they don’t like AI, they will instead scroll down to your content, where they can be exposed to your link.

    There is another layer to affiliate links mattering as well.

    AI Overviews cannot demonstrate a product or service. Yes, they can play a video, but Google search has done this for years. People, especially those who do not trust AI, will keep looking for human-created content before making the purchase. This is especially true for larger-ticket items like bikes, software, or computer systems, and demonstrations of video games before buying them. Think of parents who want to make sure it is age-appropriate, or someone who wants to see what the graphics and games are like from an actual gamer.

    This makes your affiliate links directly relevant, and in your advertising disclosure you can let them know that by clicking your link they are helping to support your business and not AI. This will resonate strongly with the anti-AI generations and shoppers. It is also required by the FTC and some international groups that you use advertising disclosures, so you might as well.

    See also: Only 28% Of Americans Trust AI Search – And That Gap Is Your SEO Opening.

    There is affordable technology from third parties like ThoughtMetrics (I have zero relationship with them, just a happy user) that shows all touchpoints in a customer journey (and repeat purchases for LTV). If you didn’t use your affiliate link, you won’t be in the running for credit or a commission. In another program, we reconcile at the end of the month and manually add anything that didn’t track. If that click didn’t happen, you would not be making as much money.

    Link clicks are always going to be an issue, but they are also still working and a first line of defense in your ability to get credit for your referrals. So yes, affiliate links and clicks still matter; there are just additional layers of protection available with more advanced tracking techniques.

    The $4 million Internet Invitational might become golf’s next substantial thing — or another bogey

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (545 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tubefilter

    • You could make the case that the most exciting golf event of 2026 involved a majority of amateurs and average joes — and the PGA wasn’t involved in the planning at all.
    • In a recent development, the driving force behind the Internet Invitational is Dave Portnoy, the provocateur and pizza lover who is best known as the owner of Barstool Sports.
    • The first Internet Invitational, organized in 2025, featured Dunkin as a sponsor and a $1 million prize.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    You could make the case that the most exciting golf event of 2026 involved a majority of amateurs and average joes — and the PGA wasn’t involved in the planning at all. I’m talking about the Internet Invitational, which recently wrapped up its second season by splitting a $4 million prize among the 16 members of the winning team.

    In a recent development, the driving force behind the Internet Invitational is Dave Portnoy, the provocateur and pizza lover who is best known as the owner of Barstool Sports. To create an event that could demonstrate the influence and appeal of the “YouTube golf” scene, Portnoy teamed up with Robby Berger and his Bob Does Sports brand.

    The first Internet Invitational, organized in 2025, featured Dunkin as a sponsor and a $1 million prize. The event was put on as a response to the PGA’s uneven investment in golf personalities. The Creator Classic that had signaled the PGA’s interest in digital partnerships was not held at TPC Sawgrass in 2026.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    Recent findings suggest that portnoy and Berger bet that they could outdo the PGA by fully embracing golf creators, and they doubled down in 2026, when they quadrupled the size of the Internet Invitational prize. “It’s all because of Dave, man,” Barstool Sports video editor Brendan Jones told Golf magazine. “Dave puts up all this money, and that changes people. That’s not good or bad — it just changes the way that people act, right? Dave’s massive thing with anything that we do at Barstool, it’s like, what are the stakes? Why do people care? How are we going to get anything out of them?”.

    In this case, people care because the proceedings were sillier, wackier, and more relatable than anything a PGA-sanctioned event could deliver. There were breakout stars like Paige Spiranac, wildly varied handicaps, and plenty of substance use during the tournament. And the fans loved it. Viewership hit 3.5 million during the first 24 hours and ballooned past 11 million views within a week.

    Recent findings suggest that “When you put the average Joe, who’s not a great golfer— that, to I think a lot of people, was riveting,” Berger told The Hollywood Reporter. “I mean, it’s kind of what Bob Does Sports was built off of.”.

    As exciting as the action may have been, the Internet Invitational wasn’t free from drama. Nelk member Salim Sirur‘s excessive drinking and Sam Heung Min‘s criticisms related to rules enforcement added controversy to the event’s conclusion. Given Portnoy’s controversial past and the indiscretions of some big names in the YouTube golf community (looking at you, Good Good), one wonders how long the Internet Invitational can sustain its positive momentum.

    Recent findings suggest that but the success of the tournament’s second iteration can’t be ignored. With the decline of LIV Golf and the presence of elite golfers on YouTube, there’s an opportunity for creators to build a viable alternative to the PGA Tour. To do that will take continued dedication from the people who made the Internet Invitational happen — and the golfers might want to cut down on the drinking, too.

    X offers to let creators chill–it’ll pay clippers for them, and give them a kickback too

    📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (617 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tubefilter

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Everyone is competing for creators’ attention lately–but X has been doing it for years.
    • Its latest bid: a clipping tool that pays both creators and clippers for reposting bite-sized pieces of longer content.
    • Industry observers note that “Grab your favorite moment from any video, add your take, and post it without leaving X,” the platform remarked in a organization post.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Everyone is competing for creators’ attention lately–but X has been doing it for years.

    Its latest bid: a clipping tool that pays both creators and clippers for reposting bite-sized pieces of longer content.

    Industry observers note that “Grab your favorite moment from any video, add your take, and post it without leaving X,” the platform remarked in a organization post. “Creators: every clip credits your original video and links back to it, so fresh viewers can find your work and keep watching. Clippers: you now have an easy, native way to share moments from your favorite creators directly on X. The best part? Both the original creator and the clipper can earn from views on the clip through Original Content Rewards. Everyone wins when great moments travel.”.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    Recent findings suggest that as you very likely know, clipping is the method du jour for creators to spread the word about their stuff. Sometimes fans clip for free/for the love of the game, but in many cases, creators pay people to clip their long-form videos and spread the shorter vids across platforms, hoping to drive more people to their full-length YouTube videos, Twitch streams, or podcast episodes.

    With its clipping tool–which, from the announcement video, looks like a basic trimmer with no real editing capabilities–X is telling creators, Hey, you don’t have to worry about hiring clippers for our platform. We’ll do it. That could be an upside for creators who don’t want to compensate people themselves.

    Grab your favorite moment from any video, add your take, and post it without leaving X.

    Creators: every clip credits your original video and links back to it, so newly introduced viewers can find your work and keep watching.

    Clippers: you now have an easy, native way to share moments from your favorite creators directly on X.

    The best part? Both the original creator and the clipper can earn from views on the clip through Original Content Rewards.

    Everyone wins when great moments travel. Clipping is one more step toward making X the best place to create, grow and earn.

    — Creators (@XCreators) November 9, 2026.

    Industry observers note that X, however, is offering a blanket green light. We’re not sure Elon Musk‘s platform will pay enough to tempt pro clippers, but it might appeal to aspiring clippers who seek a lower barrier to entry.

    Sources indicate that to be clear, though, we don’t know how much X will pay clippers. It notes they’ll earn money through its rewards program, which pays a set amount based on engagement metrics, but how will revenue be split between creator and clipper?

    Sources indicate that also worth noting: Not everyone can join the rewards program. X has to approve you first.

    Like we mentioned above, this is far from X’s first attempt to woo creators. Not long after Musk bought it, X (still called Twitter at that point…RIP) increased its max video length to 60 minutes, clearly hoping to pull some YouTubers. Musk himself personally appealed to MrBeast, who obliged and put a long-form video on X in early 2024; he did not seem overly impressed by the results, and has stayed firmly on YouTube, where he’s the biggest fish around.

    Other tweaks X has made include abolishing Twitter’s iconic character limit (thus attempting to challenge YouTube text posts as well as newsletter hubs like Substack), letting creators paywall posts, and adding a “completely redesigned livestreaming control room.” That last launch came with a promise to shell out a total of $1 million to streamers who went live on X.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Google made Gemini 4 Hydrogen the default model in AI Mode for all people worldwide, starting today.
    • In an X thread announcing the change, Robby Stein, VP of Product for Google Search, remarked Hydrogen is also “being used for your hardest questions in AI Overviews.” Google’s Search post claims the model is available globally in Search for all owners.
    • The switch came two days into the November core update, which was still rolling out as of 2:05 p.m.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Google made Gemini 4 Hydrogen the default model in AI Mode for all people worldwide, starting today. Sites that track how often AI Mode cites them now have a latest model to account for.

    In an X thread announcing the change, Robby Stein, VP of Product for Google Search, remarked Hydrogen is also “being used for your hardest questions in AI Overviews.” Google’s Search post claims the model is available globally in Search for all owners.

    The switch came two days into the November core update, which was still rolling out as of 2:05 p.m. ET today.

    The Search post says Hydrogen is able to handle multi-part inquiries, inquiries that contain typos, highly specific inquiries, and follow commands more thoroughly than previous versions of Search.

    In a recent development, the post from Search claims that Hydrogen also allows for better query fan-out. Query fan-out refers to how Search simultaneously executes multiple queries across each of the subtopics of an inquiry. According to the post, the result is what Google calls “connecting you to a broader range of helpful links than before,” and this includes websites which users may have never stumbled upon themselves. Stein’s thread says that the fan-out improvements result in showing more links to the web. Neither the post nor Stein’s thread provide counts for links or sites.

    The post references more visual aids in answers through use of images, structured responses, comparison tables and additional customized tools available to users; additionally, the answers provided will be more nuanced in all languages supported by AI Mode.

    Sources indicate that the last default change I covered was at I/O back in May when Gemini 3.5 Flash became the global default for AI Mode for everyone. Neither the Search post nor Stein’s post noted what Hydrogen replaced.

    Stein’s thread has Hydrogen handling the hardest AI Overview questions but doesn’t say which questions count as hardest or what answers the rest. The Search post doesn’t mention AI Overviews.

    Google made Gemini 3 the default model for AI Overviews globally in January. At the time, I noted that Google had described intends to send complex questions to Gemini 3 and simpler ones to faster models, and hadn’t mentioned whether that would apply to AI Overviews.

    Recent findings suggest that citation data you pull for AI Mode or AI Overviews this month now spans a model change on Nov. 12. The change applies to AI Mode’s default answers and to the hardest AI Overview questions.

    According to recent reports, nov. 12 falls inside the core update window, which began Nov. 10. Logging both dates lets you compare your tracking data before and after each one, rather than reading this month as a single change.

    It has been revealed that google’s claim that there are more links doesn’t include figures. You can check how it applies to your site by looking at the citation and referral numbers in your own reports.

    Industry observers note that although the Search Status Dashboard highlights that the November core enhancement is rolling out, its completion date will be logged as the second date, after Nov. 12.

    You should watch for an announcement from Google on which AI Overview questions are classified as hardest so you can see how much of your AI Overview tracking will reflect the change.

    #8149. Industry News: Student journalists are reporting more local news for real audiences. Their professors are exhausted.

    📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3491 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Niemanlab ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Student journalists are reporting more local news for real audiences. Their professors are exhausted.

    📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3491 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • We have sent a confirmation link to .
    • A newly introduced study finds that journalism school faculty — charged with putting more student work in front of non-student readers — often serve as a hidden infrastructure for local news.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    A newly introduced study finds that journalism school faculty — charged with putting more student work in front of non-student readers — often serve as a hidden infrastructure for local news. Burnout is a risk.

    If there’s one massive takeaway from the past two decades of local news struggle — the often perilous, occasionally brilliant transition from dominant newspapers to online media — perhaps it’s this: Passion alone isn’t enough.

    Industry observers note that A newspaper newsroom filled with committed editors and brilliant reporters still stares into the same headwinds as its more middling peers. The devotion of those leading a nonprofit outlet can mean little if revenue can’t keep the doors open. And even when the money is less important — when journalism is somewhat protected from the demands of the market — passion is still a finite resource, and it’s not always renewable.

    That truism came to mind when I was reading a recent article by Sima Bhowmik of the University of Vermont and Andrea Lorenz of Kent State. It looks at one specific corner of the contemporary news ecosystem: journalism schools that use their students to fill voids in local coverage.

    J-schools, after all, have faculties full of experience and students who need it. A few decades ago, an early-career journalist might have spent a few years covering city council meetings and school board budgets before moving up the chain to a bigger outlet. That path barely exists these days, and journalism programs know their students need the chance to do real work. What if these reporters-in-training could handle some of the local stories that the city’s daily no longer can?

    RELATED ARTICLEA “win-win” partnership brings a surge of reporting firepower to hyperlocal news outlets around BostonSarah ScireNovember 13, 2025RELATED ARTICLELen Downie: The teaching hospital model works, but it will require drastic changeLeonard Downie Jr.September 12, 2012If you happen to live near a college with a journalism program, you’ve probably seen this idea — often called the “teaching hospital” model — in action. Here in the Boston suburbs, many of the stories I read about my town are written by Boston University students. According to UVM’s Center for Community News, where Bhowmik is an assistant research professor, there were 282 such efforts as of 2025, producing local news inside 205 colleges and universities. Those numbers were up from 227 programs in 172 colleges the year before — a boom fueled by a surge in philanthropic funding for these partnerships.

    Bhowmik and Lorentz’s paper — published in Journalism & Mass Communication Educator — is the result of interviews with 118 faculty and staff at 101 of those colleges, and their major takeaway is one that will be familiar to many in local news: They’re exhausted.

    Participants repeatedly used phrases such as “at capacity,” “don’t have the bandwidth,” “not enough hours of the day,” and “it’s just a lot” to describe the workload. Several described long workdays and exhaustion, with one participant saying the amount of editing “just about kills me every semester.” At many institutions, faculty workload was intensified by staffing shortages, retirements, hiring freezes, and budget cuts. This left faculty with little time to provide the one-on-one coaching necessary to elevate student stories to publishable quality… “What’s happening in the academic ecosystem is so phenomenal, thanks to these really passionate founders on the faculty,” Bhowmik told me. “But the extra work they’re putting it isn’t always getting acknowledged within the system. A professor might be editing 10 or 20 stories a week, by students without much experience, on top of a full teaching load. There’s a lot of overwork and some dissatisfaction, even though they know how key the work is.” (See above: Passion alone isn’t enough.) Here’s how one faculty member described their situation: Think about it: Like, how many reporters does the average assigning editor at a mid-sized newspaper supervise? Half a dozen? So try, like, 20 of them, and each of them is writing for a different outlet maybe, which has its own set of deadlines and editor. And they’re all at varying skill levels, and broadly, they’re all pretty upcoming. Their copy requires a lot of work, their reporting often requires a lot of handholding. Another talked about the responsibility of getting student work up to the level a news outlet expects. You can’t just give a meh student story a C- and be done with it if a local editor is expecting publishable copy. It takes a lot of work to get student work up to the quality of professionally published work. And a lot of students start out with really good ideas, do some good reporting by the time they’re done in the semester, it needs work, and that tends to fall on the faculty person. And that’s a lot of work outside of uncompensated work…But bridging that gap between what a student produces at the end of a semester and what can actually be published is still a major gap that needs to be addressed. And aside from the editing work, faculty described the administrative burden of being the connective tissue joining two distinct worlds. Negotiating pitches, coordinating deadlines, dealing with revisions, shepherding copy flows — all of it with students who are juggling other courses, work-study jobs, and the life of college student — can be “difficult to sustain without administrative support, dedicated staff, or funding for editors,” they write. Just to save a few dozen proud Mizzou alums from emailing me: Yes, the “teaching hospital” model is not a new idea. The idea of giving journalism students real-world experience in public-facing outlets has been central to the Missouri Method for more than a century, and other major journalism schools have long done versions of this work. But Bhowmik notes that many of these new efforts are in smaller colleges with smaller journalism programs — places without the in-house infrastructure of a Columbia Missourian or KOMU, where media partnerships involve more ongoing negotiation. That can leave more of the pressure of sustainability on one or two overworked faculty members. As Bhowmik and Lorenz put it: …faculty labor is not incidental to the model; it is the hidden infrastructure that allows student work to move from classroom assignment to public-facing journalism. We argue that passion may help launch these programs, but passion alone is not a sustainable staffing model. If universities treat these initiatives as ordinary courses while expecting faculty to function simultaneously as instructors, editors, partnership managers, and newsroom supervisors, the model remains vulnerable to burnout and institutional instability. None of this, of course, is to say that these academic-publisher partnerships aren’t performing valuable roles in hundreds of communities. These programs have generated thousands of stories that otherwise might never have reached the public. But the sort of exhaustion Bhowmik and Lorenz describe reminds me a lot of what we saw in the first wave of local nonprofit news outlets in the late 2000s and early 2010s. Many of those were founded by idealistic journalists — often refugees from the local daily — who saw the opportunity to do something new and valuable for their communities. They put in long hours editing stories, selling ads, pitching foundations, and building audiences. And within a few years, a lot of them were burnt out, and their outlets suffered for it. In the decade-plus since, funders have gotten smarter about building institutional capacity — knowing that passion can only fuel so much. The world Bhowmik and Lorenz describe inside these journalism programs makes me think that department chairs and deans would be wise to consider a similar pivot to make these academic-publisher partnerships sustainable for the long term.

    Recent findings suggest that “What’s happening in the academic ecosystem is so phenomenal, thanks to these really passionate founders on the faculty,” Bhowmik told me. “But the extra work they’re putting it isn’t always getting acknowledged within the system. A professor might be editing 10 or 20 stories a week, by students without much experience, on top of a full teaching load. There’s a lot of overwork and some dissatisfaction, even though they know how notable the work is.”.

The idea of giving journalism students real-world experience in public-facing outlets has been central to the Missouri Method for more than a century, and other major journalism schools have long done versions of this work. But Bhowmik notes that many of these new efforts are in smaller colleges with smaller journalism programs — places without the in-house infrastructure of a Columbia Missourian or KOMU, where media partnerships involve more ongoing negotiation. That can leave more of the pressure of sustainability on one or two overworked faculty members. As Bhowmik and Lorenz put it: …faculty labor is not incidental to the model; it is the hidden infrastructure that allows student work to move from classroom assignment to public-facing journalism. We argue that passion may help launch these programs, but passion alone is not a sustainable staffing model. If universities treat these initiatives as ordinary courses while expecting faculty to function simultaneously as instructors, editors, partnership managers, and newsroom supervisors, the model remains vulnerable to burnout and institutional instability. None of this, of course, is to say that these academic-publisher partnerships aren’t performing valuable roles in hundreds of communities. These programs have generated thousands of stories that otherwise might never have reached the public. But the sort of exhaustion Bhowmik and Lorenz describe reminds me a lot of what we saw in the first wave of local nonprofit news outlets in the late 2000s and early 2010s. Many of those were founded by idealistic journalists — often refugees from the local daily — who saw the opportunity to do something new and valuable for their communities. They put in long hours editing stories, selling ads, pitching foundations, and building audiences. And within a few years, a lot of them were burnt out, and their outlets suffered for it. In the decade-plus since, funders have gotten smarter about building institutional capacity — knowing that passion can only fuel so much. The world Bhowmik and Lorenz describe inside these journalism programs makes me think that department chairs and deans would be wise to consider a similar pivot to make these academic-publisher partnerships sustainable for the long term.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Each week, we handpick a selection of stories to give you a snapshot of trends, updates, business moves, and more from around the creator industry.

    This week, a beloved couple has a new channel on YouTube, a vaunted exec has a new gig, and a much-memed creator is making bank (and hitting bookshelves).

    According to recent reports, welcome back to YouTube, Matthew and Stephanie Patrick. The man known as MatPat and his wife Stephanie haven’t shared many videos since they sold their Theorist brand nearly four years ago. But these crazy kids couldn’t stay offline forever, so they’re back with PatChat, a new channel featuring the couple’s conversations about internet culture. PatChat won’t upload nearly as frequently as the Theorist channels, and that’s ok. Let the Patricks live a little bit!

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    In a recent development, CNN panelist pushes back against Hasan Piker lawsuit. Piker argued that Scott Jennings defamed him by misconstruing statements that were clearly noted in jest. In response, Jennings’ lawyers argued that Piker did make those statements, sarcastic or not — so they are looking to have the $72.5 million lawsuit thrown out. If commentators can be held liable for sarcasm, the internet might be in real trouble.

    Industry observers note that whatCultureGaming rolls out new YouTube channel to pursue different types of content. After building a popular gaming hub, the WhatCulture team is trying something a little different with MegaWhat. The blueprint is to release original, personality-driven content that will give the WC team more creative freedom while still allowing them to feed the YouTube algorithm on their main channel.

    Industry observers note that anjali Sud leaves Tubi to take point at SiriusXM. As CEO of Tubi, Sud led the transformation of the Fox-owned service, which is now a major creator hub. (She was also CEO of Vimeo before that.) Now, Sud is becoming CEO of SiriusXM, giving her a chance to work her magic in the realm of digital radio. Mike Bidgoli will take over for Sud as the new top exec at Tubi HQ.

    In a recent development, elevate Communications brings in TikTok vet to expand creator operations. Elevate is elevating Sam Valentine, who previously connected TikTok with luxury fashion brands as the app’s Head of Digital, Social, and Creator Services. He’ll spearhead digital and social partnerships at Elevate, where he will work with clients that are eager to build creator programs in sectors like sports, entertainment, and healthcare.

    According to recent reports, meta brings in well-traveled exec to be the VP of its in-house content studio. After a long stint at NBC News, as well as stops at Goldman Sachs and BlackRock, Rich Latour has arrived at Meta. He will be put in charge of a studio that emphasizes Meta’s brand and highlights its impact across various communities and industries.

    Trisha Paytas has a book out (and she makes $100,000 a week on YouTube). While promoting her memoir Crying on the Kitchen Floor, which was recently published by Hachette, Paytas told Andy Cohen that her YouTube earnings can hit six figures during a good week. Oh, and she also has a upcoming dating show that is rolling out on Tubi. Slow down, Trish!

    In a recent development, hulu taps Tinx to revive The Circle (now with TikTok voting). The creator born Christina Najjar is taking the hosting role in a new version of the reality competition series that previously aired on Netflix. Tinx will have major shoes to fill replacing previous host Michelle Buteau, but with help from the voting audience, she can ensure that the Circle revival doesn’t miss a beat.

    According to recent reports, the first Clio Creator Awards will fete Dhar Mann. Actor Terry Crews will host as the notable advertising award ceremony expands to the realm of creator content. Dhar Mann, YouTube moralist and engineer of many a brand partnership, will receive an inaugural honorary award at the latest ceremony.

    Recent findings suggest that kind works with a Savannah Banana to sell a TikTok-exclusive foodstuff. Baseball player Jackson Olson has amassed a significant TikTok following after getting a roster spot on the best-known “Banana Ball” team. Olson is now parlaying his influence to sell a fresh type of Kind bar that celebrates World Kindness Day — and is only available for purchase via TikTok Shop.

    Sources indicate that GTA VI codes are flying around on Kick and Twitch ahead of launch day. All of the major platforms want creators to play GTA VI on their services once the game launches, and giving out free copies is a good way to engender that loyalty. At this point, I’m wondering if GTA VI will be able to live up to its immersurable hype, or if viewers will tire of it after it because the main topic of conversation everywhere.

    Sources indicate that barbie and Hot Wheels are on TikTok Shop this holiday season. TikTok continues to onboard name brands as it prepares for its most lucrative holiday season shopping spree. So if someone on your list has their eyes on some Mattel products, deals on those items will be hitting TikTok Shop in no time.

    Sources indicate that celebs are consenting to having their voices cloned for AI ads. Ogilvy and CAA have teamed up for a partnership that will make a-list talent more accessible for advertisers and agencies that rely on generative AI pipelines. George Clooney is a CAA client, but if he goes along with this, I’m going to have no choice but to start calling him George Cloney.

    Shaq is good at dunking, but can he hide in plain sight? The Big Diesel has a new gig: An ABC series that will ask contestants to hide the 7’1″ goliath in plain sight. I think, to be fair, the contestants should get to start by hiding Kevin Hart before working their way up to Shaq.

    Another impulse spending deterrent is taking off in China. The WeChat mini-app dubbed ‘Wallet, Please Wait’ lets customers decide whether strangers will be able to hold off on substantial purchases. I would be more interested in app that lets me vote on whether a stranger should be able to tell a stranger how to spend their money.

    Recent findings suggest that canada’s proposed federal budget includes some good news for local journalism. The federal government is extending its journalism tax credit by $501 million, expanding eligibility to audio and audiovisual news organizations, and renewing the Local Journalism Initiative, which supports journalism in underserved communities.

    RELATED ARTICLEIn Canada, a government program to support local news tries to determine who’s most deservingSarah ScireMay 8, 2020Sarah wrote about the Local Journalism Initiative in its early days. A study earlier this year found that reporters paid with LJI funding believed they maintained their roles as watchdogs and wrote balanced stories, though two-thirds of interviewees were concerned about the perception of a conflict of interest. A growing number of journalists say the benefits of government subsidies for journalism outweigh the drawbacks.

    A recent report in The Tyee suggests government support is essential to the survival of local media in Canada. (The Tyee has received support from the Local Journalism Initiative.).

    “It’s either this or death, frankly,” LJI program director and Canadian Association of Journalists president Brent Jolly told The Tyee. “It’s not about local news editors getting their marching orders from the Prime Minister’s Office like some conspiracy theorists want you to think. It’s about infrastructure.”.

    Lisa Sygutek, publisher of the Crowsnest Pass Herald in Alberta, credited the LJI with growing the publication from “a 16-page paper to a 24-page paper.”.

    Read more in The Tyee’s look at Canadian local news here.

    Latest Update: Google Ads Rolls Out Latest Invalid Traffic Overview Card via @sejournal, @brookeosmundson

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (566 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Google Ads is rolling out a fresh Invalid Traffic Overview Card that demonstrates advertisers how much invalid activity its systems filter before billing, along with credits issued after billing.
    • Until now, advertisers had to look across campaign reports and monthly billing statements to find that information.
    • Ginny Marvin, Google Ads Liaison, announced the rollout on LinkedIn and shared more details in the latest Ads Decoded newsletter.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Google Ads is rolling out a fresh Invalid Traffic Overview Card that demonstrates advertisers how much invalid activity its systems filter before billing, along with credits issued after billing.

    Until now, advertisers had to look across campaign reports and monthly billing statements to find that information. The upcoming card brings those figures into one view, with additional reporting available by day and campaign.

    Ginny Marvin, Google Ads Liaison, announced the rollout on LinkedIn and shared more details in the latest Ads Decoded newsletter.

    The global rollout began this week, and the feature is also available in Search Ads 360 for Google Ads accounts.

    Advertisers can find the newly introduced card on the Google Ads Overview page, under the Campaigns tab.

    Google has long used automated systems and manual reviews to filter invalid ad interactions, including bot activity, accidental clicks, and attempts to artificially inflate traffic.

    Most of that activity is caught before billing, so advertisers aren’t charged for those interactions.

    The new card includes three reporting areas:.

    Clicking “View details” opens a daily trend chart and campaign table. Advertisers can also access the monthly invoices where credits were applied.

    The estimated savings figure is the main addition to this information. Advertisers could already review invalid click metrics, but those reports didn’t show the estimated dollar amount Google had prevented from being charged.

    According to Marvin, Google’s systems catch the majority of invalid traffic before it reaches an advertiser’s invoice.

    Google Ads locks standard campaign metrics at month-end to match billing records. If Google detects more invalid traffic after that, any credits issued won’t change the Cost or CPA figures in the main Campaigns table.

    Advertisers who want to see those adjustments reflected in their performance metrics can use the Invalid Activity Credit: Search & PMax report.

    Available in Report editor, it includes 10 columns, such as Adjusted cost and Adjusted cost / conv. Credits are attributed to the dates the ads originally ran, even when Google issued them later.

    This gives advertisers a way to review Search and Performance Max costs with post-billing invalid activity credits factored in, without relying solely on the standard Campaigns table.

    The campaign-level breakdowns should make it easier to see where Google is filtering invalid activity, although the estimated savings figures will need some context.

    It has been revealed that A campaign with significantly more spend could show higher estimated savings simply because it’s generating more traffic. Comparing those dollar amounts alone won’t necessarily tell advertisers which campaigns have greater traffic quality concerns.

    Industry observers note that there’s also a limit to what the numbers can tell us. The card reflects activity Google’s systems have identified as invalid, but it doesn’t establish how much fraudulent traffic may have gone undetected.

    For lead generation accounts, invalid traffic reporting won’t necessarily explain why fake or low-quality leads are continuing to come in.

    Marvin addressed this in the Ads Decoded newsletter: Google’s systems can filter invalid ad interactions, but bad leads can still come from legitimate clicks or submissions that never originated from an ad.

    An account could have relatively little invalid traffic reported in Google Ads and still struggle with lead quality. Advertisers dealing with those challenges will need to compare the reporting against their CRM data rather than assuming Google’s invalid traffic figures tell the whole story.

    Featured image: Primakov (screenshot from Google Ads Decoded Newsletter) / Shutterstock.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: What Reddit Reviews Reveals About Your Products via @sejournal, @brentcsutoras

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (779 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If Reddit’s taught us anything over the last five years, it’s that people really do care about validating the assumptions that they’re making along their journey.
    • People want to see the questions, complaints, and comparisons that come up when they are deciding what to buy.
    • 10, Reddit confirmed the Reviews test with summaries of product conversations, themes about what people like and dislike, commonly compared products, and comments that lead back to their original discussions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If Reddit’s taught us anything over the last five years, it’s that people really do care about validating the assumptions that they’re making along their journey. They really want to hear from real users who have actually used something or tried something, what their experience was, even if they don’t know who those users are.

    People want to see the questions, complaints, and comparisons that come up when they are deciding what to buy. Reddit Reviews brings those conversations together on one page, giving people another way to find those experiences and click through to the original discussions.

    On Nov. 10, Reddit confirmed the Reviews test with summaries of product conversations, themes about what people like and dislike, commonly compared products, and comments that lead back to their original discussions. Reddit says the initial rollout will reach U.S. users in English on web, iOS, and Android. It covers about 10,000 products across electronics, health and beauty, home and garden, and fashion and apparel. It plans to add products and categories and expand beyond the U.S. during 2027.

    According to recent reports, that can make research easier to inspect. A shopper can move from a summary to the comment, see the community where it appeared, and follow the details that matter to them. Reddit notes some pages will also include images, prices, and purchase links supplied through brand and retailer catalogs. Those details are worth checking, especially when a page’s price or product information does not match the retailer’s current listing.

    See also: Why Your Product Feed Is An SEO Asset (And Who Should Own It).

    Reddit Reviews can help surface patterns, but there are limitations explained in the page FAQs. A verified purchase is not required; Reddit does not confirm that someone bought or used a product, and AI can miss context. The sentiment display gives a quick view of included conversations, while the detailed comments show what went into it. A review cannot represent every customer or provide an exact percentage.

    Before drawing a conclusion from a review about your brand, I would ask: Is the same complaint coming up in different threads? Is the summary missing a condition that changes the recommendation? Are people comparing your product with a competitor for a reason your team has not been tracking? That context is where the useful research is.

    It has been revealed that A moderator’s concern was raised in the launch discussion about figuring out whether product recommendations come from people with firsthand experience. One commenter said verifying whether book recommendations came from people who had read the books was “already a gigantic challenge.” The moderator’s comment does not measure how Reddit Reviews performs, but it does point to a real trust question for any system summarizing community advice.

    See also: The Review Gap: Finding Client Opportunities In Competitor Feedback.

    According to recent reports, I would treat these review pages as another place for brands to listen. Check whether a review exists for the products and categories you care about, compare its summary with the source comments, note the products people consider alongside yours, and check whether the merchant information is current. Then compare recurring questions and objections with what support, product, and research teams already hear.

    That can tell you where expectations and experience diverge. It cannot tell you what all customers think, how many people bought, or whether Reviews changed a purchase. Reddit claims the initial pages draw from eligible conversations and that businesses cannot pay for product inclusion.

    There is no conversion result to claim yet. So, watch how review pages appear in Reddit search, and check the referral and conversion data available on your own site before drawing conclusions about sales.

    This is also a reason to make the community conversations themselves better. Give people room to ask real questions, share tradeoffs, and explain what did or did not work. If your team participates, be clear about who you are and help where you are welcome. My earlier piece on Reddit and the purchase journey makes the same point: People use Reddit to validate a decision, and the experience behind the recommendation is what gives that conversation value.

    This is why we work with all of our clients to make sure that we’re building a community for them where their users have a place to come and share and talk about their products and their experiences.

    According to recent reports, when you spot a recurring product problem or a comparison buyers keep making, take it back to the team that can do something with it. That is the kind of information I think marketers can actually use.

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    It has been revealed that we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries mentioned they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary.

    In my Nieman Lab prediction this time last year, I wrote that “in 2026, the use of AI as an information gateway will only rise further.”.

    It has been revealed that as it turns out, I was right. In latest research that I published with my colleagues Rasmus Kleis Nielsen and Richard Fletcher, one of our many findings is that generative AI systems are becoming ever more significant information intermediaries, both when intentionally used and when incidentally encountered.

    For our upcoming report, “Generative AI and News Report 2026: From Standalone Tools to Information Infrastructure,”  we surveyed audiences across nine countries, including the United States, on their use of AI in their everyday lives, what they think its impact will be on different sectors of society, and what they think about its use in news and journalism specifically. I obviously think you should read the whole report, but here are some of the major takeaways.

    According to recent reports, the use of standalone conversational AI systems such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini continues to grow rapidly, with 51% of respondents across the six countries where we have past data saying they now use AI weekly (49% in the U.S.). That’s a faster spread, at least in the U.S., than smartphones or the internet saw.

    It has been revealed that many people also encounter AI through “incidental” AI exposure in the AI-infused services and platforms they’re already using. Search engines such as Google and Bing are key drivers: 57% of respondents across countries mentioned they saw or engaged with AI-generated answers or summaries in the last week. News media, too, drives AI exposure. An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries said they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary.

    Sources indicate that despite all the talk about AI agents, we find that, so far, they haven’t broken into the mainstream. The vast majority of respondents across all nine countries (67%) noted they had not used an AI agent in the last week. Fourteen percent used one for a real task and 13% tried one just to experiment.

    According to recent reports, our data provides solid evidence that a broader transformation of the information environment is afoot. Conversational AI systems have arrived as information intermediaries. Trust is not the main reason people use them. Instead, people see conversational AI systems as friction-reducing machines that get them information more rapidly.

    “Getting information” continues to be the most common use case. Thirty-eight percent of respondents across countries (35% in the U.S.) remarked they had used generative AI for getting information in the last week, up from 24% in 2025 and 11% in 2024.

    It has been revealed that we looked more closely at what people do when they say they use AI for getting information. Across the six countries we’ve surveyed since 2024, we primarily see a mixture of search-equivalent behaviors like “researching a topic” (24%) or “answering factual questions” (18%). People are also increasingly turning to AI for advice (20%).

    Industry observers note that using AI directly for news, meanwhile, remains a niche activity, as we demonstrated in the Digital News Report earlier this year. But that use is increasing: 9% of respondents across our six core countries say they use AI for news, up from 6% in 2025 and 3% in 2024.

    In a recent development, many people don’t hold clear or strong views about whether AI output is trustworthy. But people who do rely on it for information trust it. Across the nine countries, 75% of those who used AI to answer factual questions trusted the answers, as did 76% of those who used it for advice and 72% of those who used it for news. Only small minorities expressed distrust.

    At the same time, trust and trustworthiness do not, at this stage, seem to be central to why people rely on AI systems. Instead, people tend to see these systems as friction-reducing machines. The convenience of getting a faster and easier answer was chosen by 64% as the main reason they use AI, followed by the interactivity afforded by natural language interfaces (56%). Only a minority (21%) said they use AI because they get more reliable information from it than from other sources.

    As AI systems become widely used, their growing popularity is likely to affect the use of legacy content offerings and digital platforms and services. As my coauthor Rasmus Kleis Nielsen put it on LinkedIn, rapid growth in AI use isn’t just eating into what news sites have to offer. It’s eating into search, too — with people who use AI for information saying they use not just news, but search engines less, too, and by a wider margin. Challenging times may be ahead not just for news publishers, but also for the incumbent digital giants previously seen as unassailable.

    According to recent reports, as in previous years, we wanted to know what people think of AI’s use in journalism and news. We find that people’s attitudes here are remarkably entrenched and negative — though they also haven’t worsened significantly.

    People across countries remain uncomfortable with the use of AI in the newsroom, especially with the idea of news being made entirely or primarily with AI. On average across nine countries, just 12% of respondents say they are very or somewhat comfortable with news made entirely by AI. That figure rises to 19% if there is some human oversight. This has hardly changed since 2024, and the gap between human- and AI-made news appears in every country we surveyed.

    It has been revealed that this also remains true regardless of whether it is breaking news or reporting. People are even more uncomfortable with AI being used for commentary or opinion — formats where the expectation that a human should share their view is strongest.

    Our findings raise several important questions for journalists and publishers navigating the rise of generative AI.

    It has been revealed that first, generative AI is becoming an increasingly significant information intermediaries, with a number of possible knock-on effects on news. People are using AI to reduce friction by getting “good enough” outputs for some information needs — and skipping legacy platforms, established publishers, and the time and effort it takes to find the best available information. Discovery, brand attribution, data collection, and monetization all grow more challenging for publishers in this context.

    In a recent development, second, even though use continues to grow, the public remains skeptical of AI in news. This isn’t just a challenge for newsrooms’ internal adoption. It also highlights that publishers using AI need to communicate to audiences what’s in it for them.

    Recent findings suggest that third, beyond news, our findings speak to wider debates about AI’s societal impact. As in other studies on this topic, we find that uptake of AI is uneven. Weekly use is more common among people in professional occupations than those in entry-level or service occupations. Most people rely on free — usually less advanced — AI models.

    The differences in how — not just whether — people use AI may become a new dividing line. As AI researcher and OpenAI cofounder Andrej Karpathy recently argued, there is a widening “gap in shared understanding of LLM capability,” with most people not seeing what has left those inside AI firms both excited and worried.

    Expectations of what AI will do differ far more between daily people and people who have never used it than between any other groups in our survey. When two groups form very different views of the same technology because they have such different starting points, there will likely be consequences.

    According to recent reports, this doesn’t matter just for people’s individual choices around whether and how to make use of AI in their own lives. It also matters where AI is adopted and governed through collective decisions — in public services, for example — that apply to those who do not use it.

    Felix Simon is the research fellow in AI, information, and news at the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism and a research associate at the Oxford Internet Institute (OII) at the University of Oxford.

    When the Covid-19 pandemic normalized remote work, a second trend caught on: shutting down physical newsrooms.

    Recent findings suggest that A report from Northwestern University’s Local News Initiative, published Tuesday, looks at the cultural losses that news outlets face when their staff stops working together under one roof. Here’s LNI contributor and Columbia College Chicago journalism professor Jackie Spinner:.

    As pandemic-era safeguards that necessitated working from home waned, some have championed the technological advances that allow many journalists to report, edit and publish from basically anywhere with stable Internet access. But the cost savings from a smaller or nonexistent physical presence isn’t the only consideration. Less clear-cut is the impact on the elements of journalism that never appear on budgets, such as the training absorbed from looking over someone’s shoulder or the institutional knowledge gained and passed by working in proximity to others over time.

    During the pandemic, several news outlets downsized their offices — from city high-rises to co-working spaces — due to financial constraints and new hybrid work schedules.

    In a recent development, on Tuesday, I spent time looking for the local news outlets that have foregone or reduced office space and opted for primarily remote work in recent years. Here are some:.
