    #8142. Industry News: 72% Of Worker’s Say Their AI Skills Are Untested – Here’s How PPC Managers Prove Theirs via @sejournal, @gregjarboe

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1954 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: 72% Of Worker’s Say Their AI Skills Are Untested – Here’s How PPC Managers Prove Theirs via @sejournal, @gregjarboe

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1954 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, if you manage Google Ads accounts, being “good” with AI is expected, but employers probably never checked (or didn’t know how to check) if you are.
    • New research from CodeSignal surveyed 1,000 U.S.
    • Industry observers note that I sent CodeSignal 15 questions about how solid those numbers are and what practitioners should do about them.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, if you manage Google Ads accounts, being “good” with AI is expected, but employers probably never checked (or didn’t know how to check) if you are. Being able to show your judgment is a career must if you can, and a risk if you can’t.

    New research from CodeSignal surveyed 1,000 U.S. employees and 1,000 U.S. people managers about AI readiness, and two numbers sit side by side in the results. 72% of workers surveyed say their AI skills have never been formally evaluated, yet 69% of managers call AI ability a major or moderate factor in hiring. Indicating that employers are hiring for a skill they mostly don’t measure.

    Industry observers note that I sent CodeSignal 15 questions about how solid those numbers are and what practitioners should do about them. The written answers were more candid than I expected, including on the obvious conflict of interest of an assessment vendor concluding that nobody assesses anything. Here’s what holds up, what needs a footnote, and what it means for people who run paid search for a living.

    Recent findings suggest that start with what this survey is and isn’t. CodeSignal commissioned two online surveys through Pollfish in September 2026, and both samples were entirely U.S.-based. The company defined knowledge workers by the work they do rather than by job title, meaning people whose jobs run mainly on computers and digital tools. It also didn’t screen out people who skip AI. 12% noted they never use it at work.

    Sources indicate that codeSignal reports that roles where AI use is required or expected “jumped 78%.” I asked whether that meant percentage points. It doesn’t. It’s a relative increase, self-reported by employees about their own roles, measured across each person’s time in their current job. When respondents started those jobs, 9.4% mentioned AI use was required or expected of them. Today, 16.7% say so.

    Recent findings suggest that that’s nearly double. It’s also fewer than one in five.

    Industry observers note that paid search people are probably well past that curve already, since automated bidding has been Google’s default recommendation for years. So, the useful question for our field is whether anyone can tell who is using AI well.

    See also: From T-Shaped To M-Shaped: The PPC Career Evolution Nobody Is Talking About.

    62% of employees told CodeSignal they received employer training on how to use AI at work. Only 35% said employer training is where they built the AI skills they actually use.

    It has been revealed that I asked whether most of that training simply wasn’t about AI, or whether workers weren’t counting it. CodeSignal noted neither. The training was specifically about using AI at work, and the firm reads the gap as a sign that it wasn’t substantial or specific enough to apply on the job.

    Sources indicate that the follow-up number is worse. Only about one in four trained workers remarked they can apply most or all of their employer’s AI training. The other 74% apply some, very little, or none of it. Run that against the full sample and roughly 46% of all workers got AI training they can’t fully use. When CodeSignal asked what gets in the way, employees named lack of time, training that doesn’t fit their role, and lack of access to relevant training.

    So, where are people learning? The question allowed multiple answers, which is why the figures don’t add up to 100. Free resources people found on their own led at 46%, followed by trial and error on the job at 39%, and employer training at 35%. Colleagues came in at 22%, and courses people paid for themselves at 12%.

    Tigran Sloyan, CodeSignal’s co-founder and CEO, said, “Companies are buying AI courses or building their own, but if most workers are going elsewhere to learn, you have to wonder if that training is actually helping.”.

    According to recent reports, paid search has worked this way for a long time. Plenty of PPC managers learned bidding by watching their own accounts and reading practitioners on LinkedIn and X. What has changed is that the thing they now learn by trial and error is the ad platform’s own AI, and each error is paid for out of a client’s budget.

    72% of workers say their AI skills have never been formally evaluated, but 66% say the same about their skills in general. That’s a six-point gap.

    I asked CodeSignal whether the real story is that companies don’t assess much of anything, and AI just makes that visible. The answer began with “Yes, exactly.” Companies have long made people decisions on proxies such as resumes, job titles, tenure, and manager impressions. CodeSignal’s argument is that those were always weak signals, and they get costly when roles shift in months. More than six in ten managers in the survey said they make people decisions based on assumptions rather than reliable data.

    This bothers me more in paid media than almost anywhere else. We measure campaigns to the decimal point. We argue about attribution windows, incrementality tests, and conversion lag. Then we judge the people running those campaigns with a once-a-year “meets expectations.” For a discipline built on measurement, that’s a strange double standard, and AI is making it harder to defend.

    CodeSignal says the hiring side already shows the strain. When AI fluency is a criterion nobody has measured, people get judged on what’s easy to see, such as who is most visible or sounds most confident, instead of on the quality of their work.

    Recent findings suggest that anyone who has sat through an agency pitch knows how that plays out. The person who notes the automation will figure it out can sound more fluent than the person who spent the afternoon reading search terms and adding negatives. Only one of them is protecting the budget.

    “A resume is a story someone tells about their skills,” Sloyan remarked. “The work is the proof. Right now, most companies are making their biggest decisions about people based on the story.”.

    See also: PPC Automation Layering: How Smart Advertisers Combine Automation With Strategy.

    I asked CodeSignal to separate “AI fluency” from AI literacy and prompt-writing, because those terms get used as if they were the same thing. The organization drew the lines this way. Literacy means understanding what AI is. Prompt-writing is a tactic. Fluency means knowing what to delegate to AI, checking and correcting its output, and recognizing when not to use it at all.

    That is the best short job description for a modern PPC manager I’ve read this year.

    Industry observers note that map it onto a Google Ads account, and each part becomes something you can point to. Delegation is deciding which campaigns get Smart Bidding, which conversion actions you feed it, and what budget it gets to learn on. Checking is reading the search terms, placements, and automatically created assets that the system produces, then correcting what’s wrong. Knowing when not to use AI is the judgment call that rarely highlights up in a dashboard. That might mean holding back a campaign with too little conversion data, or keeping a human hand on ad copy in a regulated category.

    It has been revealed that none of that is visible in a certificate. All of it is visible in the account.

    See also: The Conversion Setup Errors That Break Smart Bidding.

    I also asked CodeSignal to critique its own product category. What can a timed, simulated assessment not tell you about whether someone uses AI well on the job? The firm answered that an assessment is only as useful as what it was designed and validated to measure. To understand how someone performs over time, it stated, you need to look at their actual work.

    In a recent development, that answer applies just as well to the credential most PPC people already hold. Google’s AI-Powered Performance Ads Certification on Skillshop is free, and third-party study guides describe it as a timed, 50-question exam. It’s worth taking, because it teaches how Google wants its AI campaign types used. But it’s written by the platform whose recommendations a good PPC manager sometimes overrides. Passing it shows you know Google’s playbook. It can’t show the afternoon you decided not to follow it, or what happened to cost per acquisition when you didn’t.

    In a recent development, then there’s the conflict of interest. CodeSignal sells assessments, and its survey concludes that skills aren’t being assessed. I asked how readers should weigh that, and what finding cut against its business.

    The company stated its interest in skills is the reason it commissioned the study. Then it volunteered a number that does cut the other way. 82% of employees said their manager understands their skills very or somewhat well. CodeSignal called that knowledge real and valuable. Its caveat is that the knowledge is informal, varies from manager to manager, doesn’t follow people when they change teams, and can’t be compared across a company.

    Agency people will recognize that last part. When an account manager moves to another client team, everything their old boss knew about their judgment usually stays behind.

    I give CodeSignal credit for offering up the 82%. I’d still want to see the full questionnaire before treating any of these figures as settled, and the firm’s launch announcement for its Agentic Skills Intelligence product doesn’t describe the survey method at all. The details above came from its answers to my questions.

    CodeSignal’s advice to individual workers was blunt. Saying you use AI for everything doesn’t prove much. Fluency is being able to explain exactly how you use it and, just as important, when you don’t. For a PPC manager, that turns into a short routine.

    If you lead a PPC team or run an agency, the firm’s advice for a 200-person business with no assessment budget translates well. Start with managers, since most employees think their managers already understand their skills. Then give those managers something more concrete than “meets expectations” by writing down what good AI use looks like for each role on the team. A specialist’s standard might be catching irrelevant search terms within a week. A strategist’s might be deciding when a client’s conversion tracking is clean enough to move to value-based bidding.

    Next, look at real account work before training and again after it. A sample of a few accounts per person is enough to see whether anything changed.

    Find your self-taught experts, too. With 46% of workers learning from free resources on their own, someone on your team has probably already worked out what the automation gets wrong. Have them show everyone else.

    Sources indicate that finally, build training around the work people do every week and give them time to practice. Lack of time was the obstacle employees named first. Track whether people use what they learned, not whether they finished the course. A Skillshop badge is a completion metric, and you’d never let a client judge a campaign on impressions alone.

    Sloyan’s version of this is worth quoting. “Training only works when it’s built around the job someone actually does.”.

    Recent findings suggest that my view is that PPC managers have an advantage most knowledge workers in this survey don’t. Our work already leaves a record. Every bid strategy change, every negative keyword, and every recommendation we dismissed is logged somewhere, with performance data attached.

    Sources indicate that most of us treat that record as housekeeping. The managers who turn it into evidence of judgment are the ones who will get promoted while their employers are still figuring out how to measure AI skills at all.

    Everyone else will be telling a story.

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    In a recent development, we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    The newly introduced budget would make a local reporting program permanent and extend a 35% tax credit on newsroom salaries. The support makes “a massive, massive difference.”.

    A Canadian program to place local reporters in underserved communities has lived from renewal to renewal. Publishers who relied on the Local Journalism Initiative couldn’t be sure whether the money would be there again.

    That changed last week when Canada proposed a federal budget that would make the Local Journalism Initiative permanent. The 2026 budget would increase LJI funding to $134 million over four years with $41 million in annual ongoing funding after that. (Figures are, naturally, in Canadian dollars.) For the budget to be finalized, it must pass Parliament. With Prime Minister Mark Carney’s party in the majority, it’s expected to.

    Expanding the LJI is not even the biggest piece of federal help for newsrooms, according to Paul Deegan, president and CEO of the news industry advocacy group News Media Canada. The same budget extends a 35% tax credit on newsroom salaries through 2028 and opens it to radio and television newsrooms for the first time. The tax credit will cost $501 million over the next five years, according to the budget. Thanks to the Online News Act, Canadian newsrooms also get funding from Google. And then there’s Canadian investment in public media; the 2026 budget added $300 million over two years to CBC/Radio-Canada “to strengthen its capacity to meet the evolving needs of Canadians across the country.”.

    I asked Deegan: How did Canadian publishers secure so much federal funding for news?

    Sources indicate that “We have a government that ‘gets it,’” Deegan said. “They see what Big Tech monopolists have done to local news. They know the labor tax credit is the leading driver of maintaining and growing newsroom headcount.”.

    RELATED ARTICLECalifornia’s significant local news bill becomes lawLaura Hazard OwenOctober 1, 2026There have been similar proposals and experiments in the United States, including a upcoming tax credit in California. But Canada is much further down the road. The country can offer lessons on what it looks like when a federal government commits to supporting journalism.

    The labor tax credit refunds 35% of a newsroom employee’s salary, up to $29,750 per journalist per year. The percentage had been scheduled to fall to 25% at the end of 2026.

    “In terms of employing the [largest] number of journalists and keeping newsroom employment stability, the labor tax credit is number one,” Deegan said.

    There’s also the Online News Act which has brought in $100 million of Google money annually. Of that amount, $63 million is set aside for news publishers. (Meta blocked news on Facebook and Instagram in Canada rather than pay under the Online News Act.) Publishers receive around $17,000 per journalist per year.

    “That’s about $47,000 per journalist per year from those two measures,” Deegan said. “That just makes a massive, massive difference.”.

    It has been revealed that in the U.S., some ideas for funding local journalism have been criticized as helping large chain newspapers — including chains that have hollowed out local newsrooms for years. Deegan — whose news industry group counts Postmedia and Torstar as members — acknowledged that the largest share of tax credit dollars goes to the largest employers.

    But News Media Canada also represents small and digital-only publications, and Deegan noted the smallest Canadian outlets face another problem. To qualify for the tax credit, an organization must produce original news content and regularly employ at least two journalists “at arm’s length” from its owners. An advisory board found the second rule excludes small “mom-and-pop” newsrooms.

    Sources indicate that the Local Journalism Initiative is a more targeted program than the tax credit. Launched in 2019, it was designed to support local and community news in underserved areas. The LJI program supports about 470 reporting positions in roughly 1,000 communities across Canada.

    Even generous government subsidies have not stopped losses in local news completely. But early results showed the LJI increased reporting capacity and local news in “news poverty” communities with limited local news offerings. The same evaluation identified reaching “news deserts” — communities with no existing local news outlets — and Indigenous communities as obstacles.

    Recent findings suggest that “Since LJI is demand driven, funding allocation across the country varies and gaps remain in some areas, such as news deserts,” the report reads. Later, the report notes that allowing news startups “could better support attraction and retainment of journalists” in the neediest communities.

    Many of the newsrooms receiving the LJI funding are small. Deegan described family-owned weekly newspapers with circulations as low as 800. Funding provides a local journalist to report on “cops, courts, city hall, and the school board.”.

    “Without those LJI journalists in some of those communities, those things simply wouldn’t be covered,” he remarked.

    Recent findings suggest that some underserved communities, particularly in northern Canada, struggle to hire reporters given high living costs and remote locations. “Even with the grant, it’s just hard to recruit and find people,” Deegan noted.

    According to recent reports, deegan points to two factors that have made Canada’s federal funding for news work. The first is distance. Publishers get LJI money from one of three administrator organizations: News Media Canada, Community Radio Fund of Canada, or the Consortium of Official Language Minority Community Media. These organizations — not the government itself — administer the funds and an independent board advises on who qualifies for the tax credit.

    “To avoid perceptions of conflict of interest, the government ensured that third parties adjudicate who receives local journalism initiative reporters and who is eligible for the labor tax credit,” Deegan said.

    The second factor applies to the Online News Act and, more generally, to Canadian politics.

    Industry observers note that “When it comes to holding those platforms to account, one of the reasons we have been successful is that we have a ban [on] corporate political financing at the federal level in Canada,” Deegan stated. “These companies sprinkle goodies around to friendly academics, think tanks, and other useful idiots to do some of their bidding, but our government sees through that nonsense.”.

    Tech Report: Google Lets Target Frequency Pair Non-Skippable Ads With Shorts via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (825 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Google has revised its help page on Target frequency campaigns, which says advertisers may now use non-skippable in-stream ads with Shorts and in-feed ads within the same campaign.
    • On this page, advertisers are allowed to “mix any combination of skippable in-stream, non-skippable in-stream (up to 20s), bumper, In-feed, and Shorts ads” in a campaign.
    • There is no date referenced on the page.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Google has revised its help page on Target frequency campaigns, which says advertisers may now use non-skippable in-stream ads with Shorts and in-feed ads within the same campaign.

    On this page, advertisers are allowed to “mix any combination of skippable in-stream, non-skippable in-stream (up to 20s), bumper, In-feed, and Shorts ads” in a campaign.

    There is no date referenced on the page. However, the capture by the Internet Archive from Oct. 14 still highlights the earlier rule: “At the moment, non-skippable ads can’t be combined with In-feed or Shorts ads in Target Frequency campaigns.” Prior to the update, advertisers who were using the Target frequency option had to choose whether to use non-skippable ads or the Shorts and in-feed ad placements options.

    Campaigns limited to in-stream formats can’t add in-feed or Shorts, which Google’s page warns “may result in less reach or a higher cost-per-thousand impressions (CPM)” for those campaigns.

    In a recent development, in the Oct. 14 version of the Target frequency page, selecting non-skippable ads would “automatically disable In-feed and Shorts ads” in the campaign. The current setup steps say to select the Non-skippable in-stream checkbox to include those ads “alongside your selected formats” in a multi-format campaign.

    The page’s “up to 20s” label for non-skippable ads wasn’t in the Oct. 14 version. On Google’s Video reach campaigns page, the recommended non-skippable length for Target frequency went from 7 to 15 seconds in the Oct. 14 capture to 7 to 20 seconds now. That page’s Target frequency table now also lists in-feed and Shorts, and recommends a vertical video of 6 to 60 seconds next to horizontal 15- and 6-second videos.

    Industry observers note that the current page lists a single frequency range of 2 to 7 per week or 4 to 12 per month. The Oct. 14 capture gave that range for multi-format campaigns and 2 to 4 per week (4 to 8 per month) for in-stream-only campaigns. When I covered Target frequency’s global launch in 2022, Google mentioned advertisers could pick a goal of up to four per week.

    The same Target frequency campaign may use both non-skippable video ads and either Shorts ads or in-feed ads; however, it will need to be limited to auction buying, as the help page makes reserve buying available on “non-mixed formats” only.

    While legacy campaigns which are in-stream-only cannot change from one ad format type to another once they are created (a rule also on the page before the patch), multi-format campaigns do allow changing the ad format types in campaign settings. At present (Nov. 12), the page does not provide information about what happens when adding non-skippable ads to a multi-format campaign created before the update to see if you can still include in-feed and Shorts ads without dropping them.

    The Target frequency campaign help page FAQ also explains that an existing campaign cannot be converted into a Target frequency campaign and instructs the advertiser to “end your current campaign and set up a newly introduced Target frequency campaign” in its place.

    Industry observers note that at the time I looked at the English Target frequency page on Nov. 12, it revealed the fresh mixing rule. However, both the UK English and Australian English versions of the Target frequency page were stating you cannot mix in-feed or Shorts ad placements and non-skippable video ad placements. The UK English version of the setup guide continues to list a separate weekly range of 2 to 4 for in-stream formats.

    In addition, Display & Video 360’s own Target frequency help page which provides assistance for those purchasing using this channel highlights that non-skippable video ads are available “up to 15 seconds” only when purchased as an in-stream-only format.

    Industry observers note that google Ads Help’s Newly introduced features & announcements section had no announcement regarding the revision as of Nov. 12. The last announcement published there was dated May 20.

    Per Google’s updated help page, brands buying Target frequency at auction no longer have to choose between non-skippable ads and Shorts or in-feed reach.

    Prior to developing a campaign for Target frequency using auctions, you should create a new Target frequency campaign, open the Ad formats drop-down within that campaign and verify if selecting Non-skippable in-stream leaves both in-feed and Shorts selected within your account.

    The Video reach page says that horizontal video can serve on Shorts (when there is no vertical video in the ad group) and eligible horizontal videos may be served vertically when video enhancements are turned on.

    Google suggests creating vertical video content for Shorts and horizontal video content for feed ads and non-skippable ads.

    In a recent development, watch for the UK and Australian versions of the Target frequency page to match the English page, and for any change to Display & Video 360’s page. Also watch the English page for a note on adding non-skippable ads to campaigns created before the enhancement.

    ONA, OpenNews, and others see troubled times ahead, so it’s goodbye to “rubber chicken dinners.”.

    Recent findings suggest that RELATED ARTICLEWe know coronavirus has wrecked the events business for media in 2020. But will it come back post-virus?Joshua BentonMarch 25, 2020When the pandemic forced conferences to go virtual, the question was whether people would come back in person post-Covid.

    Sources indicate that for a while, they did. For a couple years after the pandemic, people were excited to be in person together again. U.S. journalism organizations saw their revenue climb, as sponsors and funders spent generously.

    Sources indicate that at the end of 2026, though, the situation is less rosy. Combine surging jet fuel prices, inflation, media companies cutting costs, and declining sponsor and funder dollars, and the future appears grim not just for journalism conferences but, in some cases, for the organizations behind them.

    It has been revealed that revenue is the total revenue line on each organization’s IRS Form 990. The 990s are from ProPublica’s Nonprofit Explorer. ONA’s 990 for 2025 was not available as of November 12, 2026.

    The Online News Association said on Tuesday that it is “pausing” its 26-year-old conference and laying off its five staffers.

    In a recent development, “Before the pandemic, the annual conference was ONA’s biggest source of revenue, and together with grants, it sustained the organization. This is no longer true,” Niketa Patel wrote. “The costs of large convenings have climbed sharply while professional development and sponsorship budgets have shrunk.”.

    LION Publishers remarked in September that it’s getting out of the large conference business for now. “Philanthropy is famously fickle, and funding priorities have shifted, making this kind of conference a very tough lift,” executive director Chris Krewson added.

    Industry observers note that LION barely broke even on the conferences it held in 2025 and 2026, Krewson told me. The organization may still hold smaller events next year, it’s not cutting staff or programming, and it’s expanding its Audit program. But it “won’t be taking on the responsibility for an independent event at a hotel with a food and beverage minimum and hotel room block for 400-plus people.”.

    “Every dollar I spend on rubber chicken dinners and microphones/WiFi for three days is money I can’t spend on programs that make publishers’ businesses stronger,” Krewson said.

    OpenNews said in October that it’s switching into “emergency mode”1 and cutting back on “work that distills journalism craft: no more community calls or Source articles for at least the rest of 2026 and maybe longer.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the future of OpenNews’s annual conference, SRCCON, is uncertain. “We usually make our decision about SRCCON at about this time every year, but this year is different as we consider the news from both LION and ONA and the funding pressures that we know all too well,” Jessica Morrison, co–executive director of OpenNews, told me in an email. “We are opening a community conversation today — emails going out very soon — to gather input about SRCCON, our other programs, and where we go next with OpenNews.”.

    The three-year-old Organization for Accessible Journalism stated Thursday that it is shutting down. “Financial support never reached a level that allowed us to build beyond an all volunteer effort — including my full-time effort,” founder Stacy Kess wrote.

    Journalism conferences in the United States are certainly not gone. IRE and NICAR will hold their annual data journalism conference in Denver in March. The Institute for Nonprofit News is “talking about what INN Days will look like in 2027” and will know more by early next year. And the International Symposium on Journalism is on for 2027 — its 28th year, founder (and Nieman Foundation board member) Rosental Alves told me. But things have gotten harder, he remarked. “It’s not only the difficulty of finding sponsors, but also the rising costs of venues, hotels, airfares, etc., compounded by shrinking travel budgets in newsrooms and even the problems international attendees face in coming to the U.S.,” he told me in an email. ISOJ cut costs, in part by moving to a different venue, and it benefits from being relatively small. “It’s very sad that foundations and corporations that funded journalism conferences in the past have pulled back their support,” Alves added. “The need for these gatherings is as great as ever.” a play on Emergency Mode for News, its initiative to support journalists working during disasters [↩].

    Industry News: AI Bot Management: Why SEOs Need More Than Block Lists via @sejournal, @chrisgreenseo

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that for years, bot management in SEO was relatively straightforward.
    • AI search has made that approach increasingly inadequate.
    • It has been revealed that today, websites are accessed by traditional search crawlers, AI training crawlers, retrieval bots, user-initiated fetches, and autonomous agents.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that for years, bot management in SEO was relatively straightforward. You either allowed crawlers to access your website or blocked them. That model was never perfect, but it was generally sufficient for what we needed.

    Image from author, November 2026.

    AI search has made that approach increasingly inadequate.

    It has been revealed that today, websites are accessed by traditional search crawlers, AI training crawlers, retrieval bots, user-initiated fetches, and autonomous agents. These serve very different purposes, yet we regularly lump them together under the term “AI bots.”.

    Blocking a crawler used for model training has different consequences from blocking one retrieving content for search answers – this distinction really matters!

    Robots.txt remains useful, but as it’s voluntary actual enforcement happens through CDNs, web application firewalls and bot mitigation services, which can contradict your robots.txt rules without the SEO team even knowing.

    Image from author, November 2026.

    Agents complicate matters further. They can browse websites like real users, trigger analytics tracking, and become increasingly difficult to distinguish from human visitors. Block an agent performing a product comparison, and you might not simply lose a ranking. You could disappear from the answer entirely.

    Sources indicate that my argument is that we need to move from block lists to deliberate bot policies. Policies that consider who’s accessing our content, why they’re doing it and the consequences of allowing or blocking them.

    Recent findings suggest that these decisions increasingly involve SEO, engineering, security, legal, and commercial teams. They need to be coordinated, consistently enforced and regularly reviewed.

    Image from author, November 2026.

    It has been revealed that I’ve covered these challenges, their implications, and some practical approaches in my GEO Elite presentation. Hope you find it useful:.

Tech platforms would have to pay even when they surface news link previews or story snippets in their products, including AI search products. The law would also force platforms to compensate publishers when their journalism is used to train AI models.

    Any compensation would be paid through a state-run management organization, which would then distribute the funds to publishers. Platforms that don’t comply could face sanctions, including the loss of their local business permits.

    Social media and search engine companies have come out in force against the bill, with Google leading the campaign.

    Indonesia is a massive market for global digital platforms with roughly 230 million internet customers. In 2023, Indonesia had the fifth-most Google users of any country in the world, with traffic reaching 4.42 billion searches.

    On Wednesday, a Google official argued that the bill would limit access to news, according to Reuters.

    Berni Moestafa, Meta’s head of public policy in Indonesia, testified that if the bill is passed “publishers could lose readership traffic as well as potential advertising and subscription revenue.”.

    Back in 2023, Canada passed the Online News Act, its own, albeit narrower law which required platforms like Google and Meta to pay publishers for sharing or linking to their content. Meta responded by blocking news links on Facebook and Instagram in Canada altogether.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Google created a page on Search Central which lists the HTTP Referer values that are passed on when a user clicks to get to another website using Google Search. The page is listed as upcoming in Google’s update log, added to document “how site owners can identify and track traffic from Google Search” within their analytics.

    It has been revealed that the same HTTP Referer values are also passed on by Discover and Google Images, the page states. That means a google.com referrer shows that Google sent someone, without showing whether they came from Search, Discover or Images.

    Recent findings suggest that google Search is using the origin referrer policy, so all that appears in the header is the scheme and host of the referring page. In other words, no information about the path of the page, the query parameters and the actual search query is sent; instead, Google’s page points to Search Console’s Performance report for queries.

    Google Search on the web sends either https://www.google.com/ or one of a number of local Google domains, such as https://www.google.co.uk/. Similarly, the Google app on iOS sends this. The Google app on Android sends either of these options or android-app://com.google.android.googlequicksearchbox/https/www.google.com if the app opens the link in a browser tab.

    According to the webpage, Discover traffic carries the values of whichever surface it was viewed on, “such as the Google app or Google Search on the web,” and other services available through Google from the same origins, for instance Google Images, send them too.

    In February 2021, Google began moving Discover traffic for Chrome to be sent via the google.com origin referrer instead of a googleapis.com referrer so that it would match Discover within the Google app.

    Visits from Google Search can come to your website without a referrer. The page explains how browsers or operating systems might remove that header for privacy reasons when someone is using private mode, opening in a latest tab (depending on the browser), or switching from a mobile search widget to an external browser.

    According to recent reports, when traffic carrying Google’s referrer values reveals up in your analytics software, it is generally referred to as organic traffic coming from Google Search, according to the page. However, when you find it classified as Referral or Direct traffic, it could mean that your custom channels, referral exclusions, or filters have reclassified the traffic.

    You should count only the requests to your landing pages and not include requests for images, CSS and JavaScript files in your counts of Google Search referrals; these requests carry the URL of your landing page as their referrer.

    In a recent development, when you use client-side redirects on your site, your redirects may be replacing the referrer with your site’s URL. When you do a redirect that drops the query string, it will take away parameters like gclid, which the page describes as commonly used in ad tagging. A redirect with a stricter Referrer-Policy header could remove the referrer altogether.

    Sources indicate that google Search Console shows a click every time someone has selected a link, but analytics tools will show a visit only after the page has loaded and executed the tracking script, which ad blockers, consent choices and privacy settings can block. Google Search Console only tracks organic clicks, whereas analytics totals may or may not include Google Ads traffic depending on how the website was set up.

    You can separate Discover clicks from Search clicks by using the Discover report in Google’s Search Console and not referrer data.

    It has been revealed that the last revision for this page was made on Nov. 12; it does not cover AI Mode or AI Overviews. The standard Performance report in Search Console counts clicks in both categories. As I reported on Nov. 2, it does not have a search appearance type that separates those clicks.

    If your paid landing pages are being redirected, make sure that the redirects are passing along the query string, because losing a gclid is another gap the page names.

    Teams that keep their own list of Google referrer values now have Google’s version to compare against. As of Nov. 13, the page doesn’t mention the google.com/goto redirect links in results, which DataForSEO dates to late August and which I covered last week. Google’s documentation updates log is where a revision to the page would show up.

    From latest majors to search traffic, newspapers to impeachment: Have you kept up with this week’s media news?

    In a recent development, it’s been another busy week. Recap it with the second edition of the Nieman Lab News-About-News Quiz, your weekly incentive to keep up with the latest happenings in the world of digital journalism. All questions are based on the week’s Nieman Lab stories or articles elsewhere that we’ve linked to in What We’re Reading. The quiz will appear here through November as a trial run; if people seem to like it, we’ll keep it going in 2027. Good luck!

    What journalism organization announced this week that it was canceling its annual conference and laying off most of its staff?

    “Since we gathered in Chicago for ONA26, many of you have asked when we will be together again,” CEO Niketa Patel wrote. “Unfortunately, it will not be in 2027. ONA has decided to pause our in-person events and will not host a conference in 2027.”.

    Recent findings suggest that for the first time ever, the press freedom group Reporters Without Borders (RSF) has officially called for the impeachment of a U.S. official. Which one?

    Industry observers note that “RSF does not take the question of impeachment lightly. In fact, our organization has never before called for the removal of a US official. But the severity and persistence of Carr’s misconduct as FCC chairman demand an extraordinary response. Congress has a constitutional responsibility to hold him accountable. Restoring the FCC’s independence must be central to that effort.”.

    Emerson College recently unveiled a fresh degree program aimed at helping students build “a career across a rapidly changing media landscape.” What’s the program’s name?

    “Our upcoming Content Creation major prepares students to be a part of the evolving creator economy, teaching them not only how to produce compelling digital content but also how to build a successful entrepreneurial career.”.

    What news organization — after a challenging few years — claims it is now “within striking distance of break-even,” financially?

    Recent findings suggest that “I’ll be honest,” executive editor Matt Murphy noted at a conference. “We had years of losses, and steepening losses. That’s the truth. We’re a private manufacturer and don’t share the figures, but it was hundreds and hundreds of millions of dollars. Now we’re within striking distance of break-even, and I expect next year will be our best year in seven years. We’ve done the right-sizing we needed, which was tough.”.

    According to recent reports, the Echo-Pioneer — the local newspaper in the town of High Level, Alberta (population 4,000) — has an unusual business model. What is it?

    According to recent reports, town officials signed a two-year “advertising and readership agreement” in 2025. It’s one of the many ways local Canadian news outlets are trying to stay afloat — most notably the federal Local Journalism Initiative.

    Which online publisher’s CEO announced that Google search traffic had “dropped by more than 1 million referrals on average per week” in October?

    As a result of the search decline, CEO Steve Huffman announced Reddit would be shifting to a primarily “logged-in experience.”.

    The Asia-Pacific outlet The Diplomat retracted an interview with a South Korean CEO last week. Why?

    Sources indicate that “The author presented themselves as a South Korean freelance journalist and claimed to have interviewed Newtype’s CEO. We now know that the journalist fabricated the interview and may not even be who they claimed to be.”.

    According to recent reports, the parliament of an Asian nation is debating requiring tech companies like Google and Meta to pay news outlets when they direct customers to their stories. Which nation?

    The proposed law would also require compensating news publishers when AI models are trained on news content.

    Which international news outlet, sensing a political opening, is expanding its reporting team in the United States?

    In a recent development, “Market research indicated there was room to grow among politically liberal Jews in the United States. Gali Arnon, who became the chief executive of Haaretz Group last year, said she wanted the newspaper to become in other countries what it is in Israel: an ‘identity brand.’”.

    According to recent reports, this photo reveals an early editorial plan from one of the first important publications on the World Wide Web, a mononymic website that has recently been in the news. What site was it?

    Recent findings suggest that the photo is from Salon co-founder Laura Miller, laying out some early “challenges” of the influential web “magazine” which closed last week. “People sometimes tell me about reading Salon avidly in their youth, how it felt like connecting to something exhilarating and cool and a bit crazy in the strange latest expanses of the internet. All I can say is: That’s exactly how it felt to work there.”.

    The most important stories about journalism and the future of news, delivered to your inbox every afternoon.

    ONA, OpenNews, and others see troubled times ahead, so it's goodbye to "rubber chicken dinners.".

    The upcoming budget would make a local reporting program permanent and extend a 35% tax credit on newsroom salaries. The support makes “a massive, massive difference.".

    #8127. Breaking: Meta & OpenAI Agents Made Nearly 90% Of Agent Requests In Bot Data via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    Breaking: Meta & OpenAI Agents Made Nearly 90% Of Agent Requests In Bot Data via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (947 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • AI agents from Meta and OpenAI made nearly 90% of the agent requests reaching sites and apps protected by HUMAN Security in October, according to the company’s monthly State of Agentic Traffic report.
    • According to recent reports, in October, total agent requests were approximately 8 times greater than in August and roughly 2.6 times greater than September’s.
    • The majority of these requests accessed product and search content.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    AI agents from Meta and OpenAI made nearly 90% of the agent requests reaching sites and apps protected by HUMAN Security in October, according to the company’s monthly State of Agentic Traffic report. Meta’s Muse accounted for 59% on its own.

    According to recent reports, in October, total agent requests were approximately 8 times greater than in August and roughly 2.6 times greater than September’s. This report includes agent requests on HUMAN-protected sites and apps but does not include all internet traffic; each request represents an action by the agent, such as a page load or a search.

    The majority of these requests accessed product and search content. There was a very small portion that reached the checkout area.

    In a recent development, muse’s share of agent requests rose 19 percentage points from September, and the number of requests it sent nearly quadrupled. The report says Muse now sends 3.7 times as many requests as ChatGPT Agent, the next-largest agent. Meta introduced Muse on Sept. 8.

    OpenAI accounted for about 30% of total requests with three of the top 10 agents. ChatGPT Agent had 28.5% of requests in September, but despite sending 44% more requests, its share dropped to 15.9% as Muse grew faster, according to the report. The Codex Browser application increased from 7.7% to 8.8% and the Codex Chrome extension went up from 3.3% to 5.2%.

    The Claude Chrome extension had a 50% drop in share, going from 7% to 3.5%, though it had a 30% increase in number of requests. Google’s newly released Gemini agent (launched Oct. 8, per HUMAN) came in at No. 8 with 0.8%. xAI’s Grok Agent was new to the top 10 at No. 9 with 0.7%.

    Recent findings suggest that genspark’s browser-based agent dropped off the top 10 list entirely; Perplexity’s Comet agent accounted for 41% of all agent requests in August but this figure declined to only 9.4% in September and then further to only 3.6% by October. Comet was also the only top-10 agent that experienced a drop-off in request volume during October, with a decline of approximately 30% since August. In addition, OpenAI discontinued its standalone ChatGPT Atlas browser in August.

    The report attributes this downward trend to users selecting an agent based on either their familiarity with the platform or having used another product offered by the same tech giant.

    According to recent reports, in October, 85% of all agent requests in the report were directed toward product and search pages. This represents an increase over the previous month’s percentage when such requests totaled 81%. During the same period, requests made to checkout and payment pages decreased from 2.4% of the total to 1.9%.

    According to the report, agents “still browse far more than they buy” but the number of requests making their way to checkout has been increasing at a rapid pace. The report’s page categorizations represent where a request ended up rather than what action was being taken, so a request arriving on a checkout page does not signify an order had been placed.

    Ecommerce websites generated a stable share of approximately 60% of agent requests during this period, and travel was the second highest category, according to the report. Media generated the third largest portion among all categories tracked, marking the first time in this series that travel websites have outperformed media.

    Recent findings suggest that HUMAN uses a combination of behavioral data along with user-agent strings and, when available, publisher-level integration to determine what is agent generated, and it excludes crawler activity. The report says AgenticTrust has identified and verified Muse using HUMAN’s own proprietary research and digital signature validation. The report does not provide further breakdown on the percentage of Muse detected through each method.

    In Meta’s engineering post on Muse, the company claims Muse’s browsing “will appear as your activity” to the sites it visits.

    It has been revealed that muse transferred its Web Bot Auth signatures from Meta’s key directory (meta.com) to its own (muse.ai) between Nov. 7 and Nov. 9, according to DataDome’s reporting on Nov. 11. Web Bot Auth allows agents to identify themselves by signing the request they are sending to a site, allowing the receiving site to verify the identity of who is making the request. At the time of my review on Nov. 13, the muse.ai key directory was active.

    As of Nov. 10, half of Muse’s requests on DataDome’s network were being made without being signed, so there would be no signature to verify the source of the request. According to DataDome, sites that verify signatures and only accept those based on meta.com will now see Muse’s requests as having no verification. Both DataDome and HUMAN sell bot and agent identification services.

    For ecommerce and travel teams, HUMAN’s October report narrows down whose agents are sending most agent requests. In HUMAN’s data, two companies’ agents account for nearly nine in ten.

    Industry observers note that as Slobodan Manic wrote for SEJ in October, an agent like Muse gives robots.txt no name to match, so the decision about letting it in moves to bot protection. A bot rule that verifies signatures now needs Muse’s muse.ai directory, and in DataDome’s Nov. 10 count, about half of Muse’s requests carried no signature to check.

    HUMAN’s report also notes analytics tools on most sites can’t tell AI agents from human visitors. Muse and OpenAI’s three agents make a short list to raise with whoever runs bot protection before Black Friday.

    The thing to watch is whether more of Muse’s requests start arriving signed. HUMAN states next month’s report will show how agents behaved over Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • Industry observers note that we will never sell your address.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    Industry observers note that we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    Sources indicate that we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    The Cornell Daily Sun saw traffic spike by almost 500% in September.

    RELATED ARTICLESearch traffic has declined so much that some publishers are considering opting out of Google entirelyNeel DhaneshaJuly 22, 2026We’ve now been publishing roundups of local newspaper traffic for a full year, so we can compare this year’s traffic to last year’s. Almost across the board, local newspapers are seeing traffic decline as Google referrals drop. For July, August, and September, traffic to the most-visited sites is lower than at this time last year, according to our Similarweb data.

    RELATED ARTICLEHow did newspapers in places like Harrisburg, Birmingham, and Syracuse become some of America’s most-read online?Joshua BentonJuly 23, 2025A good example is Advance Local’s Harrisburg Patriot-News, PennLive.com. Josh has written about Advance publications punching above their weight in traffic. They still are: Advance outlets like AL.com, Mlive.com, and NJ.com, among others, continued to feature prominently in the top sites by estimated monthly visits in July, August, and September. In August 2026, PennLive’s traffic growth stood out even among Advance peers; it gained 3.6 million visits in August compared to July, a 78% spike. But in total, PennLive saw a little over 8.2 million monthly visits for August 2026 — down from about 12.5 million in August 2025.

    Still, publishers large and small are finding ways to bring more readers to their sites. In August, the Bozeman Daily Chronicle grew its traffic by about 96,000 monthly visits, a 49% jump. Managing editor Jack Reaney attributed the growth to the newspaper launching a new website Aug. 3 designed for improved functionality, with “fewer, more intentional news categories,” lighter page design for faster load times, and a more modern layout. The Chronicle is one of more than 150 newspapers owned by Adams MultiMedia. The parent firm is rolling out the new website design across its newspapers, but Bozeman was the “guinea pig,” Reaney remarked.

    In Florida, Cape Coral Breeze, a small weekly, saw its traffic spike about 139% in August. The network of local weeklies has tried to adopt a daily, real-time mindset after decades of posting once a week, Breeze Newspapers publisher Ray Eckenrode told me. The August spike was driven by participation in Cape Coral Breeze’s “Best of Cape Coral” contest, where readers vote on favorite local businesses in more than 200 categories. According to the team’s internal count, a little over 150,000 “Best of” votes were cast this year, up from 92,000 last year. The team made an effort this year to “drive traffic to our homepage first to reach the contest voting page to expose some of those casual website people to our news coverage,” Eckenrode said, and had some success with that strategy.

    In September, The Cornell Daily Sun gained 1 million visits, almost a 500% jump from August, when it broke the story of the Cornell 7 lawsuit (and published an editorial naming the defendants). Other local news sites in New York also saw meaningful growth in September; traffic to NNY360.com jumped 84%, while the Gannett-owned Democrat and Chronicle gained about 762,000 visits, a 35% jump.

    According to recent reports, on the opposite coast, the San-Jose-based Mercury News gained around 690,000 monthly visits in September, a 14% jump. “Our traffic is volatile like everyone else’s, but we had a strong September mainly because a couple of stories performed very well,” stated Annika Toernqvist, MediaNews Group’s managing editor for digital for Northern California. Environmental beat reporter Paul Rogers‘ story about a new California law that will ban watering artificial turf “performed exceptionally well on Google and Google Discovery”; 62% of traffic to the story came from search. Stories about the local impact of new state laws consistently do well with the outlet’s readers, according to Toernqvist, and this was “a hot topic with a strong headline.” The story was also the top subscription converter in September. Another story by Rogers covering the proposed renaming of Fremont State Park also drove traffic that month; 86% came from search, mostly from Google Discovery.

    Meanwhile, celebrity reporter Martha Ross‘ story about a latest book on King Charles’ valet performed well in part thanks to a bump from…the Drudge Report. (“Yes, the Drudge Report still drives traffic,” Toernqvist said; it accounted for 43% of visits to that story.).

    #8122. United Lets Search Engines Index Its Site, Makes AI Agents Ask First via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1000 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    United Lets Search Engines Index Its Site, Makes AI Agents Ask First via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1000 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, united Airlines’ website terms, updated Nov.
    • The changes came with United’s announcement that it is restricting unauthorized third-party AI agents on its own platforms and through travel agencies and booking sites.
    • For those on SEO and ecommerce teams who have created their own rules for AI agents, the airline’s rules are an example of what a massive firm has done.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, united Airlines’ website terms, updated Nov. 11, allow search engines to index its public pages. However, any AI agent that searches, books, or makes purchases on united.com or in its app needs written permission. The terms also bar anyone from using fares, schedules, availability, pricing or other data from United’s site or app to “train, fine-tune, ground, evaluate, or otherwise develop” an AI model.

    The changes came with United’s announcement that it is restricting unauthorized third-party AI agents on its own platforms and through travel agencies and booking sites. The airline updated its contract of carriage (the passenger agreement that comes with buying a ticket) on the same day.

    For those on SEO and ecommerce teams who have created their own rules for AI agents, the airline’s rules are an example of what a massive firm has done. The rules for the AI agents can be found in both the terms and conditions and the contract. As of Nov. 14, United’s robots.txt file named no crawlers or agents for any AI.

    The announcement from United states that sharing account login credentials with an outside third-party AI assistant can expose customers’ sensitive information. Furthermore, according to the announcement, there are potential risks of “unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles.” In addition to these risks, automated actions by the AI assistant may violate Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and Department of Transportation (DOT) regulations. United points to check-in as an example, saying it requires a person to acknowledge that their bags hold no banned items like explosives.

    United’s FAQ on its Digital Trust Center calls any AI agent, bot, browser extension or browser feature unauthorized if it searches, books, buys, manages or collects information on united.com or the United app without United’s permission. Using AI to research and initiative a trip is allowed as long as the tool doesn’t access united.com or the app.

    In a recent development, united doesn’t work with any third-party AI agents yet, according to the FAQ, and bookings that agents made before Nov. 11 won’t be canceled.

    In The Wall Street Journal’s report, CEO Scott Kirby said at an event in Chicago, “I don’t want to create another middleman.”.

    It has been revealed that united’s terms of service define an Automated Agent as any software, service or feature that, with full or partial autonomy, searches, books, buys or manages items on the United website or app, or extracts or copies data from those websites or apps. This includes AI assistants, bots, scrapers, browser extensions and features built into browsers or apps, even if a person supervises or approves the actions of the Automated Agent.

    No Automated Agent shall be permitted to access United’s site or app without prior written permission from United, and United reserves the right to block or impede an Automated Agent at any time, regardless of who operates it (the user, a third party or an artificial intelligence tech giant).

    One of the uses United’s terms of service bar for data pulled from its site or app is grounding, which involves an AI system pulling in outside content to build a response.

    Search engines that index the public pages of united.com are exempt under the terms of service. The terms of service also exempt assistive technology and standard browsers used by a person. However, built-in agent features of a browser are not exempt. Additionally, the terms of service do not address how they treat answers created by AI systems from search engines’ indexes.

    Use of an Automated Agent on United’s site results in acceptance of the agreement by the user, whoever runs the agent and the person for whom the agent acts. In September, Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse agent based on its Conditions of Use, which bind the shopper rather than Meta, as Slobodan Manic reported for SEJ. eBay has added “buy-for-me agents, LLM-driven bots” to its User Agreement‘s list of automated tools that need eBay’s permission, in an patch it posted in January.

    The highlighted excerpts below show United’s permission requirement and its search-indexing exception.

    It has been revealed that the contract of carriage uses its own term “AI Agent” to describe all computer-based applications (software) utilized on behalf of a traveler or other individuals, to locate, research, book, purchase or otherwise manage any offer from or through United, regardless of whether an individual is monitoring or approving such activity. Examples include assistant capabilities built into social media, messaging or search platforms, browsers utilizing AI capabilities, stand-alone AI-enabled agents, and third-party AI assistants connected to United via some type of interface provided by a travel agency or other intermediary.

    According to recent reports, rule 6.J.6 adds using AI agents to “make, modify or service a Ticket,” or to buy any service or product, to the contract’s prohibited practices, next to hidden-city and throwaway ticketing. Rule 5.H lists bookings that AI agents made, changed or serviced among the improper bookings United will cancel without notice.

    Recent findings suggest that according to the FAQ, travel agencies and booking platforms aren’t permitted to use third-party AI agents to search for, book, or manage United travel on behalf of customers. Agencies also need to get United’s permission before using their own third-party AI tools.

    United’s terms separate search indexing from AI agent access, and none of it depends on robots.txt. Personal agents like Muse publish no user agent for a robots.txt rule to name, as Manic wrote in October. Reviewing your robots.txt, terms, and bot protection together can help you see whether they’re aligned on what an AI agent is allowed to do on your site.

    United claims it will keep reviewing how AI assistants work with its services and will upgrade its FAQ if it starts working with third-party agents. United’s release, FAQ, terms and contract don’t say how it detects an agent, so watch how the rules are enforced for travel agencies and agent makers, and whether other airlines write similar rules.

    Over the next two years, NPR will address a longstanding listener plea: improving its app.

    Industry observers note that during a November 12 board of directors meeting, NPR CEO Katherine Maher noted the organization will rebuild its digital offerings to be a “service-first, app-first destination” as part of NPR’s 2027-2029 strategic plan, Current reported on Thursday. One goal of the plan is to reach “five million weekly active people on its platforms by 2029” and “to build a monthly engaged digital audience of 40 million.” According to Current, Maher said that the NPR network — which includes more than 200 member radio stations — at the moment reaches 39 million weekly listeners across broadcast and digital, but the “total potential addressable audience, weekly consumers of news, information and culture who are open to our work, is roughly 153 million Americans. That is nearly four times our current reach.”.

    Sources indicate that in Apple’s App Store, NPR’s app has a 4.7-star rating and more than 78,000 reviews, of which the majority are positive. But reviewers have quibbles.

    According to recent reports, bryan Moffett, NPR’s senior vice president of transformation, mentioned NPR+, the broadcaster’s subscription program, brought in $8 million in the 2026 fiscal year, up from $5.5 million in 2025. (NPR+ is available with a donation of $8 a month or more, and offers perks like podcasts without ads.) Maher said upcoming investment in the app will help reach younger audiences and shift NPR’s “median audience age from 60-plus toward 40-plus.”.

    “We love radio, but we have been so wildly successful there that we’ve largely exhausted its further financial growth,” Maher told the board. “And as it shrinks, we must invert our revenue engine to ensure sustainability across all of our platforms, including radio, but to build a wider funnel through digital offerings, third-party platforms, and upcoming investments in marketing and communication that will tell our story and share our value with the world.”.

    Industry observers note that RELATED ARTICLENPR, the quintessential audio news brand, adapts to a video-first futureSarah ScireSeptember 29, 2026Overhauling the app is just one part of NPR’s strategy to keep up with users’ changing consumption preferences. In September, Sarah Scire reported on the broadcaster leaning into video podcasts with the acquisition of Kevin Roose and Casey Newton’s technology podcast Machine Gods. NPR chief operating officer Ryan Merkley told Current in June that NPR was already working on redesigning the app to better serve member stations and their listeners.

    “Fix the app,” departing public editor Kelly McBride told NPR leaders during the meeting. “It’s not a great experience for the audience and it’s key to moving forward, but you guys seem like you’re on it. So I won’t dwell on that.”.

    Nieman Lab requested a copy of the approved strategic plan but did not receive it by publication time. Read the full story in Current here.

    #8119. Core Upgrade, ChatGPT Business Hub & AI Mode’s Upcoming Model – SEO Pulse via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1310 w)

    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Core Upgrade, ChatGPT Business Hub & AI Mode’s Upcoming Model – SEO Pulse via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1310 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Welcome to the week’s Pulse: what’s changing affects how you read ranking movement, which data ChatGPT will report back to businesses, and how larger sites believe search traffic will perform.
    • It has been revealed that this week saw Google announce its core update while it also changed the default model that is used by AI Mode.
    • Sources indicate that google started rolling out the November 2026 core patch on Nov.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Welcome to the week’s Pulse: what’s changing affects how you read ranking movement, which data ChatGPT will report back to businesses, and how larger sites believe search traffic will perform.

    It has been revealed that this week saw Google announce its core update while it also changed the default model that is used by AI Mode. OpenAI revealed that Business Hub is available in beta, and three company earnings calls dealt with decreasing search referral numbers and paid crawl hints.

    Here’s what matters for you and your work.

    Sources indicate that google started rolling out the November 2026 core patch on Nov. 10.

    Sources indicate that key facts: This is the third Search core update of the year. According to the Search Status Dashboard, the update “applies globally and to all languages”. Per the dashboard, the update “may take up to 2 weeks to complete”. At 10:06 a.m. PT on Nov. 10 the rollout had just begun and as of Nov. 12, the update was still in progress. Google’s Search Central team also referred to the update as “a regular update” on their LinkedIn page.

    Google advises waiting at least a full week after a core upgrade has rolled out, then trying to compare your Search Console data from that week (the week after rollout) to the week prior to when the rollout began. Going by Google’s estimate of two weeks, the first full week after rollout would include U.S. Thanksgiving Day, Black Friday and Cyber Monday, so online retailers making this comparison would be comparing their holiday traffic to their average non-holiday week.

    Read our full coverage: Google’s November 2026 Core Upgrade Starts Rolling Out.

    In a recent development, openAI opened Business Hub in beta on Nov. 10, letting businesses claim their ChatGPT profiles and see how often ChatGPT mentions them and sends clicks to their websites.

    Key facts: Any eligible business located where ChatGPT is available can claim its business, according to OpenAI’s announcement. Once the claim and identity verification are approved, Insights show aggregated mentions, website clicks and discovery topics for the past 28 days. OpenAI’s setup guide says a mention for an online business counts when ChatGPT references the business’s website, and the brand name alone doesn’t count. Vahan Petrosyan, SEJ’s director of technology, submitted Search Engine Journal and reported 353,356 mentions and 2,663 website clicks from Oct. 14 to Nov. 10.

    According to recent reports, for an online business, OpenAI counts in Business Hub’s Insights how many times a reference is made to this business by ChatGPT and how many clicks are generated from those references. A recorded click isn’t a confirmed visit, so those clicks are the numbers to put next to the number of referrals you see in your analytics for the last 28 days. The setup guide also indicates that a blank metric doesn’t always mean there was no activity, and simply claiming a business will not guarantee increased visibility within ChatGPT’s responses.

    Read our full coverage: How to Submit Your Website to ChatGPT Business Hub.

    Google made Gemini 4 Hydrogen the default model in AI Mode on Nov. 12 and is using it for some AI Overview questions too.

    Sources indicate that key facts: Robby Stein, Vice President of Product at Google Search posted the announcement about the change on an X thread and noted Hydrogen is “being used for your hardest questions in AI Overviews”. Google’s Search post states the model is available everywhere in Search to everyone, and that it has better query fan out, connecting people to “a broader range of helpful links than before”. The Search post and the thread do not give link numbers, and the thread did not say what would be considered the hardest AI Overview questions.

    Citation tracking for AI Mode and AI Overviews in November now spans a model change on Nov. 12, two days after the core revision began. Logging both dates makes it easier to compare what happened before and after each one, while your citation and referral numbers can help you assess Google’s claim of a broader range of links for your site.

    Read our full coverage: Google Makes Gemini 4 Hydrogen The Default Model In AI Mode.

    Ziff Davis CEO Vivek Shah said on the firm’s third-quarter call that it is “not planning on a search recovery”. Tripadvisor CFO Mike Noonan said on his company’s call that SEO will still be a headwind to growth in 2027.

    Key facts: Shah said organic Google referrals to Ziff Davis properties fell about 37% year over year in the quarter. He also put about 2.7 billion AI Overview and AI Mode impressions in Search Console for the quarter at nearly 10 times “the clicks those same sites received from Google Search”. Tripadvisor took a $369.5 million non-cash goodwill impairment on its Hotels and Other segment in the quarter, which its earnings release attributes largely to traffic headwinds from “changes in the search landscape”. Marketing took 48.8% of Tripadvisor’s revenue from continuing operations, up from 43.3% a year earlier, and Noonan tied the rise to a move from free to paid channels.

    In a recent development, shah’s comparison of the number of AI feature impressions versus the overall clicks in Google Search does not represent an AI click-through rate, since Search Console counts clicks on those features (AI Overview and AI Mode) inside the overall total. Similar comparisons are available to sites that have access to the generative AI report, as they too may be able to measure these types of ratios based upon their own data. On the Tripadvisor side, the planning number is marketing’s share of revenue, which the company connects to its move from free search traffic to paid channels.

    Read our full coverage: Ziff Davis CEO: ‘Not Planning On A Search Recovery’ and Tripadvisor Notes SEO Will Still Weigh On Growth In 2027.

    Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince said on the organization’s third-quarter call that OpenAI is paying for hints that tell its crawler when web pages change.

    Key facts: Prince said the quarter brought the organization’s first revenue from Act 4, its name for products aimed at a new business model for the internet, with OpenAI’s payments as one example. On the call, neither that revenue nor OpenAI’s payments came with a figure. For customers that want more traffic from AI agents, he called Cloudflare’s help “sort of the new version of SEO”. He also expects some form of micropayments, with sites possibly charging agents less when the agents explain why they’re visiting.

    Recent findings suggest that the Act 4 payment Prince referred to was paid to Cloudflare for improving the efficiency of OpenAI’s web crawling, and the call had no discussion about sharing revenue with owners of the sites providing these hints. Welcoming crawlers or blocking them are options existing Cloudflare customers have for each individual crawler (AI Crawl Control exists on every plan).

    Read our full coverage: Cloudflare CEO Likens AI Agent Optimization To A Fresh Version Of SEO.

    Several of the AI search metrics reported this week were defined by the platforms themselves; each platform’s metric is based on that platform’s specific definition. For example, Business Hub uses OpenAI’s definitions to determine how many mentions exist, while Shah’s comparison puts the AI impressions (as defined by Google Search Console) next to all of Google Search clicks. Google described a broader range of links for Hydrogen but did not provide an actual count. Cloudflare acknowledged that OpenAI does pay for crawl hints, but it did not give the dollar amount. Both Ziff Davis and Tripadvisor are already building their strategies around reduced amounts of free search traffic. Any report built on these numbers should carry the platform’s definition next to each one, and the dates of the core upgrade and the Hydrogen switch belong in your own log.

    #8114. YouTube’s Clips Tool Turns Podcast Episodes Into Shorts via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📖 Baca
