    YouTube’s Clips Tool Turns Podcast Episodes Into Shorts via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (706 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that youTube has expanded the video clips tool in YouTube Studio to Shorts, so creators can turn segments of long-form videos, such as podcast episodes, into vertical Shorts.
    • In an April post, YouTube remarked it would be “rolling out Video Clips to Shorts” later in the year.
    • The help page explains that each Short created using this tool has the original video as its related video.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that youTube has expanded the video clips tool in YouTube Studio to Shorts, so creators can turn segments of long-form videos, such as podcast episodes, into vertical Shorts. TeamYouTube announced the change Nov. 12 in a YouTube Help Community post aimed at podcast creators.

    In an April post, YouTube remarked it would be “rolling out Video Clips to Shorts” later in the year. The tool’s help page has described the Shorts option since at least Sept. 10, according to an Internet Archive capture.

    The help page explains that each Short created using this tool has the original video as its related video. A clickable link of the source video will be located underneath the channel handle. However, if the Short is either private, unlisted or Made for Kids, then the tool won’t add the link.

    The automatic link gives teams with a video podcast or webinar series a way to send viewers from a Short back to the whole episode.

    Recent findings suggest that when they are in YouTube Studio, creators open one of their pre-existing long-form videos. On the left-hand side of the screen is a list of options including Clips and Shorts. If they choose Short, they have two ways to create the Short.

    Here’s an example from YouTube’s demo showing the Short creation option in Studio.

    They can enter timestamps into the timeline editor. Alternatively, they may select some text in their video’s transcript to create the Short.

    According to recent reports, where available, the left-hand panel also shows AI-powered suggestions and an outline of the transcript that AI generates. YouTube’s post states it picks “moments in your episode that can be watched independently” so creators can review and edit them.

    The selection screen places suggested Shorts beside the transcript and the original video.

    The post describes how a widescreen episode becomes a Short:.

    “For Shorts, your 16:9 podcast episode will be transformed into a verticalized video, keeping the most crucial parts of the video in the frame.”.

    The help page indicates captions are added automatically where available, and creators can change their color, font, styling and position or turn them off.

    Here’s the vertical preview from the same demo, with captions and a Create draft button.

    Industry observers note that for standard video clips, which the tool still makes, the help page’s tip is to add a link to the source video in the clip’s description. YouTube also recommends keeping only full episodes in podcast playlists.

    YouTube’s help page for the clips tool lists AI-powered suggestions and outlines for creators in Brazil, Canada, France, Germany, India, Mexico, South Korea, Spain, the U.K. and the U.S. The supported languages are English, French, German, Hindi, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish.

    According to recent reports, in an April capture, the page limited suggestions to English-language videos in a podcast playlist in the U.S. and Canada. The current page doesn’t mention podcast playlists for suggestions.

    Recent findings suggest that on Oct. 1, YouTube stated it would reduce the reach of channels that mainly aggregate or re-upload other creators’ clips without significant changes. In my coverage, I wrote that YouTube’s video on the change didn’t discuss creators cutting Shorts from their own long-form videos.

    Unless it’s private, unlisted, or Made for Kids, a Short created with the clips tool will automatically link to its full-length episode. When you create a Short on another platform and upload it yourself to YouTube, YouTube’s related video help page has you add that link manually after uploading. To do this requires advanced feature access.

    Beyond stating that creators won’t be penalized for using their own content in a clip or Short, the help page’s note didn’t address recommendations, which was specifically what the Oct. 1 Shorts changes were about.

    According to YouTube’s post, they are right now working to expand the AI suggestion system to more of their creators in the near future but do not include specific countries, languages, nor time frames. If you have a YouTube channel located outside of the 10-country limit or the seven-language limit included on the help page, then this will be the list to reference prior to developing a clipping routine based on suggested content.

    #8111. Industry News: Higher Spend Came With Pricier Clicks For 14 B2B Google Advertisers via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1200 w)

    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Higher Spend Came With Pricier Clicks For 14 B2B Google Advertisers via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1200 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • To determine how much more the same non-branded Google Ads keywords cost 14 B2B advertisers per click during the months of April through September compared to the same time period last year, Grey Matter reviewed their Google Ads Search campaigns.
    • According to the agency report by Grey Matter issued in October, there was an increase of about 21% in cost-per-click (CPC) for the same keywords used by these 14 B2B advertisers, after accounting for changes in their spending, ad position and Quality Score.
    • Andy Hendricks, Grey Matter’s head of search, writes that he wanted to isolate what portion of the overall price change all advertisers experienced versus what portion was due to actions taken by each advertiser individually.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    To determine how much more the same non-branded Google Ads keywords cost 14 B2B advertisers per click during the months of April through September compared to the same time period last year, Grey Matter reviewed their Google Ads Search campaigns.

    According to the agency report by Grey Matter issued in October, there was an increase of about 21% in cost-per-click (CPC) for the same keywords used by these 14 B2B advertisers, after accounting for changes in their spending, ad position and Quality Score. The report gives a likely range of 1% to 44% for that figure. It is based on client Google Ads Search campaign data only, so it does not include Performance Max, Shopping or Display campaigns. All 14 come from the agency’s client base, and its search team runs SEO and paid search programs for B2B companies.

    Andy Hendricks, Grey Matter’s head of search, writes that he wanted to isolate what portion of the overall price change all advertisers experienced versus what portion was due to actions taken by each advertiser individually. Most available CPC benchmarks, such as published averages, do not account for this differentiation and simply provide an overall average CPC.

    In a recent development, grey Matter excluded broad match keywords since the searches they get matched to can change over time; keywords within Maximize Clicks campaigns also do not fit into the analysis. Brand and competitor keywords were also excluded from the overall estimate.

    Industry observers note that grey Matter’s analysis is based on tracking 1,349 non-brand keywords, each within one account, for six quarters (April 2025 to September 2026). The year-over-year comparison covers April through September 2026 versus those months a year prior.

    According to recent reports, the headline estimate was derived from a regression model using data from all 14 advertisers in the report which controlled for campaign spend, impression share lost to budget, top-of-page position, and Quality Score. Every advertiser was given equal weight regardless of how much it spends.

    Recent findings suggest that with no controls applied, the same keywords cost 29% more year over year. Adding the two spend-related controls lowered that to 22%, and position and Quality Score took it to 21%.

    According to recent reports, A second estimation technique used in this analysis was a keyword price index. This measure covered 11 advertisers who had sufficient matching keywords from quarter to quarter.

    Industry observers note that the report’s regression ties every 10% increase in campaign spend to about 1.4% higher CPCs, on top of the market increase, or roughly 11% for doubled spend. The report doesn’t give a likely range for that figure.

    Recent findings suggest that the most extreme case in the sample nearly quadrupled its non-brand Search spend year over year, and its same-keyword CPCs rose 132%. The report states that advertiser’s brand keywords, on a flat budget, rose about 4% year over year in the third quarter.

    The report sees a correlation between this pattern and automated bidding. It explains that a campaign using a strategy like Maximize Conversions spends a bigger budget by entering auctions it previously skipped, including higher positions, more competitive searches, and pricier times of day.

    In a recent development, for the 11 advertisers covered by the keyword price index, the overall year-over-year increase in average non-brand CPC was 36%, including the advertisers’ own choices. Of that, 22 points were attributed to the market, and three additional points were attributed to increased spending. There was a three-point deduction due to various types of keyword, match type and bid strategy changes, leaving 14 points that the report’s first three parts don’t explain.

    Grey Matter illustrates that breakdown in the chart below.

    The majority of those 14 points occurred at a few of the advertisers who saw an approximate doubling of their CPCs, which the report stated probably represented competition in their respective categories.

    Actual CPC changes ranged from a 30% decrease to a 121% increase. Ten of the 11 paid more for the same keywords, and nine paid more overall. One advertiser kept its spending flat and saw the same keywords rise by 20%. After shifting some of its budget to pricier phrase-match keywords, its overall CPC increased by 40%.

    It has been revealed that with only 14 advertisers in this report, the likely range for the 21% estimate is wide. When the biggest spender is removed from the report’s data, the estimate drops to around 17%, and its likely range of -2% to +40% includes zero. When broad match keywords are included, the estimate rises to around 31%. According to Hendricks, compared with a year ago, that same click most likely costs about 20% more currently, and the true figure “could be meaningfully higher or lower”.

    The report calls its findings correlation (and not proven causation). There are no references on the report page or in the PDF to the industries or markets of the advertisers used in the report, nor their currency.

    The report doesn’t provide any conversion rate or cost per lead information; so, it can’t show whether these advertisers saw better or worse results along with higher CPCs. Jyll Saskin Gales argued in an April column for Search Engine Journal (SEJ) that under Smart Bidding, a high CPC is often a sign of a healthy account, and that accounts should be evaluated based on CPA or ROAS.

    It has been revealed that alphabet’s third-quarter 10-Q reports that cost-per-click on Google Search & other properties rose 4% year over year in the quarter. Alphabet has defined this metric as click-driven revenue divided by total paid clicks and has cited several factors such as changes in the devices users access the internet on, geography, advertiser spending, and product mix as variables that affect it.

    The metric is based on paid clicks through Google Search properties and other platforms owned by Alphabet, so it will track with the price of the clicks and also the mix of clicks being counted. Grey Matter’s estimate instead tracks the same keywords across 14 advertisers.

    There is no direct confirmation or contradiction between the two figures since they measure entirely different things.

    Grey Matter’s report holds the keyword and the account constant, while raw CPC averages also rise when advertisers buy different clicks. With 14 clients of one agency and a range from 1% to 44%, the report is a reference point for B2B non-brand Search, not a forecast for any single account.

    You can run a same-keyword check on your own account by comparing the year-over-year change in what the same non-brand keywords cost with the change in the account’s average CPC. The report reads the gap between those two as the effect of keyword, match type and bid strategy changes. A same-keyword rise can still include the effect of higher spending.

    Grey Matter’s data runs through September, so it doesn’t include fourth-quarter auctions. For 2027 budgets, the report’s guidance is to scale them gradually and assess each step by how much the additional clicks cost. For campaigns on automated bidding such as Maximize Conversions, the report also suggests deciding what the additional conversions are worth before raising the budget, and setting a target to match.

    #8109. ChatGPT Ads Vs. Google Search Ads: What Early Data Shows via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2454 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    ChatGPT Ads Vs. Google Search Ads: What Early Data Shows via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2454 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that this past week, OpenAI rolled out cost-target bidding in its ChatGPT Ads platform.
    • The question for a paid search team is whether ChatGPT Ads now compete with Google Search Ads for advertising dollars, and whether the early results make a case for moving some of their budget to ChatGPT Ads.
    • According to recent reports, chatGPT Ads are competing for advertisers’ budgets.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that this past week, OpenAI rolled out cost-target bidding in its ChatGPT Ads platform. These ads first debuted in February. By Aug. 31, OpenAI reported that its ads product had achieved a $1 billion annualized run rate.

    The question for a paid search team is whether ChatGPT Ads now compete with Google Search Ads for advertising dollars, and whether the early results make a case for moving some of their budget to ChatGPT Ads.

    According to recent reports, chatGPT Ads are competing for advertisers’ budgets. However, the revenue metrics, survey data, and Google’s disclosures I reviewed give no indication of how many dollars have been diverted away from Google Search Ads to ChatGPT Ads.

    In terms of performance metrics, a ChatGPT ad click visit to an advertiser’s website generated about one-third the revenue of a paid search visit in U.S. traffic. The working paper in my Nov. 2 coverage provided the pooled revenue metric from 102 different websites with transaction and revenue tracking. The authors of that paper called the comparison descriptive. One of the authors’ universities also released a press statement saying that for every dollar an advertiser spends on ChatGPT Ads, they receive $0.52 back in revenue (compared to $3.40 for every dollar spent on Google Search).

    It has been revealed that only the first of these performance metrics was actually measured. The second figure combined that measured performance metric with the average cost-per-click pricing from one ChatGPT account and the median cost-per-click pricing from 16 paid search accounts. So the second figure varies with what an advertiser pays per click on each of those channels.

    Sources indicate that an Oct. 21 engineering post from OpenAI puts the run rate above $1 billion, with more than 100,000 advertisers having run ads since launch. Alphabet reported $63.35 billion in Search & other revenue for the third quarter, up 12%, which I covered on Oct. 28.

    On Alphabet’s earnings call, Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler cited “the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode” as one factor in slower Search growth, without giving a figure or a baseline.

    Google Search was the most-mentioned potential source of future ChatGPT ad spending in a Bank of America survey of 117 advertisers and agencies, TheStreet reported on Oct. 14. I haven’t seen the bank’s note, and the survey asked about plans. It doesn’t measure money that has moved.

    Industry observers note that neither company’s revenue figures show spending that shifted from one platform to the other. Google can continue to grow even as some advertisers move part of their budgets elsewhere.

    Industry observers note that in U.S. traffic, paid search generated $2.45 in revenue per session versus $0.89 with ChatGPT ad sessions, and transactions per session came to 1.17% against 0.37%.

    In a recent development, these pooled figures are based on a total of 60 weeks (through Aug. 22). For U.S. traffic, there were up to 28 weeks of ChatGPT ad sessions available for analysis.

    Sources indicate that kaiser and Schulze built a statistical model that controlled for website, device type, and week, and found that ChatGPT ad sessions generated lower rates of conversion and lower revenue per session than paid search. These results were robust even after removing individual advertisers. Out of 87 different advertisers who used both paid search and ChatGPT ads in U.S. traffic, 84 produced less revenue per session using ChatGPT ads.

    About 20% of the 102 websites studied were services, software, education, or finance websites. A table footnote explains that these websites report online conversions as bookings, leads, licenses, or sign-ups. However, the appendix calls a transaction a completed order, and it does not explain how the authors defined the relationship between these two types of metrics.

    Because advertisers chose to buy ChatGPT ads, the authors do not argue causally that ChatGPT is worse for advertisers than paid search. Rather, the authors view their work as “descriptive rather than causal,” a record of what these websites received from each advertising channel. They do not provide any evidence as to whether switching advertising dollars from paid search to ChatGPT under matched campaigns would be beneficial or detrimental to specific advertisers.

    Recent findings suggest that data for this study were donated by Grips Intelligence, where Kaiser, a former employee, works as a scientific advisor. The authors disclose that Kaiser has received a salary and virtual manufacturer shares from Grips Intelligence. The authors add that Grips Intelligence played no role in conducting the research described in this study.

    I contacted OpenAI about this study and received an email response from an OpenAI spokesperson saying the study “captures an earlier period of ChatGPT Ads’ development and extrapolates platform performance from a small sample.” The statement also says OpenAI has kept launching products since the ads launched, with Target CPA and Target CPC among the recent ones.

    Kaiser and Schulze express the difference in terms of value for money, revenue per session divided by click price. Treating each session as a paid click, that works out to about $0.52 per ad dollar for ChatGPT ($0.89 ÷ $1.72) and $3.40 for search ($2.45 ÷ $0.72), the two figures in the Frankfurt School release. The authors report that an ad visit from ChatGPT returns about one-third the value of a search visit at about 2.4 times the price. In their abstract, they state that ChatGPT ads are worth less than a sixth the value for money of Google Search. A table provides a reported ChatGPT price of 6.57 times what would be necessary to produce the same return on investment as Search.

    The Frankfurt School release cites the difference as “6.6 times better value for money” for Google and reports this in revenue per ad dollar. Its $0.52 and $3.40 figures are not provided within the body of the paper, and the release itself gives no explanation of how they were calculated.

    Recent findings suggest that there is no single price given for search, but rather a median price of $0.72, which comes from 16 mostly U.S. accounts that have linked Google Ads cost records. This price was not matched to the revenue each site generated.

    Sources indicate that the ChatGPT price is $1.72, which Opascope, an agency that runs paid media for clients, published in June. It covers one account and about $60,000 in spend over 15 days, on campaigns the agency scaled after they showed promise. Opascope wrote that the numbers aren’t an average of every test it launched, and it reported a 1.49x ROAS.

    Just one website in the sample did as well as Opascope’s account on both conversion rate and implied revenue per visit, and it had only nine ChatGPT ad sessions.

    In a recent development, the authors suggest that $1.72 is a conservative price as it is toward the low end of what practitioners report and below the $3-$5 OpenAI suggests be used as a starting maximum bid. Also, bidding is based on a maximum value, which is simply the cap an advertiser sets, not necessarily what each click will cost.

    In a recent development, resampling advertisers, while keeping the search price constant, gives the authors a range of $0.05 to $0.57 around a ChatGPT click price of about $0.26 that would match search’s return. Neither the ChatGPT click price nor the search price was changed.

    Advertising agencies have provided reports about their individual ChatGPT Ads campaign data for one advertiser, and separately, Brooke Osmundson reported in September that advertisers lacked the context to assess what they were being told by the numbers in such reporting.

    StubGroup provides ChatGPT ads management services. It ran Google ad campaigns and ChatGPT Ads campaigns for an advertiser who is a B2B compliance firm, for 30 days. The clicks on ChatGPT ads cost $0.76 a click. The clicks on Google search campaigns cost $10.46 a click. The cost per lead with ChatGPT was $92.21; with Google it was $157.57. The conversion rates were 0.8% with ChatGPT, and 6.64% with Google.

    The agency stated that while the advertising campaigns run through Google have years of optimization behind them, the leads generated through those campaigns appear to be converting to customers at a greater rate so far than the leads generated through ChatGPT ads. As a result of this, the cost per customer appears to be lower for Google. How many customers will be ultimately generated from the leads created through both platforms, StubGroup does not yet know, due to the client’s long sales cycle. Additionally, the agency said that the $0.76 per click was low when compared to the CPCs of some of its other clients.

    Workshop Digital used its own funds to pay for $2,319 worth of clicks on ChatGPT Ads. Workshop Digital’s CPC for ChatGPT ads was $3.14. For Google Search the CPC was $6.76. The CTR for Workshop Digital’s ChatGPT ads was 1.1%. For Google, the CTR was 5.2%.

    It has been revealed that workshop Digital received zero qualified leads from its ChatGPT ads, and two qualified leads from Google. The agency called the two types of advertising campaigns “not a direct comparison,” although it didn’t provide the spend amount or dates for Google Search as part of the comparison.

    Recent findings suggest that brafton, which sells ChatGPT Ads services, ran one click campaign with one ad from June 17 to Aug. 28. It spent $1,524.11 for 263 clicks and one form submission. Its Google and LinkedIn comparisons are outside benchmarks, and its director of paid media, Zach Shah, stated ChatGPT ads are “priced like search, but seem to behave like paid social.”.

    All three agency reports came down to what happened after the click, the stage with the fewest results.

    Additionally, OpenAI pointed me to some customer success stories via its ad page. One such example is from Jotform. According to this example, their cost per signup is approximately 30% less than with paid search. This figure is based on Jotform’s internal data collected during July; however, no costs are provided behind it, nor does it detail how the sign-ups were attributed. Sign-ups do not equal sales.

    Industry observers note that A paid search team may be asked to shift some portion of search spend to ChatGPT on the strength of a per-dollar figure based upon another party’s click costs. For an account paying a number of dollars per click on search, a number greater than the median of the paper’s data, there are differing starting points for making such comparisons. The basis for comparison that makes sense begins with actual spend and attributed revenue on each channel for the same period of time and using the same attribution settings.

    It has been revealed that the size of the test will affect how much an ecommerce account testing ChatGPT Ads can learn from a weak result. In all, 18 of the paper’s 102 sites recorded transactions resulting from ChatGPT ads; a single zero does not distinguish a weak channel from a small test. So when reporting to stakeholders, the number of sessions associated with each ad campaign belongs beside the revenue figures, because what a zero means is quite different depending on whether there were a few dozen or a few thousand visits.

    To compare results, lead-gen accounts also need to define a qualified lead in exactly the same terms on both channels and give those leads sufficient opportunity to convert. This is why StubGroup’s customer comparison is still open, since its lower-cost leads have not yet turned into lower-cost customers. While a cost per signup was used by Jotform as the metric in their case study, it is further removed from revenue than a cost per customer.

    Industry observers note that A team planning to present Ads Manager results either against the paper’s data or against its Google Ads performance metrics will first need to document its attribution settings. On OpenAI’s Measure Results page, Ads Manager conversion totals may include eligible view-through conversions, and advertisers select from a 7-day, 14-day, or 30-day click window. The view-through window can be set to one day or disabled, and both windows employ last-touch logic. The paper tracked visits that were attributable to the ad.

    Industry observers note that ads Manager tracks clicks, while analytics uses sessions. There can be differences between these two numbers. On OpenAI’s basics page, the company states ad-review crawling programs may access landing pages that contain tracking parameters, and analytics tools may report these visits as paid traffic even if they do not represent billable clicks. The Measure Results page provides additional explanations for these discrepancies, including redirects, consent settings, and browser-based blocking. Only by assuming clicks and sessions align can the release’s $0.52 be calculated from reported revenue per session and cost per click.

    Recent findings suggest that openAI’s ads FAQ says that they do not presently provide performance benchmarks. In addition, all four OpenAI help pages I reviewed provided a suggested starting bid, but none provided any information about click prices across advertisers. Neither did OpenAI’s statement. One advertiser’s cost is documented in the research paper. Each agency CPC was unique to its specific case.

    In a recent development, there were no monthly or bid-type breakdowns within the research paper, so it could not establish if the outcomes had been affected by OpenAI adding conversion-optimized campaigns in June. Data from the research paper ceased prior to when OpenAI implemented bid adjustments, which went into effect this month.

    It has been revealed that on Oct. 28, Google published an ads post stating that CTR for sponsored and organic product listings in AI Mode were similar. This was based on two weeks of internal U.S. data. Google gave no absolute rates. That was the single performance figure for AI Mode ads in my review of Google documentation.

    Industry observers note that two of the bid options now offered for latest ChatGPT Ads campaigns didn’t exist during the paper’s data window. Since Nov. 9, new conversion campaigns that want a cost target use Target CPA, and new click campaigns can use Target CPC, as I covered this week. The option with no cost target is Intelligent bidding, previously named Maximize Results, according to OpenAI’s bidding page. Beginning with Nov. 18, all values submitted using the legacy API bid fields are treated as the average-cost target when creating a new campaign or changing an ad group’s bid type. Max Bid and Max CPC will officially retire for existing campaigns on Jan. 1, 2027.

    Performance improvement is not shown in the upcoming options. Noting which objective, bid strategy, and attribution windows produced each fourth-quarter result will help a team decide if the metrics generated this year have enough similarities to compare next year.

    #8104. When The WordPress Plugin Patch Is The Security Risk: Why SEOs Should Pay Attention via @sejournal, @cshel

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1483 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    When The WordPress Plugin Patch Is The Security Risk: Why SEOs Should Pay Attention via @sejournal, @cshel

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1483 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I’ve worked with WordPress for more than 20 years, and for most of that time, keeping plugins updated has been among the first recommendations I’ve made when discussing website security.
    • For SEOs, this is more than an abstract concern about application security.
    • There have now been several recent WordPress incidents in which the trusted delivery mechanism was part of the problem, so let’s look at them together.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I’ve worked with WordPress for more than 20 years, and for most of that time, keeping plugins updated has been among the first recommendations I’ve made when discussing website security. It’s still good advice. Known vulnerabilities don’t become less dangerous because updating a site is inconvenient. The advice does carry an assumption that most of us rarely bother to examine: The revision we’re installing is the software its developer actually intended to release.

    For SEOs, this is more than an abstract concern about application security. When someone gets unauthorized access to a website, they may change the pages search engines see, introduce spam, tamper with redirects or indexing directives, or alter content without the editorial team’s knowledge. We can spend days investigating those symptoms as routine technical SEO problems while completely missing the reason they’re happening.

    There have now been several recent WordPress incidents in which the trusted delivery mechanism was part of the problem, so let’s look at them together. Examining them as a group is more illuminating than treating any single developer’s bad week as the big story.

    In a recent development, in June 2024, malicious updates appeared in several WordPress.org-hosted plugins, including Social Warfare. Wordfence’s investigation traced the compromise to developer accounts that used previously exposed credentials. The injected code could create administrator accounts and exfiltrate information, and researchers also found code designed to inject SEO spam. Roughly 35,000 installations were potentially exposed, although Wordfence couldn’t say how many had actually received the malicious updates. This is an especially useful example for our profession because the search-related damage wasn’t hypothetical: SEO spam was part of the attacker’s toolkit.

    According to recent reports, the following July, Gravity Forms disclosed that some copies of versions 2.9.11.1 and 2.9.12 available for manual download had been modified maliciously. According to Gravity Forms’ incident notice, the exposure was confined to particular manual downloads and Composer installations during July 9-10, 2025. Its separate automatic-patch service was not compromised. That distinction is notable. Two organizations could have been using ostensibly the same software while facing different risks because they obtained it through different channels.

    The more recent incident involved Rank Math SEO PRO. Rank Math’s incident disclosure notes a subset of version 3.0.123 packages downloaded or updated from October 15 at 20:02 UTC through October 16 at 07:12 UTC contained malware capable of compromising sites if activated. Rank Math removed the affected files, provided a clean 3.0.124 release, and advised affected customers to treat their installations as compromised. Wordfence’s advisory classified the matter as critical, with a CVSS score of 9.8. The free Rank Math plugin distributed through WordPress.org was not affected.

    Recent findings suggest that the three cases aren’t identical. One involved compromised developer accounts and poisoned repository updates, another concerned certain official manual downloads, and the third affected specific packages of a commercial SEO plugin. They do, however, share a problem that ordinary patch advice doesn’t adequately address: the site owner could get into trouble while obtaining software from a source they had good reason to trust.

    The Rank Math release timeline makes this unusually clear. According to the Rank Math changelog, version 3.0.123 appeared on Oct. 7, but the affected distribution window didn’t begin until Oct. 15. A site reporting that version number might have received the original clean files or a compromised package, depending on when it was updated. The installed version alone cannot resolve the question.

    Imagine managing a hundred client sites, or an enterprise portfolio with different brands, teams, and hosting providers. A security advisory comes out and somebody asks which properties are exposed. You can generate a tidy plugin inventory in minutes, but a spreadsheet of version numbers may not tell you what was actually installed. You need deployment timestamps, a record of the package source and, where possible, a way to compare the installed files with verified clean artifacts. Gravity Forms presented a related challenge because the installation method determined whether a particular download was implicated.

    According to recent reports, I don’t expect SEO practitioners to start auditing build pipelines. I do expect us to understand the limits of the information we routinely use to assess the health of a site. A dashboard that says a plugin is current doesn’t certify that the underlying files are trustworthy, and installing a clean update doesn’t necessarily remove accounts, backdoors, or stolen credentials left behind during a compromise.

    See also: From Plugins To Performance: What CMOs Need To Ask About Their WordPress Stack.

    In a recent development, in an enterprise environment, ownership of the website is often split across several groups. Marketing may choose the SEO software, development handles deployments, a hosting provider manages updates, and security gets called when someone notices suspicious activity. The SEO team is nevertheless expected to account for what the search engines can crawl, index, and understand. Those responsibilities overlap whether the organizational chart acknowledges it or not.

    Consider how a compromise might first appear in our regular work. Search Console begins reporting unfamiliar URLs. A crawl finds redirects that weren’t present last week. Canonical tags have changed without a corresponding release, or the rendered page no longer matches what the content team published. Depending on the attacker’s access, visitors, and crawlers might even be served different content. None of those observations proves a security breach, and I am not suggesting they were documented outcomes of the Rank Math incident. They are reasons to include compromise in the set of explanations we consider instead of assuming every unexpected technical change is a configuration error.

    In a recent development, that can be particularly consequential when an SEO has spotted a symptom but doesn’t know whom to tell. We don’t need to become the malware response team. We do need an established route for escalating suspicious changes, preferably one worked out before an incident has everyone comparing logs and asking who owns what. The 2024 SEO-spam injection case demonstrates why that coordination belongs in an SEO conversation rather than being filed away as somebody else’s security problem.

    See also: Who Owns Web Performance? Building A Framework For Digital Accountability.

    According to recent reports, wordPress itself has been looking at the trust problem. In June 2026, Matt Mullenweg declared Protect the Shire, initially describing a cooldown for latest plugin and theme releases before they reached sites through WordPress.org’s automatic-enhancement infrastructure. WordPress has also documented an automated security review process intended to identify potentially risky changes. The appeal is straightforward: a period of scrutiny may catch a compromised release before it is distributed widely, although delaying a genuine emergency fix creates a competing risk.

    It has been revealed that that protection has boundaries. Commercial plugins delivered by their vendors’ own enhancement systems don’t necessarily pass through the same WordPress.org review process, even though all the plugins appear in the same administrative interface. The FAIR project, operating under Linux Foundation governance, is taking a different approach by developing federated and independent software repositories. Protect the Shire focuses on checks within one major distribution route, while FAIR focuses on diversifying and verifying the routes themselves. Neither approach should be mistaken for a guarantee that every package reaching a website is safe.

    For people responsible for websites, the practical question is less about choosing a philosophical side in the distribution debate and more about knowing where each update originates and what checks apply along the way.

    Recent findings suggest that an SEO team doesn’t need to turn every plugin upgrade into a full security review. It would be useful, though, to know whether the organization retains update dates and deployment records, whether its commercial plugins use separate delivery systems, and who can verify file integrity when a vendor identifies an affected download window. It is equally worth knowing whether the recovery strategy extends beyond restoring yesterday’s backup to checking for unauthorized accounts, persistence mechanisms, and exposed credentials.

    I would also ask who receives reports of suspicious URLs, unexpected redirects, or changes to indexing instructions. We already know how to inspect rendered pages, compare crawls, review logs, and investigate search performance anomalies. Those skills make us quite capable of noticing that a website isn’t behaving as it should. They don’t automatically tell us why, which is where an agreed escalation process becomes useful.

    None of this is a reason to stop updating plugins, or an excuse to infer that a particular vendor is incompetent because it experienced an incident. The root cause of a compromise cannot responsibly be guessed from the fact that malware turned up in a package. What these examples do show is that familiar revision channels and reassuring version numbers aren’t the whole story. We spend a great deal of time checking what a website actually serves rather than trusting what a configuration screen states it should serve. It seems reasonable to apply some of that same curiosity to the software we’re installing on it.

    #8102. Yahoo becomes first licensee of ‘Spotify-like’ collective AI content licensing model

    📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1052 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    Yahoo becomes first licensee of ‘Spotify-like’ collective AI content licensing model

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1052 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that join us Dec.
    • AI content licensing has largely comprised of one-off deals between publishers and tech companies.
    • The deal means publishers of all sizes can license their content for use in Yahoo’s AI-powered search engine Scout and get paid based on how that content is used.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    AI content licensing has largely comprised of one-off deals between publishers and tech companies. RSL, which is being renamed The Internet Licensing Collective (ILC), is pursuing a collective model instead, with Yahoo as its first licensee.

    The deal means publishers of all sizes can license their content for use in Yahoo’s AI-powered search engine Scout and get paid based on how that content is used.

    Digiday spoke with ILC co-founder Doug Leeds about how this model works and how publishers can earn revenue.

    Industry observers note that A licensee like Yahoo pays a blanket licensing fee for access to content in the collective. Leeds declined to say how much Yahoo was paying, but the fee is tied to the “demand-side revenue.”  Yahoo declined to be interviewed for this story.

    As a licensee’s business scales, the amount available for publisher compensation can grow as well.

    “It allows businesses that are making a lot of money off of the content to keep that content in place and sustainable. But it also allows for entrants,” Leeds said. “As the revenue scales, the percentage scales. So more money comes out. But that also means that entrants can come in, and there can be fresh use cases and new players and new products, and all of that’s vital to the evolution of what we’re doing to the market.”.

    Sources indicate that A new report out today from publishing analytics firm Mather Economics estimated that collective licensing for AI could generate publisher compensation equal to 15% to 35% of AI company revenue, a potential market that in three years could surpass the U.S. display advertising market. The analysis was based on the current annual revenue from the two biggest frontier models, OpenAI and Anthropic, and an economic model created by Mather Economics incorporating AI training-data scaling laws.

    Leeds likened the licensing collective to a Spotify-like model.

    Sources indicate that “It’s kind of like Spotify, but also a song is a song is a song, and content is very different. And so we had to come up with these rules that made sense specifically for digital content,” Leeds remarked.

    Leeds stated ILC worked closely with its publisher collective to figure out those rules. The first step was to define a “segmented royalty pool.” This separates licensing revenue by AI company, rather than combining payments into a single fund shared by all participating publishers. That means publishers only receive a share of the revenue generated by AI products that actually use their content.

    Recent findings suggest that more AI and tech companies are testing pay-per-value licensing models. Digiday has previously reported that Google and Microsoft are testing and developing these models, which compensate publishers when their content meaningfully contributes to AI-generated responses, rather than paying based on how frequently their content is used. It’s a shift from flat-fee licensing deals to more dynamic pricing, based on the value publishers’ content delivers to AI companies.

    When an AI manufacturer signs a licensing agreement with ILC, that money goes into its own royalty pool. Rather than combining all these payments into one enormous fund and distributing them across participating publishers, ILC keeps the royalty pools separate.

    In a recent development, this protects specialized publishers from having their revenue diluted, Leeds explained. A general-purpose AI search engine like Yahoo Scout might use large quantities of content from hundreds or thousands of publishers, but a specialized healthcare AI product might use a much smaller amount of content from a handful of medical-focused publishers, and that specialized content could be considerably more valuable to the healthcare tech giant, he said.

    ILC wanted to ensure that a publisher’s compensation reflects the value of the AI product using its content, not simply how much content it contributes to the overall licensing ecosystem.

    Industry observers note that “An AI vertical in health might be very low volume, but much higher specific value. So if your content gets used in that, you should split that high value, not get diluted by all the content that got used by Yahoo,” Leeds said.

    Over 3,000 publishers are now part of the ILC, he noted.

    The payments are determined by what Leeds called “allocation rules.” These take into account how much content is used, like grounding, retrieval or displayed in an AI response, and whether the publisher is credited or cited as a source.

    Sources indicate that for example, an AI product that uses a publisher’s content to check a fact might receive a lower allocation than one that displays detailed election results and explicitly credits the Associated Press, Leeds said. He did not disclose the exact formula used to calculate each publisher’s share.

    The allocation rules are intended to discourage AI companies from choosing content simply because it’s cheaper, and instead incentivize them to use what they consider the highest-quality sources, he noted.

    RSL, which stood for the Really Simple Licensing (RSL), was two things: a group of publishers working on a collective licensing agreement, and the organization behind the RSL Protocol, a standard that publishers can use in robots.txt to describe in machine-readable language what their terms of service are. Publishers can ask AI companies for a pay-per-crawl or pay-per-inference fee through the RSL Protocol, for example. “Thousands” are currently using this standard, Leeds mentioned.

    But Leeds wanted a new name for the non-profit organization that reflected the publisher collective, to make it clear that this is a licensing model that any publisher can join, he noted.

    Recent findings suggest that leeds remarked ILC is presently in talks with “some” of the major AI companies interested in the licensing collective. He declined to name which ones.

    It has been revealed that “You can do a deal with a one-off, and that’s fantastic. But that doesn’t invest in the infrastructure of content in general,” he said.

    More brands are gravitating toward live shopping, a growing channel that is set to play an outsized influence on shopping trends.

    Bustle Digital Group has teamed up with Profound to help brands like Pampers and Innisfree boost their visibility in AI recommendations in a newly introduced GEO-offering.

    Twitch is swinging big with a new short-form content push that should help more creators get discovered on-platform.

    #8100. CMS Market Share Trends: Top Content Management Systems (Nov 2026) via @sejournal, @theshelleywalsh

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1945 w)

    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    CMS Market Share Trends: Top Content Management Systems (Nov 2026) via @sejournal, @theshelleywalsh

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1945 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • WordPress might remain the dominant force in content management systems (CMS) for now, but market share has dropped since its peak in 2022 to under 60%.
    • WordPress still remains a substantial lead over its nearest rival, Shopify, but is this an indication of a downturn for WordPress, or for the general usage of CMS?
    • In a recent development, shopify has continued its growth across all surveyed websites, with Wix and Squarespace also maintaining their growth trajectory.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    WordPress might remain the dominant force in content management systems (CMS) for now, but market share has dropped since its peak in 2022 to under 60%. According to W3Techs on Nov. 13, 2026, WordPress now has a CMS market share of 57.9%. Looking at historical data, WordPress dipped under 60% in 2016, 2017, and 2019, but this is the lowest drop since 2013.

    WordPress still remains a substantial lead over its nearest rival, Shopify, but is this an indication of a downturn for WordPress, or for the general usage of CMS?

    In a recent development, shopify has continued its growth across all surveyed websites, with Wix and Squarespace also maintaining their growth trajectory. In fact, apart from Joomla and Drupal, which fell, and Webflow, which held flat, all other top CMS have increased market share, indicating WordPress is on a downturn to the benefit of other platforms.

    This report breaks down the current CMS landscape, compares the top platforms, and outlines the latest shifts in market share and usage.

    According to W3Techs, 67.7% of websites have a CMS, and Netcraft reports over 323 million domains.

    From this, we can assume that the current market size for content management systems has risen to 218.8 million websites.

    *Approximations extrapolated from W3Techs and Netcraft data.

    There are two different measures throughout this report: usage is a platform’s percentage of all surveyed websites, while market share is its percentage of websites with a known CMS.

    Sources indicate that data from W3Techs, Nov. 13, 2026. (WooCommerce and Elementor are not listed in the table above as they’re WordPress plugins and not standalone CMS platforms.).

    *Graphs are separated due to the dominance of the WordPress market share.

    According to recent reports, wordPress remains the most widely used CMS. Its usage across all surveyed websites rose from 23.3% in January 2015 to 43.2% in January 2022, before falling to 39.2% today.

    Sources indicate that but its long-standing growth curve is now in a downturn. Its CMS market share has fallen by approximately 7.3 percentage points from the January 2022 figure of 65.2%. Since Jan. 1, 2026, it has declined from 60.2% to 57.9%, while all-website usage has dropped from 43.0% to 39.2%.

    According to recent reports, those figures do not show why individual sites changed platforms. For teams using WordPress, plugin compatibility, core updates, and security management remain practical considerations.

    Read more: Should You Still Use WordPress?

    It has been revealed that as the second-most popular standalone CMS in W3Techs’ current listing, Shopify’s market share stands at 7.9%, and it is used by 5.4% of all websites surveyed. Both measures have increased from Jan. 1, 2026, when they stood at 7.0% and 5.0%, respectively.

    Market share is not a performance benchmark. For a separate, historical comparison of technical performance, see our 2025 Core Web Vitals CMS rankings.

    From an SEO and business perspective, Shopify’s growing footprint makes it a platform worth evaluating alongside the features, costs, and technical requirements of an online store.

    According to recent reports, wix now powers 4.2% of websites surveyed and holds 6.2% of the known-CMS market. Its market share has increased from 5.8% at the start of 2026, but its all-website usage remains at 4.2% at the displayed precision.

    Wix has benefited from its positioning beyond a lightweight website builder that consistently invests in branding and platform capabilities, making it a viable contender for mid-market adoption.

    Squarespace’s CMS market share has grown from 0.5% in January 2015 to 3.6% today, with 2.4% of all websites surveyed now using the platform.

    Its growth could be attributed to the increasing demand for low-maintenance, design-forward platforms that are easily accessible to small businesses and individuals.

    In a recent development, read more: WordPress Vs. Squarespace – Which One Is Better?

    It has been revealed that in contrast to all the other top CMS surveyed, Joomla and Drupal have continued to lose CMS market share, now accounting for 1.6% and 0.9%, respectively. At the start of 2026, those figures were 1.9% and 1.1%.

    Once platforms in favor with web developers and amateur coders, this shift likely reflects a broader trend where more user-friendly, SaaS-based platforms capture the attention of small businesses and non-technical users.

    Recent findings suggest that webflow, which last year looked like a growing contender, now holds at 1.2% of the known-CMS market, unchanged from Jan. 1, 2026. Its usage across all surveyed websites has slipped from 0.9% to 0.8%.

    Between Jan. 1 and Nov. 13, 2026, the proportion of websites using none of W3Techs’ monitored CMS platforms rose from 28.6% to 32.3%, an increase of approximately 3.7 percentage points. During the same period, WordPress usage fell from 43.0% to 39.2% of all surveyed websites.

    In a recent development, that reverses the earlier downward trend in the “no CMS” category. It is not proof that those sites are custom-coded or have abandoned a CMS, as the category means that no monitored CMS was detected.

    According to recent reports, since January 2024, Joomla’s CMS market share has fallen from 2.5% to 1.6%, while Drupal’s has declined from 1.6% to 0.9%. Over the longer period, Joomla has dropped from 8.6% in January 2015 and Drupal from 5.1% in the same month.

    Recent findings suggest that they’ve slipped from the No. 2 and No. 3 spots to No. 5 and No. 10, overtaken by faster-growing platforms like Wix and Squarespace in 2022.

    Joomla, in particular, had strong momentum early on – briefly surpassed WordPress in search interest until around 2008, according to Google Trends – but it hasn’t kept pace with modern platform demands.

    Shopify is the platform with the most interest overtaking WordPress.

    Why did these popular content management systems decline so much?

    It has been revealed that it’s most likely due to the strength of third-party support for WordPress with plugins and themes, making it much more accessible. But the rise of supported themes and plugins for Shopify is starting to gain on WordPress.

    The growth of website builders, such as Wix and Squarespace, indicates that small businesses want a more straightforward managed solution, and they have started to nibble on market share from the bottom. Although, it does not establish that customers moved directly from Joomla or Drupal to those platforms.

    Over the period from November 2025 to November 2026, the CMS market share of:.

    Growth has slowed sharply for Wix and Squarespace, while Shopify’s has accelerated from 4.6% to 16.2% and taken the lead against the others in a reversal from the last reported period (Wix was growing by 32.6%, Squarespace 9.7%, and Shopify by 4.6%).

    In a recent development, as mentioned above, SaaS web builders don’t require coding knowledge and offer an opportunity for a small business to get a web presence swiftly. The rise of Shopify could be attributed to an influx to the platform from WooCommerce, as the WordPress alternative.

    Recent findings suggest that wordPress is not known as a complicated platform to use, but it does require some coding knowledge and an understanding of how websites are built. On the other hand, a website builder is a much easier route to market, without the need to understand what is happening in the back end.

    Elementor is the most widely used WordPress page builder, installed on 18.2% of all websites with a known CMS and 12.3% of all sites surveyed (not shown below) – more than Wix and Squarespace combined – though it functions as a plugin within WordPress, not a standalone CMS.

    It has been revealed that while not a CMS on its own, it is a major part of the WordPress ecosystem. Its figures overlap with WordPress and should not be added to WordPress’s market share or usage.

    W3Techs also compares platforms by overall popularity and traffic rank. The ranking bars measure a platform’s share among sites with a known CMS within each ranking tier, rather than its share of all websites.

    The WordPress, Joomla, and Drupal comparison above shows Drupal with a smaller overall footprint but a stronger presence among highly ranked sites. WordPress remains much more widely used overall.

    Wix and Squarespace have lower representation in the top-ranked groups than in the overall known-CMS sample. That is a traffic-ranking distinction, not a direct measure of business size or the quality of the software.

    Elementor gives site owners a visual way to build within WordPress. For businesses comparing drag-and-drop tools, the practical question remains how the builder fits their design, maintenance, and SEO requirements.

    WooCommerce has seen a decline to 11.4% of websites with a known CMS, while Shopify has increased to 7.9%.

    Industry observers note that wooCommerce powers 7.7% of all websites surveyed, compared with Shopify’s 5.4%. As a WordPress-based ecommerce platform, it is included within the WordPress ecosystem rather than listed as a separate standalone CMS in the top 10 above.

    Recent findings suggest that W3Techs’ separate ecommerce-system survey uses a different denominator: websites using an ecommerce system that W3Techs monitors. On that measure, WooCommerce has a 47.0% share and Shopify 32.7%. Those figures do not measure sales, revenue, or every online store worldwide.

    In comparison to other ecommerce CMS platforms, WooCommerce is still dominant right now.

    Recent findings suggest that it has more market share than its competitors combined: Shopify (7.9%) + PrestaShop (0.7%) + OpenCart (0.4%). But it is losing ground, and this could be correlated to the decline of WordPress and users moving to other platforms. It will be interesting to see if Shopify overtakes in the next year.

    In a recent development, the ranking comparison also shows why overall adoption is only part of the picture. Shopify has a stronger presence than WooCommerce in several of the higher-ranked groups, even though WooCommerce has the larger overall share of the known-CMS sample.

    Shopify surged during the pandemic, with market share growing by 52.9% from 2020 to 2021 and then 26.9% from 2021 to 2022, outpacing every other platform. After a dip in 2023, it recovered in 2024 and has reached 7.9% market share this year.

    As the market changes, platform choice affects site architecture, plugin availability, and technical SEO flexibility.

    WordPress continues to lead, but its gradual decline marks a turning point. SaaS competitors such as Shopify, Wix, and Squarespace are steadily gaining traction, offering streamlined platforms that appeal to most businesses.

    If more SMBs are switching to website builders, understanding the limitations and intricacies of these platforms for SEO could be a competitive advantage. CMS adoption determines how efficiently teams can build, secure, and optimize sites at scale.

    The one area I am most interested in is how AI and vibecoding might impact CMS platforms and if there will be a rise in websites without a CMS.

    Shopify now runs on 5.4% of all websites surveyed, not just sites with a CMS. With its increasing footprint, specializing in Shopify SEO could be a strategic move for an SEO professional.

    It has been revealed that wix and Squarespace remain crucial alternatives, too. Getting fluent in their ecosystems could help you serve businesses with different development and maintenance requirements.

    The reality is that WordPress remains the largest ecosystem in this survey, while other platforms give business leaders and SEO professionals an opportunity to diversify their expertise.

    Understanding the strengths and limitations of various CMS platforms can inform strategic decisions and align with evolving market demands.

    It has been revealed that CMS usage and market-share data collected from W3Techs on Nov. 13, 2026. Historical comparisons use the dates stated in the text. Percentages are rounded by the source, so calculated changes are approximate. See the W3Techs methodology page for how the survey is compiled. Google Trends measures search interest separately.

    Why user-first ad experiences build the strongest app businesses

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (949 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
    • Today’s mobile consumers are searching, streaming, scrolling and shopping in bursts as they go about their day.
    • Industry observers note that capturing value in those seconds is remarkably difficult.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Today’s mobile consumers are searching, streaming, scrolling and shopping in bursts as they go about their day. According to RealityMine, the average smartphone user interacts with around 18 different apps per day, racking up to 200 app sessions daily.¹ In each of those moments, attention is won second by second — and lost just as swiftly.

    Industry observers note that capturing value in those seconds is remarkably difficult. When audience acquisition is expensive, and engagement is just as hard to earn, app studios cannot afford ad experiences that cause churn.

    It has been revealed that in-app ads are a core part of the overall app experience, yet monetization and user retention are still too often treated as competing priorities. The assumption is that earning more revenue requires heavier ad loads, which damages the user experience, while protecting that experience means leaving money on the table.

    “Disruptive ads have a severe, compounding negative impact on both current engagement and future user acquisition,” mentioned Scott Sheffer, vp of global partnerships on Google’s sell-side monetization team. “Disruptive ads not only drive current users away but also prompt negative reviews, discouraging future users from downloading the app. Seems intuitive, but now there is data to back that.”.

    According to a Deloitte and Google AdMob study, a single encounter with a disruptive ad increases a user’s likelihood to churn by 6% to 7%.² When those experiences repeat, 52% of gamers say they leave the app for good.³ On the flip side, high-quality, user-first ad experiences actively protect engagement: 72% of gamers keep playing when ads are high quality⁴ and 20% report playing more often.⁵ These metrics demonstrate how ad quality serves as a fundamental growth engine beyond a cosmetic choice.

    “App economics are not an either-or,” Sheffer said. “With quality ad experiences, customers can stay engaged longer and you can naturally unlock more opportunities for other revenue streams, like in-app purchases and subscriptions.”.

    Sustainable revenue growth doesn’t come from aggressive ad strategies that disrupt audiences. It comes from pairing global, premium demand with uncompromising quality controls. This foundation protects in-app experiences and grows long-term revenue opportunities.

    To truly scale revenue, safety cannot be restricted to a single network. Google built its advanced ad quality protections to extend across the AdMob network and participating third-party bidders. This means studios can filter out unwanted categories, block problematic creatives and apply brand rules across their bidding partners from a single interface.

    Toss, a financial app manufacturer from South Korea’s Viva Republica, chose AdMob as its mediation partner to grow revenue through quality ad experiences. By using AdMob’s real-time ad review and rigorous A/B testing capabilities, Toss grew ad revenue 891% year over year while driving a 17% uplift in next-day retention for one of its app’s features.⁶.

    Across the wider app ecosystem, SensorTower data shows that apps primarily using AdMob’s mediation platform have a 25% higher 60-day and 90-day user retention rate than apps primarily using competing platforms.⁷˒⁸.

    Recent findings suggest that “Our focus on quality and long-term growth explains why, in recent research, Kantar found that app developers rank Google AdMob No. 1 in both providing high-quality ads and in maximizing revenue — ahead of other leading app monetization platforms,” said Sheffer.⁹˒¹⁰.

    As app development cycles continue to accelerate, monetization operations must keep pace.

    Industry observers note that instead of losing critical hours to manual creative review, app developer teams can lean on Google’s intelligent brand safety systems to help. For example, improved AI models in the Ad Review Center can swiftly flag off-brand creatives for removal. In parallel, click-through-rate-based filtering helps to block deceptive ad behaviors like forced redirects, fake buttons or hidden close icons. This tactic helps developers eliminate these formats across all bidding sources before they trigger player frustration.

    For ads that need a closer look, revamped search filters in the Ad Review Center help teams find creatives faster — such as sorting creatives by revenue to prioritize the reviews that impact the bottom line.

    By protecting both developer velocity and creative safety, teams can more easily grow revenue and focus on the user experience. That balance of automation and control is why a Kantar analysis showed app developers rate Google AdMob 1.5x higher than the competitor average for making it easy to monetize apps.¹¹.

    Delivering on ad quality and making monetization simple is only the start. Google is building new tools to help teams catch performance anomalies, implement and validate ad placements and preserve player retention.

    “We believe enterprise-grade AI and monetization requires secure, native integration across the tools you already use today,” Sheffer noted. “That is why Google AdMob is continuously expanding what an advanced monetization platform can do. By shifting routine diagnostics, complex yield optimizations and brand safety into intelligent, automated workflows, we are bridging the gap between app development and ad operations — so you can build, test and ship ad setups with the same speed and safety as your app code.”.

    Partner insights from Google Publisher Connections.

    It has been revealed that publisher Connections brings together publishers, buyers and their audiences. Across a suite of trusted platforms — from Google Ad Manager, AdMob and AdSense, to their buyer solutions — they deliver continuous innovation and powerful results.

    The e-commerce giant is central for many consumer brand advertisers, but measurement changes could throw a wrench into their aims for next year.

    More brands are gravitating toward live shopping, a growing channel that is set to play an outsized influence on shopping trends.

    A latest product manager role will explore ad-related monetization, suggesting the platform could make ads a bigger part of its business.

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1370 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    Future of Marketing Briefing: Inside Guinness’ go-slow approach to creators

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1370 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that join us Dec.
    • Recent findings suggest that this Future of Marketing Briefing covers the latest in marketing for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Friday at 10 a.m.
    • For a brand that takes nearly two minutes to pour, Guinness is in no great hurry where creators are concerned.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Recent findings suggest that this Future of Marketing Briefing covers the latest in marketing for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Friday at 10 a.m. ET. More from the series →.

    For a brand that takes nearly two minutes to pour, Guinness is in no great hurry where creators are concerned.

    It has been revealed that it has little interest in signing up creators en masse the way some of its rivals have. Rather, that side of its marketing will build organically, at the brand’s own pace, said global marketing manager and head of sport Paddy Carberry.

    Speaking during a live recording of the Unofficial Partner sports business podcast in partnership with agency Sid Lee, the marketer made the case for why: “The minute we start getting involved in trends and social media stuff, all of a sudden we become the dad dancing at the disco.”.

    Sources indicate that few things kill a brand’s cool faster than chasing it — and Guinness has plenty to lose these days. Carberry traces much of the turnaround to the pandemic. With the pubs shut and most suppliers chasing unpaid bills, Guinness “extended our credit to all of our customers,” he continued, and it sent its unsold beer off to fertilize Christmas trees. Landlords and bar staff noticed, and that counted for a lot, since in Carberry’s view nobody has more sway over what gets ordered than the person pulling the pint. The brand’s ads played up the wait for the pub to come back so by the time the doors reopened, Guinness was one of the pints people had missed.

    Guinness’ apprehension toward creators, therefore, is understandable. Its cool was earned behind the bar and a flood of sponsored posts could undo that work faster than a badly poured pint. Creators still played their part in the revival, mind. Most of them, however, weren’t on the payroll. London’s pint-rating accounts turned judging other people’s pours into a spectator sport and Kim Kardashian and Olivia Rodrigo did the brand plenty of favors without a Diageo brief. “Splitting the G” had been doing the rounds in pubs since at least 2018 when it earned an Urban Dictionary entry.

    It has been revealed that over that period Guinness has nudged things along where it made sense. Its social team spent 2014 amplifying rituals drinkers had already invented and adding a layer of curated influencer partnerships. As Carberry tells it, the skill lies in knowing which moments to touch and which to leave well alone.

    “While we lean into creators in appropriate ways we probably do less than you’d expect,” said Carberry.

    And yet Carberry and his team seem more connected with how people view the brand than ever. Its “Singing Pints” campaign, which launched in 2023 but was revived over the summer, was inspired by the viral #SingingGuinness TikTok Trend where pubgoers poked faces into the creamy foam head of their pints and blew across them to make the foam “mouths” open and close.

    “We took what was the consumer playing with the brand and amplified it into a TV spot,” remarked Carberry. “That was one of most successful pieces of content for the last 10 years.”.

    Industry observers note that creators are clearly part of Guinness’ future, just in a smaller role than the creator economy narrative would have it. Guinness seems more focused on community management and how creators fold into that. That puts it closer to where influencer marketing began. Before follower counts became a media currency, brands courted bloggers with tight-knit readerships and locals whose word carried on their own patch. The industry then spent a decade turning those relationships into a reach game. Guinness still takes part but it does so carefully.

    “Guinness might not consciously be signing people up as creators, but ‘splitting the G’ has turned plenty of ordinary drinkers into exactly that,” said Jon Williams, founder and chief creative officer at Freedom Works. “They’re creating something to show their mates, in a pub, around a brand. That should be an ambition for any marketer: giving people something they want to do in real life, which then gives them something worth sharing on a screen.”.

    It also has less room for error than most brands. In the U.K., anyone drinking in an alcohol ad has to be, and look, over 25. The brand also can’t advertise anywhere where more than a quarter of the audience is under 18 and that’s a hard thing to promise on TikTok. The Advertising Standards Authority banned Au Vodka ads last year for exactly that, and Cranberry noted that advertising regulations are “stricter and stricter around the world.”.

    “While these results are above what we expected for this quarter, this level of growth is, of course, well below the level of growth that we expect from ourselves in the future… I’m encouraged by our progress, and I am proud of our team. But I want to be very clear, we are not satisfied.”.

    — The Trade Desk’s CEO Jeff Green when discussing the tech giant’s quarterly revenues during the Q3 2026 earnings call.

    34%: Average percentage of a brand’s video that TikTok viewers watch on the app.

    $3.4 million: Amount by which The Trade Desk’s revenue declined during Q3 2026.

    $34.1 million: Total CTV revenue that Nexxen reported during its Q3 earnings.

    14%: Percentage by which Nvidia’s stock dropped following the resignation of its CEO.

    OpenAI’s fresh business agents give brands a free way into the conversation it’s also selling as an ad.

    OpenAI now lets brands publish a free “business agent” in ChatGPT, the organic twin of the sponsored agent it’s been selling as an ad since September.

    Why brands like Anthropologie are commissioning creator-created shows instead of posts.

    Brands like Anthropologie are paying creators to make original series, such as short comedy shows, rather than one-off sponsored posts, betting it builds lasting audience habits, sometimes with money moved out of traditional influencer budgets.

    LinkedIn brings its B2B ad targeting to U.K. connected TVs.

    LinkedIn is bringing its CTV ads to the U.K., letting advertisers target streaming viewers by job role, industry seniority, though agencies doubt the premium pricing and targeting accuracy are worth it.

    Reddit dangles seasonal ad credits but advertisers still want better proof it works all year round.

    Reddit is offering Q4 ad credits to win advertisers, but doubts about its measurement and ad tools make it hard to turn seasonal spend into year-round budgets, and slowing ad revenue growth and falling search referral traffic don’t help.

    EU indicates ‘rabbit hole’ video feeds on TikTok violate its digital rules.

    The EU says TikTok’s For You feed breaks its digital rules by pulling consumers into harmful content “rabbit holes”, and it’s demanding redesigns, with fines up to 6% of revenue possible, per AP News.

    Microdrama Platform Canvas Aims to Build a Netflix-Style Brand Around Creator-Led Shows.

    Recent findings suggest that canvas, a Latest York microdrama studio, wants to build a Netflix-style brand by fully funding short series made with creators, per Net Influencer. Creators get a 30% to 50% share of the IP, and Canvas makes its money from app subscriptions.

    Sources indicate that just a quarter of U.S. adults trust creators to always disclose brand deals.

    A Morning Consult survey of about 2,000 Americans found only around a quarter of U.S. adults think creators reliably disclose paid brand deals, which points to a sizeable trust gap, per Tube Filter.

    ByteDance reportedly prepares a Muse-like AI agent within weeks.

    Industry observers note that byteDance is reportedly weeks away from launching a Muse-style AI assistant, according to The Next Web. Co-founder Zhang Yiming has reportedly told staff it may take until 2029 or 2030 to compete with Anthropic and OpenAI at the frontier.

    A fresh product manager role will explore ad-related monetization, suggesting the platform could make ads a bigger part of its business.

    CEOs have never cared much for holdcos. Enterprise solutions, on the other hand, get a meeting.

    Marketers expect their 2026 holiday revenue to increase 1% to 31% or more in comparison to their 2025 holiday revenue.
