    10 Stylish Sofa Covers to Totally Refresh Your Living Room Before the Holidays

    📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1823 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housebeautiful

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that life at home gets messy with its regular residents, and it gets even crazier when guests come over.
    • According to recent reports, whether you opt for a tightly-fitted silhouette or a looser, blanket-style slipcover, a high-quality sofa cover can totally refresh your space.
    • There are hundreds of sofa cover options available, so below, our shopping team did the hard part for you.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that life at home gets messy with its regular residents, and it gets even crazier when guests come over. Hosting season demands the most of our couches, as they become extra seats for family dinner or makeshift beds for overnight stays. It’s not always feasible to swap out your sofa just because the upholstery has seen better days. That’s where the mighty sofa cover comes in.

    According to recent reports, whether you opt for a tightly-fitted silhouette or a looser, blanket-style slipcover, a high-quality sofa cover can totally refresh your space. Just think about it: a dated, yellowing couch suddenly looks fresh and brand new. You can even go bold and experiment with patterned options, without the commitment of buying a whole new piece. Pro tip: patterns are also a great way to hide stains.

    There are hundreds of sofa cover options available, so below, our shopping team did the hard part for you. We hunted down nine options for different types of couches, including an editor-tested and approved option. Plus, we chatted with interior designer Tiffany Leigh for tips on styling sofa covers, keeping them clean, and more.

    Additional copy from Jessica Cherner.

    Sources indicate that velvet couches are having a moment, so if you want in on the trend but don't want to toss out your current sofa, enter this sumptuous sofa slipcover. Stretch the base piece to fit around a sofa measuring 72 to 96 inches, then cover three cushions with the included covers. The fabric is extra soft, so you feel like you're sitting on a high-end sofa at a fraction of the price. "My family used this velvet slipcover to bring a dated, faded blue sofa back to life in a trendy ivory velvet that looked like it could be at home in any furniture showroom," Associate Shopping Editor Janae McKenzie states. "Even better: it was so soft against my skin that I fell asleep on it during movie night more times than I'm proud of.".

    Material: Velvet | Colors: 23 | Care: Machine washable.

    Recent findings suggest that full-blown tassels might feel like too much texture to add to your everyday sofa, but some subtle fringe is a welcome inclusion. This blanket-style cover drapes easily over a two-three cushion couch, and it’s made of a non-slip fabric designed to stay in place. Even with the rowdiest kids and pets.

    Material: Chenille | Colors: 18 | Care: Machine washable.

    Just because you want to protect your couch doesn’t mean you have to give up dreams of elegant white furniture. This extra-large cream couch cover actually comes in two pieces, so it’s perfect to cover an L-Shaped or U-Shaped sectional. You can protect the chaise arm with ease, and it’s still stain-resistant and machine-washable.

    Material: Chenille | Colors: 11 | Care: Machine washable.

    Sofas are often the center of your family room, which means they can be a high-traffic, mess-prone area. Whether you're worried about pet or kid accidents, or an errant wine spill during book club, this waterproof cover could be a great solution to protect your beloved furniture. The stretchy jacquard fabric is leakproof and fits snug to your cushions and frame.

    Material: Polyester-spandex | Colors: 16 | Care: Machine washable.

    According to recent reports, want to add trendy bouclé upholstery to your home but are hesitant to commit to it 24/7? This slipcover offers the best of both worlds. The fitted fabric makes it appear as though you bought the sofa in this style, but you can easily swap it out when you want a different look or feel. It's all in one piece for your sofa's frame, so you can still add the throw pillows of your choice.

    Material: Polyester-spandex | Colors: One | Care: Machine washable.

    This couch cover is basically your favorite waffle blanket, but it covers the entire sofa. The linen is stonewashed, so it's already soft from the first time you sit on it. We love the neutral and earthy tones it's available in, especially this cinnamon color. If you're unsure whether you'll love it, take advantage of the 30-day trial period.

    Material: Cotton-linen blend | Colors: Two | Care: Machine washable.

    The stretchy spandex of this sofa cover makes it a great choice for an inexpensive, colorful refresh. The textured jacquard fabric comes in seven sizes and a wide range of 30 colors, so you're sure to find something that suits your sofa and style. It's also machine washable, so feel free to enjoy a few wine nights on your sofa, especially if you opt for one of the darker colors.

    Material: Polyester-spandex | Colors: 30 | Care: Machine washable.

    In a recent development, for a much more casual look (and application process), this geometrical sofa cover fits like a big textured blanket, so it'll avoid pooling on one end of the sofa. Plus, it can be used for several purposes: it's a great picnic blanket whenever you decide to change up the look of your sofa. It's bordered with adorable tassels, and the chenille fabric is also durable enough to withstand your furry friends.

    Material: Chenille | Colors: 48 | Care: Machine washable.

    Sources indicate that if the idea of investing a small fortune in a white couch sounds like a risky idea, opt for a white sofa slipcover instead. This blanket-like cover is oversized for a luxurious, draping look, and it's available in two light linen shades. It will give your living room that coveted clean, modern feel without triggering your anxiety. The best part? This one is machine washable, so anytime you notice a mark or stain, simply pop it in the wash, and it will be good as latest.

    Material: Chenille and linen | Colors: Two | Care: Machine washable.

    If you want something that'll truly protect your sofa from the wrath of your pets, Pottery Barn's pet furniture throw is a no-brainer. Available in three sizes, this lucky find can also be customized in a variety of fabrics, including tweed, bouclé, and chenille, among others. Of course, they're all performance-grade.

    Material: Basketweave, Linen, Boucle, Velvet, and more | Colors: 95 | Care: Depends on the fabric material you chose.

    How to Measure and Buy a Sofa Cover.

    The size of your sofa cover will depend not only on the size of the sofa or couch you want to protect, but also on the properties of the fabric itself. Leigh indicates that with a stretchy fabric, you may want a cover with measurements slightly smaller than the dimensions of your sofa for a tighter, more fitted look. For sofa covers with corner ties that allow you to tighten or tie bows, the fabric may have a bit less give, so you'll want to allow for a little extra room in the cover size.

    Some styles lend themselves to being covered more effectively than others. Leigh states that sofas with thinner or rolled arms tend to look nicer with a slipcover than those without. You can also choose between having a skirt on your sofa cover or showing off the legs of your furniture, depending on your aesthetic preference. “I like when they go right to the floor because a skirt cover is a much more traditional, covered look,” Leigh says. “If you have a little bit more of a modern style, having a slipcover that stops at the legs can be a fresher, kind of more updated take.”.

    What Fabrics Are Best for a Sofa Cover?

    Natural fabrics, such as chenille or linen, are typically a great choice when selecting a sofa cover fabric. For family rooms or homes with pets, indoor/outdoor fabrics like Crypton that have been treated to repel dirt and debris are safer bets for those wanting something stain-resistant. The stretchiness of the fabric also plays a role in selecting a sofa cover. "If you wanted something a little bit more durable, canvas or cotton would be a really great material on there," Leigh says.

    Do You Need to Prewash Your Sofa Cover?

    It's always a good idea to pay attention to the care instructions for whatever cover you buy, as fabric care really depends on the individual material. For example, a heavier cotton material can likely withstand more washing. “I would say only wash when you really need to, just like with a really nice sweater,” Leigh indicates. “Don't wash it every time you wear it because washing breaks down fibers. So, it could reduce the longevity of your sofa cover. Most are designed to be removed and washed. So if and when you feel like 'oh, you know what, it's looking a little bit dingy, it's time,' that's the time to do it.” Additionally, it's essential to consider the size of your cover, as larger ones may necessitate the use of a commercial washing machine.

    Industry observers note that additionally, the cover may wrinkle over time, especially with linen, which softens with each wash. “Linen does get a little bit wrinkly, but I think that's kind of the charm of a slipcovered sofa, having that kind of rumpled, you know, 'someone just took a nap here' look,” Leigh indicates.

    According to recent reports, “An oatmeal linen slipcover is that very quintessential, relaxed coastal style that you see a lot of slipcovers used in, and I think it's a classic choice that you'll never go wrong with,” Leigh states. Don't run away from patterns either, though—Leigh is seeing a rise in patterned upholstery in the design industry, and it's a chance to push the envelope and have fun with your design choices. “A cover can be a great way to, you know, try out a pattern without necessarily committing to it forever, because if in five years you say, ‘okay, this pattern was fun, but I'm ready for something different,’ you can just change the slipcover as opposed to having to get an all-latest sofa,” Leigh says.

    Sources indicate that at House Beautiful, we are experts in reviewing and buying anything for the home, from mattresses for back pain to reclining sofas. For this story in particular, we asked our staff members to share their favorite sofa cover (if they own one) and spent hours combing the internet, reading hundreds of reviews about the best ones currently available on the market. While we haven't personally tested every product on this list, we've thoroughly outlined the pros and cons of each sofa cover to provide you with all the necessary details before you make a purchase.

    For further insight into how to best place sofa covers in your home, we consulted interior designer Tiffany Leigh. Leigh runs her eponymous firm in Ontario, Canada, where her team helps clients bring their dream homes and cottages to life. Since 2019, they have designed approachable and livable interiors that feel welcoming and elevated, focusing on quality craftsmanship, emotional connection, and natural elements.

    #8065. Media Buying Briefing: Buyers grapple with incoming Amazon reporting changes

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (961 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    Media Buying Briefing: Buyers grapple with incoming Amazon reporting changes

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (961 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that join us Dec.
    • This Media Buying Briefing covers the latest in agency news and media buying for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Monday at 10 a.m.
    • Changes in the way that key media platforms measure impressions mean that performance and pricing benchmarks may be thrown into disarray come the newly introduced year.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    This Media Buying Briefing covers the latest in agency news and media buying for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Monday at 10 a.m. ET. More from the series →.

    Changes in the way that key media platforms measure impressions mean that performance and pricing benchmarks may be thrown into disarray come the newly introduced year.

    According to recent reports, amazon has estimated brands will see 63% fewer impressions for display ads appearing across its retail properties, including its homepage, product pages and search results, according to a notice distributed among advertisers seen by Digiday. It’s due to the platform’s decision to shift from counting impressions the moment they begin downloading to a user’s device, to when they actually render on the user’s screen, from Jan. 1. Google declared a similar transition at the beginning of September, effective Feb. 17; spokespeople from both tech companies declined to comment.

    In turn, six buyers who spoke to Digiday said they’re working to amend reporting methodologies and soothe client nerves.

    Buyers fear that a reduction in reported impressions could mean that supply is constrained, driving up CPMs. “If there’s going to be fewer impressions, your CPMs will be higher,” explained Hannah Schatz, vp of programmatic operations at Coegi.

    At the same time, the stricter impression reporting methodology means that lower-impact display placements further down Store pages will become even less desirable for advertisers — while top-of-page slots that stand a greater chance of influencing shoppers will see an increase in demand.

    “There’s going to be probably more competition on the platform,” stated Nola Ladd, awareness media supervisor at media agency Collective Measures.

    Amazon has not issued guidance regarding the expected impact on pricing or costs, or whether it might upgrade its billing methodology around the latest impression reporting, according to Stagwell Media Platform’s global product managing director, Dru Sil.

    “The implications are up to us to discover,” he remarked.

    Recent findings suggest that while the drop in impressions might unnerve some clients, it’s unlikely to provoke advertisers to reduce spending. Sil suggested that most advertisers will maintain spending levels, in order to establish latest performance benchmarks in January and February.

    Recent findings suggest that “I don’t expect clients to like dramatically scale up budgets to try to get ahead of the curve. You’re likely going to continue to run what you’ve been running because you have an expected outcome that you’re trying to obtain from Amazon, regardless of the specific ad format,” said Sil.

    He added: “You need to build that baseline anyway, right? And the only way to build that baseline is to be running ads.”.

    Benchmarking may be the real problem buyers face when they shake off the latest year’s hangover.

    Recent findings suggest that automated reporting processes, or media mix models that use impressions as a key input, might need to be recalibrated to account for the expected drop in reported impressions. “If you have a lot of automated processes, optimizations, reconciliations, built around these data sets already, you’re going to have to do a little bit of work,” said Paul DeJarnatt, vp and head of investment at Novus.

    For most buyers, Amazon’s and Google’s tinkering with impression reporting merely underlines the importance of focusing on outcomes, rather than media KPIs, to understand campaign performance.

    “The bottom line is, we don’t expect this to change campaign results. The shift will make reporting metrics look different, but it shouldn’t move ROAS or CPA, which are the outcomes our clients care about,” remarked Jared Smith, senior director of strategy and innovation, January Digital.

    Recent findings suggest that “Impressions, CPMs, they shouldn’t be north star metrics,” noted Ernie DeColte, svp of media at indie agency Level. “They’re tool metrics we use to optimize towards business impact. This might be a wake-up call to a few advertisers. Maybe it’s time to think about buying differently.”.

    Still, communicating this change to clients who might be alarmed when they see impression counts fall off a cliff (or CPMs spike) is something media buyers across the industry are attempting to get ahead of.

    “The client, even though that metric is misleading, is used to seeing a big number,” mentioned Ladd.

    It has been revealed that “They’re used to seeing really low CPMs. They’re used to seeing really great impression volume, and that change and that difference is going to require agencies and media experts to really think about the way that they present success to the client,” she added.

    Just because it’s got a donut graph doesn’t mean a report is saying very much. According to an Experian survey of 400 marketers, the profusion of dashboards and data isn’t helping marketers back up their decisions.

    “In the past, a company like Unilever, buying big media in Brazil from TV Globo, had a significant competitive advantage. Now you are buying from Meta or from Google or from Amazon or from Walmart or from TikTok, and that model doesn’t favor a scale of purchase. It favors the quality of engagement you generate on the platform.”.

    —Unilever CEO Fernando Fernandez, speaking during its Capital Markets Day last week, on why better creative could be the secret to making its marketing operation work harder.

    Industry observers note that local sports rights have gotten more complex and confusing as the regional sports network business changed. The leagues are now looking to simplify that offering.

    As AI automates advertising workflows, the contest is shifting to who can make the decisions that deliver results.

    IAB Tech Lab’s Rowena Lam joined the Digiday Podcast to break down how Trusted Server works and address questions about the user privacy implications of ad tech’s server-side shift.
